lessons.title: Números incríveis
lessons.summary: O zero, o π, os números primos e o infinito.

cards.title: A invenção do zero

events.l: Fibonacci leva os algarismos à Europa

cards.text: O zero como número, e não apenas como um espaço vazio, foi desenvolvido na Índia; Brahmagupta escreveu regras para ele por volta de 628 d.C. Ele chegou à Europa por meio de estudiosos árabes, junto com os algarismos indo-arábicos.

deep.x: Zero plays two different jobs, and they were invented at different times. The first is a **placeholder**: an empty slot that tells you 205 is not 25. Babylonian scribes used a mark for this by about 300 BCE, and the Maya invented their own zero independently. The second job is zero as a number in its own right, something you can add, subtract and multiply. That idea came from India.

In 628 CE the astronomer Brahmagupta, working in Rajasthan, wrote down rules for calculating with zero. Most of them are exactly what we use today. One was not: he said zero divided by zero is zero, a question mathematicians now leave undefined.
The long road to Europe

The Indian digits, zero included, travelled west through the Islamic world. Around 825 CE al-Khwarizmi wrote a book in Baghdad on calculating with them. In 1202 Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, promoted them in Europe in his *Liber Abaci*.
The word itself made the same journey: Sanskrit *śūnya* (empty) became Arabic *ṣifr*, then Latin *zephirum*, then Italian *zero*. The same Arabic root gave English "cipher".
In 1299 the bankers' guild of Florence banned the new numerals in its account books, partly because a 0 could easily be changed into a 6 or a 9.
Zero turned "nothing" into a number you can calculate with, and that made modern arithmetic possible.

cards.title: Valor posicional
cards.text: Em 352, o 3 significa três centenas por causa da sua posição. Os números romanos não tinham valor posicional, o que tornava as contas um sofrimento: tente fazer CCCLII × XLVII.

deep.x: In a place-value system, the same digit is worth different amounts depending on where it sits. In 352 the 3 is worth 300, the 5 is worth 50 and the 2 is worth 2. Each step to the left is worth ten times more, because we count in base 10, probably because we have ten fingers.
Why Roman numerals were hard work

Roman numerals add up symbols: CCCLII is 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 1 + 1. There is no zero and no columns, so you cannot line numbers up and multiply digit by digit. Romans and medieval merchants did real calculations on an abacus or counting board and only wrote the result in numerals.
In place-value notation that sum takes a few lines on paper. With Roman numerals you would end up with XVIDXLIV, and no simple written method to get there.
Our minutes, seconds and 360° circle are leftovers of the Babylonians' base-60 place-value system, over 4,000 years old.
Place value lets ten symbols write any number, and lets you calculate column by column.

cards.title: Pi
cards.text: π é a razão entre a circunferência de qualquer círculo e o seu diâmetro: cerca de 3,14159. Seus dígitos nunca terminam nem se repetem. Arquimedes o estimou por volta de 250 a.C.

deep.x: Take any circle, from a 2-euro coin to the Equator. Divide the distance around it by the distance across it and you always get the same number, about 3.14159. That constant is **π** (pi). It is the same for every circle because all circles are scaled copies of each other.
circumference = π × diameter

x: one turn moves it π × 70 cm

deep.x: Squeezing pi between polygons

Around 250 BCE Archimedes drew regular polygons inside and outside a circle. Their perimeters are easy to calculate, and the circle's lies in between. Going up to 96 sides, he showed that π is between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7, that is between about 3.1408 and 3.1429.
Endless digits

In 1761 Johann Lambert proved that π is irrational: no fraction equals it exactly, so its decimals never end or settle into a repeating pattern. In 1882 Ferdinand von Lindemann went further, which settled an ancient puzzle: you can't "square the circle" with ruler and compass.
NASA's navigation engineers use only about 15 decimal places of π. Around 40 would give the size of the observable universe to within the width of an atom.
π is the same for every circle, and no fraction or finite decimal can ever pin it down exactly.

cards.title: Números primos
cards.text: Um número primo tem exatamente dois divisores: 1 e ele mesmo. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13… Euclides provou, por volta de 300 a.C., que eles são infinitos.

deep.x: A prime is a whole number greater than 1 that only 1 and itself divide exactly. Every other whole number above 1 is a product of primes, and in only one way: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5, whatever order you find the factors in. That is why primes are called the atoms of arithmetic.

deep.w: 1 is a prime number
deep.r: 1 is not prime. If it were, 6 = 2 × 3 = 1 × 2 × 3 = 1 × 1 × 2 × 3, and factorisation would no longer be unique.

deep.x: Finding them: the sieve
Eratosthenes, a Greek scholar in Alexandria around 240 BCE, gave a simple method. List the numbers, then cross out every multiple of 2, then of 3, then of 5 and so on. What survives is prime.
You only need to check divisors up to the square root of a number. To test 97, try 2, 3, 5 and 7; since 11 × 11 = 121 is already too big, 97 is prime.
They thin out as numbers grow, but they never stop. Euclid proved that around 300 BCE.
The largest known prime, found in 2024, is 2 to the power 136,279,841, minus 1. It has over 41 million digits.
Every whole number is built from primes in exactly one way, and the supply of primes never runs out.

cards.title: Os primos protegem seus dados
cards.text: Multiplicar dois primos enormes é fácil; fazer o caminho inverso para descobri-los é extremamente difícil. A criptografia RSA, usada na internet, depende disso.

deep.x: Some calculations are easy one way and brutally hard in reverse. Multiplying two primes is quick even when they have hundreds of digits. Taking the answer and finding the two primes that made it, called **factorising**, has no known fast method on ordinary computers.
With a four-digit number you can grind through the options. With a 600-digit number, all the computers on Earth would need far longer than the age of the universe using the best known methods.
How RSA uses this
RSA was published in 1977 by Rivest, Shamir and Adleman (the British codebreaker Clifford Cocks had found it secretly in 1973). It uses two keys.

steps: Pick two huge primes p, q

x: The **public key** contains n, the product. Anyone can use it to encrypt a message to you.
The **private key** depends on knowing p and q. Without them, decrypting needs n factorised.
Typical keys today are 2,048 bits, a number about 617 digits long.

deep.x: Much of today's web traffic uses newer elliptic-curve methods for the key exchange, but RSA is still common for the digital signatures and certificates that prove a website is genuine.
A big enough quantum computer could factorise quickly using Shor's algorithm. That is why in 2024 the US standards body NIST published new "post-quantum" encryption standards.
Your online security rests on a lopsided puzzle: multiplying primes is easy, unmultiplying them is not.

cards.title: A sequência de Fibonacci
cards.text: Cada número é a soma dos dois anteriores: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21… Ela aparece nas espirais das sementes de girassol e nas pinhas.

deep.x: Leonardo of Pisa, called Fibonacci, posed a puzzle in 1202 about breeding rabbits. Its answer is the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… Indian scholars had described the same numbers centuries earlier, when counting rhythms in Sanskrit poetry.
next number = previous + the one before
The golden ratio hiding inside
Divide each Fibonacci number by the one before it and the answers settle down towards 1.618…, the **golden ratio**.
Why plants show it

A growing sunflower adds each new seed at a turn of about 137.5°, the "golden angle", from the last. This angle packs seeds evenly with no wasted gaps. The spirals that appear then come in Fibonacci counts, often 34 one way and 55 the other, or 55 and 89 in big heads.

deep.w: The Parthenon and the Mona Lisa were designed on the golden ratio
deep.r: There's no good evidence for either. You can find 1.618 almost anywhere if you choose which points to measure.

deep.x: Add the last two numbers to get the next: a simple rule that sunflowers and pine cones follow because it packs best.

cards.title: Números quadrados
cards.text: Os números quadrados vêm de multiplicar um número por ele mesmo: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Somando números ímpares, você chega a eles: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.

deep.x: A square number is what you get when you multiply a whole number by itself: 4 × 4 = 16, written 4². The name is literal: 16 dots fit into a 4-by-4 square.
Why odd numbers build squares

Start with one dot. To grow it into a 2-by-2 square you add an L-shape of 3 dots. To reach 3-by-3, add an L of 5. Each new L is two dots longer than the last, so the odd numbers stack up into squares.
That formula says the gap between neighbouring squares is always the next odd number: 6² − 5² = 36 − 25 = 11.
Spotting a square
A square number can only end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9 (5 and 0 come from numbers ending in 5 and 0). So 2,437 and 5,618 cannot be squares, without any calculation.
In 1770 Joseph-Louis Lagrange proved that every whole number is the sum of at most four squares: 7 = 4 + 1 + 1 + 1.
Square numbers are literally squares, built layer by layer from the odd numbers.

cards.title: Infinito
cards.text: Alguns infinitos são maiores que outros. Georg Cantor mostrou que existem mais números reais (todos os decimais) do que números inteiros, embora ambos sejam infinitos.

deep.x: Infinity isn't a very big number; it is the size of a collection that never ends. The surprise, discovered by Georg Cantor in the 1870s and 1890s, is that endless collections come in different sizes.
Same size: pairing up
Two collections are the same size if you can pair them off one to one with nothing left over. That works even for endless lists, with strange results.

So there are exactly as many even numbers as whole numbers, even though the evens are "half" of them. David Hilbert's famous imaginary hotel, with infinitely many rooms, all full, can still fit a new guest: everyone moves from room n to room n + 1.
Cantor's diagonal argument

Suppose someone claims a complete numbered list of all decimals between 0 and 1. Build a new decimal: make its first digit differ from the first number's first digit, its second digit differ from the second number's second digit, and so on. Your new decimal differs from every number on the list somewhere, so the list was not complete. No list can ever be.

steps: Change digit n of number n

deep.x: Is there a size of infinity between the whole numbers and the decimals? Gödel (1940) and Paul Cohen (1963) showed the usual rules of mathematics can neither prove nor disprove it.

deep.w: Infinity is just one thing
deep.r: There are endless sizes of infinity, each bigger than the last.

deep.x: Some infinities can be counted off one by one; the decimals cannot, so they form a bigger infinity.

cards.title: Números negativos
cards.text: Os números negativos já eram usados na China há mais de 2,000 anos para registrar dívidas. Os europeus resistiram a eles até o século XVII. Hoje eles estão em todo termômetro e extrato bancário.

deep.x: Chinese mathematicians used negative numbers over 2,000 years ago. *The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art*, compiled during the Han dynasty, used red counting rods for positive amounts and black ones for negative, and gave rules for combining them. In 628 CE Brahmagupta in India described them as debts against fortunes.
Europe's long suspicion

Many European mathematicians found negatives absurd: how can you have less than nothing? In 1544 Michael Stifel called them "absurd numbers", and René Descartes in 1637 called negative solutions "false roots". Bookkeepers and the number line, which treats negatives as positions below zero, gradually won the argument.
Using them today
A negative number is just a position or a change in the other direction: below zero, below sea level, money owed.
The shore of the Dead Sea lies about 430 m below sea level, the lowest dry land on Earth: a height of roughly −430 m.
A negative number is a direction as much as an amount: below, behind, or owed.

cards.title: Um truque com o 9
cards.text: Multiplique 9 por qualquer número de 1 a 10 e os algarismos do resultado somam 9: 9 × 7 = 63, e 6 + 3 = 9.

deep.x: The digits of every multiple of 9 add up to a multiple of 9. For the first ten, the total is exactly 9.
Why it works

9 is one less than 10. Multiplying by 9 is the same as multiplying by 10 and taking one lot away: 9 × 7 = 70 − 7. Moving up one step adds 1 to the tens digit and removes 1 from the units, so the digit sum stays the same.
It keeps going
For bigger multiples, keep adding the digits until you get one digit, and you'll land on 9.
The reverse is also true, which gives a quick test: a number divides exactly by 9 if its digits add up to a multiple of 9. For 4,374: 4 + 3 + 7 + 4 = 18, so it divides by 9 (it's 9 × 486).
Hold up ten fingers and fold down the 7th: you see 6 fingers to the left and 3 to the right, which reads 63 = 9 × 7.
Because 9 is 10 minus 1, its multiples always have digits that add up to 9.

cards.title: Noções básicas de probabilidade
cards.text: A probabilidade é um número de 0 (impossível) a 1 (certo). A chance de uma moeda honesta dar cara é 1/2; a de tirar um seis no dado é 1/6.

deep.x: A probability measures how likely something is, on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). When every outcome is equally likely, it's a simple fraction.
P = favourable outcomes ÷ all possible outcomes
Three ways to write the same chance
Bookmakers use **odds** instead, which compare the chances against with the chances for. A probability of 1/6 is odds of 5 to 1 against: five ways to lose for one way to win.
The complement
The chance that something does **not** happen is 1 minus the chance that it does. That is often the easiest route.

v.unit: ways to score each total, 2 dice

deep.x: That's why 7 matters so much in dice games like craps: it's the most common total.

deep.w: A 30% chance of rain means it will rain for 30% of the day
deep.r: It means that on days with forecasts like this, it rains at your location about 3 times in 10.

deep.x: Probability counts the ways something can happen out of all the equally likely ways things could go.

cards.title: "E" e "ou"
cards.text: Para eventos independentes, multiplique no caso do "e": duas caras = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Some no caso do "ou", se os dois não puderem acontecer juntos: um 1 ou um 2 num dado = 2/6.

deep.x: Two events are **independent** when one tells you nothing about the other: two coin flips, or a die and a coin. Then the rules are simple.
When "or" overlaps
Adding only works if the two things can't happen together. If they can, you'd count the overlap twice, so take it off once.
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)

x: Draw a heart or a king from 52 cards

deep.x: "At least one": use the complement
"At least one six in four rolls" has many ways to happen. Its opposite, "no sixes at all", has only one, so work that out and subtract from 1.

In the 1650s the gambler Chevalier de Méré asked why betting on at least one double six in 24 rolls of two dice lost money. Blaise Pascal worked it out: the chance is only about 49%, and modern probability theory was born from the letters that followed.

deep.w: Two independent 50% chances make a 100% chance
deep.r: Adding only works for outcomes that can't both happen. For "at least one heads in two flips", it's 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.

deep.x: "And" means multiply; "or" means add, minus any overlap; "at least one" means 1 minus "none".

cards.title: A falácia do apostador

items.w: "Deu vermelho 5 vezes, agora vai dar preto"
items.r: Cada giro é independente: mesmas chances

cards.text: Depois de cinco caras seguidas, a coroa não "está devendo". Moedas não têm memória; o próximo lançamento continua 50/50.

deep.x: The **gambler's fallacy** is the belief that after a run of one result, the other is "due". A coin, a die or a roulette wheel has no memory, so each go starts fresh.

x: Chance of 6 heads in a row, before any flips
Chance of a 6th head, after 5 heads

deep.x: Both numbers are right. A run of six is rare looking forward, but once five have already happened, only the next flip is uncertain.

items.w: This number hasn't won for ages

deep.x: The Monte Carlo night

In August 1913, at the Monte Carlo casino, the roulette ball reportedly landed on black 26 times in a row. Gamblers bet heavily on red, sure the streak must end, and lost millions of francs. On a European wheel the chance of 26 blacks in a row is roughly 1 in 137 million, but with thousands of wheels spinning over decades, some extraordinary streaks are bound to appear.
Why we fall for it
Our brains expect short sequences to look like the long-run average, so we think randomness should "balance out" quickly. Genuine randomness is lumpier than we think.

items: The law of large numbers dilutes

deep.x: People asked to write down a "random" sequence of 100 coin flips almost never include a run of six or more. In real flips, such a run turns up most of the time.
Coins, dice and lottery balls have no memory: the past doesn't change the next go.

cards.title: O paradoxo do aniversário

viz.unit: % de chance de aniversário em comum

cards.text: Num grupo de apenas 23 pessoas, há mais de 50% de chance de duas fazerem aniversário no mesmo dia. Com 70 pessoas, passa de 99,9%.

deep.x: It feels as if you'd need about 183 people (half of 365) for a good chance of a shared birthday. You need only 23. The trick is that the question is about **any** pair, not about you.

x: = 253 different pairs, each a chance of a match

deep.x: Working it out
Calculate the chance that everyone has a different birthday, then subtract from 1. The second person must avoid one date, the third must avoid two, and so on.
Your birthday is different
For someone to share **your** birthday, you need far more people: about 253 for a 50% chance, because now only the pairs including you count.
A football match has 22 players plus the referee: 23 people. In roughly half of all matches, two people on the pitch share a birthday.
The same maths matters in computer security: "birthday attacks" find two inputs that give the same digital fingerprint much faster than you'd expect.
Shared birthdays come quickly because the number of pairs grows much faster than the number of people.

cards.title: Valor esperado
cards.text: Multiplique cada resultado pela sua probabilidade e some tudo. Um bilhete de loteria que custa €2 com prêmio esperado de €1 perde, em média, €1.

deep.x: **Expected value** is the average result per go if you repeated a bet many, many times. You rarely get exactly that amount on any one go, but it tells you which way things drift.
expected value = Σ (outcome × its probability)

x: = 3.5, a value you can never actually roll

deep.x: Roulette
A European wheel has 37 pockets: 18 red, 18 black and one green zero. A €1 bet on red wins €1 or loses €1.
That 2.7% is the casino's edge. A bet on a single number pays 35 to 1, and gives exactly the same −2.7%. The casino doesn't need to know who will win; over millions of bets, it will collect.
When a negative EV is still sensible

Home insurance has a negative expected value too: insurers pay out less than they collect. People buy it because a small certain loss is better than a rare ruinous one. Expected value measures the average, not the risk.
Expected value is the long-run average per go: a quick way to see which bets drain your money.

cards.title: Loterias
cards.text: A chance de ganhar o prêmio máximo do EuroMilhões é de cerca de 1 em 140 milhões. É muito mais provável você ser atingido por um raio ao longo da vida.

deep.x: EuroMillions asks you to pick 5 numbers from 50 and 2 "Lucky Stars" from 12. The order doesn't matter, so you count combinations.
So one ticket has a 1 in about 140 million chance of the jackpot. Portugal has played since 2004, through Jogos Santa Casa.
How long you'd wait
There are two EuroMillions draws a week. Buy one ticket for every draw and you'd play 104 times a year.
Where the money goes

About half of ticket sales go to the prize fund; the rest funds good causes, taxes and running costs. In Portugal, prizes above €5,000 also pay 20% stamp duty. Expected value per €1 ticket is therefore well under €1, typically about 50 cents.

deep.w: Picking numbers that haven't come up for a while helps
deep.r: Every draw is independent. Choosing less popular numbers can't raise your chance of winning, only the size of your share if you do.

deep.x: A lottery ticket buys a dream, not an investment: on average, half the stake is gone.

cards.title: O problema de Monty Hall
cards.text: Você escolhe uma de três portas; o apresentador, que sabe onde está o prêmio, abre uma porta perdedora e oferece a troca. Trocar ganha em 2/3 das vezes. Até matemáticos erraram no início.

deep.x: On a game show there are three doors: a car behind one, goats behind two. You pick a door. The host, who knows where the car is, always opens one of the others to show a goat, then offers you the chance to switch. Should you?
Why switching wins 2/3 of the time

When you first pick, you have a 1/3 chance of the car. That doesn't change, because the host can always open a goat door whatever you chose. So the remaining 2/3 must now sit on the one other closed door.
Make it 100 doors

Imagine 100 doors. You pick one, and the host opens 98 goat doors, leaving yours and one other. Would you still believe your first random choice is as good as the one door he carefully avoided? Your door has a 1/100 chance; the other has 99/100.

When Marilyn vos Savant gave the correct answer in *Parade* magazine in 1990, she received thousands of letters, many from people with PhDs, telling her she was wrong. Even the great Paul Erdős was only convinced after seeing a computer simulation.
The key detail is that the host **knows** and never reveals the car. If he opened a door at random and happened to show a goat, switching would only be 50/50.
The host's choice carries information: switching wins whenever your first guess was wrong, which is two times in three.

cards.title: Taxas de base
cards.text: Um teste tem 99% de precisão para uma doença que afeta 1 em cada 1,000 pessoas. Se o seu resultado der positivo, a chance de você ter a doença é de só cerca de 9%, porque os falsos positivos entre pessoas saudáveis superam os casos reais.

deep.x: The **base rate** is how common something is to begin with. Ignore it and even an accurate test can mislead you badly. The clearest way to see this is with counts of people rather than percentages.
Why the answer is so low
The test is wrong only 1% of the time, but it's used on a huge number of healthy people. One per cent of a huge number beats 99% of a small one.
Testing again helps
Doctors usually confirm with a second, independent test. After a positive result, your chance is about 9%; that becomes the new starting point. A second positive pushes it to about 91%.
The formal rule for updating probabilities with new evidence is **Bayes' theorem**, named after the English minister Thomas Bayes and published in 1763, after his death.

deep.w: A 99% accurate test means a positive result is 99% certain
deep.r: It depends on how rare the condition is. For rare conditions, most positives can be false.

deep.x: The same error, called the "prosecutor's fallacy", has appeared in courts: a 1-in-a-million match can still point to the wrong person if millions could have been tested.
Before trusting a positive result, ask how common the thing was in the first place.

cards.title: Lei dos grandes números
cards.text: Em poucos lançamentos, os resultados podem ficar desequilibrados. Em milhares, a proporção de caras fica muito perto de 50%. Os cassinos contam com isso.

deep.x: The **law of large numbers** says that as you repeat a random experiment more and more times, the share of each outcome settles towards its true probability. Jacob Bernoulli proved a version of it, published in 1713.
The typical wobble shrinks with the square root of the number of tries: 100 times more flips gives about 10 times less wobble.
Proportions settle, gaps don't vanish
The gap between heads and tails, counted in flips, doesn't shrink. It usually grows. It just becomes tiny compared with the total.
During the Second World War, the mathematician John Kerrich, interned in Denmark, flipped a coin 10,000 times. He got 5,067 heads: 50.67%.
Why casinos always win

A casino with a 2.7% edge can lose to individual players every night. Across millions of bets, its takings settle very close to 2.7% of everything staked. For a single gambler playing a few rounds, luck dominates; for the house, maths does.

deep.w: Luck "evens out" by correcting past results
deep.r: Past results are never corrected. They're simply swamped by many new ones.

deep.x: Repeat something often enough and the averages become predictable, even though each single go stays random.

cards.title: O risco em perspectiva
cards.text: "Dobra o risco" parece assustador, mas passar de 1 em 10,000 para 2 em 10,000 é uma mudança absoluta minúscula. Sempre pergunte: em quantos?

deep.x: A **relative risk** says how much a risk changes ("doubles", "up 50%"). An **absolute risk** says how many people are actually affected. Headlines prefer relative risks because they sound dramatic; decisions need absolute ones.

x: Risk goes from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000
absolute: +1 person in 10,000, or 0.01 percentage points

deep.x: A real scare

In 1995 the UK warned that certain contraceptive pills doubled the risk of a type of blood clot. The absolute risk rose from about 1 in 7,000 women to about 2 in 7,000. Many women stopped taking the pill, and in the following year there were an estimated thousands of extra unwanted pregnancies and abortions. Pregnancy itself carries a higher clot risk than either pill.
Questions to ask

items: What's the risk of the alternative?

deep.x: Natural frequencies help

People understand "2 in 1,000" much better than "0.2%" or "a 100% increase". Doctors often use the **number needed to treat**: how many people must take a treatment for one of them to benefit. If a drug cuts a risk from 2% to 1%, you need to treat 100 people to prevent one case.
Always turn a scary percentage into "how many out of how many" before deciding whether to worry.
