cards.title: O teorema de Pitágoras
cards.text: Num triângulo retângulo, o quadrado do lado mais longo é igual à soma dos quadrados dos outros dois. Os construtores usavam triângulos 3-4-5 para fazer cantos em esquadro.

deep.x: Label the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle a and b, and the longest side, opposite the right angle, c. That longest side is the **hypotenuse**. Pythagoras' theorem links them.
a² + b² = c²
Using it
Whenever you need a straight-line distance and know two distances at right angles, Pythagoras gives the shortcut.

x: Walk 300 m east, then 400 m north
A 5 m ladder, foot 1.5 m from the wall

deep.x: The same idea measures screens. A "55-inch" TV is 55 inches (about 140 cm) along its diagonal, not its width.
Older than Pythagoras

Pythagoras lived in the 500s BCE, but the rule is much older. A Babylonian clay tablet called Plimpton 322, from about 1800 BCE, lists sets of numbers that fit it. It was also known in ancient India and China. No proof by Pythagoras himself survives.
There are hundreds of different proofs. One was found in 1876 by James Garfield, five years before he became US president.
Those are **Pythagorean triples**: whole numbers that fit the rule exactly. Multiply any of them, and you get another: 6, 8, 10.
In any right-angled triangle, the two short sides' squares add up to the long side's square, so distances can be found without measuring them.

cards.title: O triângulo 3-4-5
cards.text: Meça 3 m ao longo de uma parede e 4 m ao longo da outra. Se a diagonal tiver exatamente 5 m, o canto é um ângulo reto perfeito.

deep.x: Since 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5², a triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 must have a right angle between the 3 and the 4. That makes it a perfect tool for checking corners with only a tape measure. The rule works backwards too: if the squares fit, the angle is 90°.
Scaling it to the job
Any multiple works, so builders pick the size that fits.
Bigger triangles are more accurate, because a 1 cm measuring slip is a smaller share of a longer side.
How sensitive is it?
So each 5 cm of error on the diagonal is about 1.2° off square. Over a 4 m wall, that's about 8 cm out at the far end, enough to show up as a wedge-shaped gap along tiles or skirting boards.
The diagonals check
For a whole rectangle, such as a slab or a room, builders also compare the two diagonals. If they're equal, every corner is square.

It's often said that ancient Egyptian "rope-stretchers" laid out right angles with a rope knotted into 12 equal parts (3 + 4 + 5). It's a lovely story, but historians have found little direct evidence for it.
Measure 3, 4 and 5 and you have a right angle: Pythagoras working in reverse.

cards.title: Ângulos de um triângulo
cards.text: Os ângulos de qualquer triângulo somam 180°. Os de uma figura de quatro lados somam 360°.

deep.x: Draw any triangle, tear off its three corners and place them side by side. They always make a straight line: 180°.
Why it's true

Draw a line through the top corner parallel to the base. The two angles that the sides make with this line match the two base angles (they're "alternate angles"). Together with the top angle, they fill a straight line.

steps: Draw a parallel line on top
With the top: a straight line

deep.x: Any polygon
Split a shape into triangles from one corner. A shape with n sides always gives n − 2 triangles.
angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°
Not on a globe

On a curved surface the rule breaks. Start at the North Pole, go down to the Equator, turn 90°, travel a quarter of the way round the Earth, turn 90° again and go back to the pole. Your triangle has three right angles: 270°.
Around 1820, Carl Friedrich Gauss is said to have measured a huge triangle between three German mountain tops to check whether space itself is curved. It came out at 180° within his measuring error.
On a flat surface, a triangle's angles always add up to a straight line, 180°.

cards.title: Área do círculo
cards.text: A área de um círculo é π vezes o raio ao quadrado. Dobrar o raio deixa a área quatro vezes maior: é por isso que uma pizza de 40 cm vale mais do que uma pizza e meia de 30 cm.

deep.x: Cut a circle into many thin slices, like a pizza, and lay them alternately point-up and point-down. They form a shape close to a rectangle: one side is half the circumference, π × r, and the other is the radius, r. Multiply and you get the area.
A = π × r²
Why size grows so fast
The radius is squared, so doubling it multiplies the area by 4. Even a modest increase in diameter adds a lot of pizza.
So one 40 cm pizza is about 1.78 times a 30 cm one, though two 30 cm pizzas (about 1,414 cm²) are still a bit more.
Compare price per area

deep.w: A pizza twice as wide is twice as much food
deep.r: It's four times as much. Area grows with the square of the size.

deep.x: Of all shapes with the same perimeter, the circle encloses the most area. That's one reason pipes, tins and tree trunks are round.
Area grows with the radius squared, so a little extra width means a lot of extra area.

cards.title: Hexágonos na natureza
cards.text: As abelhas constroem células hexagonais porque os hexágonos cobrem uma superfície sem deixar espaços, usando o mínimo de material de parede para a área delimitada.

deep.x: Only three regular shapes tile a flat surface with no gaps: equilateral triangles, squares and hexagons. That's because only their corner angles, 60°, 90° and 120°, divide 360° exactly. Pentagons (108°) leave gaps.
The most area for the least wall
Of the three, the hexagon is the roundest, so it encloses a given area with the shortest perimeter. For a bee, wall means wax, and wax is expensive: bees must eat a lot of honey to make it.

v.unit: perimeter for 1 cm² of area, cm

deep.x: Circles would be even better on their own, but they leave wasted gaps between them. In 1999 the mathematician Thomas Hales proved that hexagons are the best possible way to divide a flat surface into equal areas with the least total wall: the "honeycomb conjecture", suspected since Roman times.
Hexagons elsewhere

x: Basalt columns, like the Giant's Causeway, crack into rough hexagons as lava cools and shrinks
Snowflakes, from the six-sided way water molecules lock together
A giant hexagonal cloud pattern at Saturn's north pole
Bubbles squeezed in a single layer settle into hexagons

deep.x: Biologists still debate how much of the honeycomb's perfect shape comes from the bees and how much from warm wax being pulled into hexagons by surface tension, the way bubbles are.
Hexagons fill space without gaps while using the least wall: maximum storage for minimum wax.

cards.title: Sólidos de Platão
cards.text: Só cinco sólidos têm faces regulares idênticas, com o mesmo número delas se encontrando em cada vértice: tetraedro, cubo, octaedro, dodecaedro e icosaedro. Os dados usam essas formas.

deep.x: A **Platonic solid** has every face the same regular polygon, with the same number of faces meeting at every corner. There are exactly five, and Euclid proved it in the last book of his *Elements*, around 300 BCE.
Why only five?
At least three faces must meet at each corner, and their angles must add to less than 360°, or the corner lies flat.

x: Triangles (60°): 3, 4 or 5 at a corner, giving 180°, 240° or 300°. Six would make 360°: flat.
Hexagons (120°): 3 already make 360°, flat. Nothing bigger fits.

deep.x: That's 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 possibilities, and each one really exists.
Euler's formula
For each of them, and for any solid without holes, corners minus edges plus faces equals 2.
Where you meet them

Role-playing games use all five as dice: d4, d6, d8, d12 and d20. Every face is identical, so each is equally likely to land facing up. Many viruses build their protein shells as icosahedra, and some minerals, such as pyrite, grow as cubes.
Plato linked four of them to the classical elements (fire, earth, air and water) and the dodecahedron to the heavens. That's why they bear his name, though he didn't discover them.
Only five solids can be built from identical regular faces meeting the same way at every corner.

cards.title: Simetria
cards.text: Uma forma tem simetria se um movimento, como uma reflexão ou rotação, a deixa com a mesma aparência. Os flocos de neve têm simetria de ordem seis; o seu rosto é mais ou menos simétrico como num espelho.

deep.x: In maths, **symmetry** means you can do something to a shape and it ends up looking exactly the same. There are a few basic moves.
Counting rotational symmetry
The **order** of rotational symmetry is how many times a shape looks the same during one full turn.

x: Equilateral triangle: order 3; regular hexagon: order 6
Letters S, N and Z: order 2, with no mirror line at all; H has order 2 and two mirror lines

deep.x: Why snowflakes have six arms

Water molecules freeze into a hexagonal crystal. As a snowflake falls, each arm meets almost exactly the same temperature and humidity at the same moment, so all six grow alike. No two flakes are identical, because each takes a different path through the cloud.

steps: Same air at the same time

deep.x: Patterns on walls and pavements

Repeating patterns combine these moves. In 1891 the Russian crystallographer Evgraf Fedorov proved there are exactly 17 distinct types of flat repeating pattern. Portuguese **azulejos** and *calçada portuguesa* pavements, and the tilework of the Alhambra in Granada, show many of them.
Faces aren't perfectly symmetric. A photo made from two copies of your left half looks noticeably different from one made of your right half.
Symmetry is anything you can do to a shape that leaves it looking unchanged.

cards.title: Escala
cards.text: Se você dobrar o tamanho de um objeto, a área fica quatro vezes maior e o volume, oito vezes. É por isso que insetos gigantes não conseguiriam sustentar o próprio corpo.

deep.x: Scale an object up by a factor k, keeping its shape, and different measurements grow at different speeds.
This is the **square-cube law**, set out by Galileo in 1638.
Why giants can't exist

A leg's strength depends on its cross-section, an area. The weight it carries depends on volume. Make an animal twice as big and its legs get 4 times stronger but it's 8 times heavier, so every bit of bone carries twice the load.

x: legs carry 100 times more per bit of leg

deep.x: That's why elephants have thick, pillar-like legs while a spider can have spindly ones. Insects also breathe through tiny tubes that work by slow diffusion, which only reaches so far into a body. Around 300 million years ago, when the air held more oxygen, dragonfly-like insects reached about 70 cm across the wings.
Heat and size
Heat escapes through the skin (area) but is made by the body (volume). Small animals lose heat fast relative to their size: a shrew must eat close to its own body weight in food each day.
Crushed ice cools a drink faster than one big cube of the same weight, because chopping it up adds lots of surface area.
Double the size and the area quadruples, but the volume goes up eight times; that mismatch shapes everything from bones to ice cubes.

cards.title: Projeções cartográficas
cards.text: Não dá para achatar uma esfera sem distorção. O mapa de Mercator mantém os ângulos corretos para a navegação, mas faz a Groenlândia parecer tão grande quanto a África, que é cerca de 14 vezes maior.

deep.x: In 1827 Carl Friedrich Gauss proved that you cannot flatten any part of a sphere without stretching or squashing it. Try flattening an orange peel. Every flat map must give up something: true areas, true angles, true distances or true shapes.
Why sailors loved Mercator

Gerardus Mercator published his map in 1569. A line of constant compass bearing appears on it as a straight line, so a navigator could draw a course with a ruler. To keep angles correct, the map stretches everything more and more towards the poles.
On Mercator they look about the same size, and the poles can't be shown at all: they'd be infinitely far away.
A Portuguese connection

The Portuguese mathematician **Pedro Nunes** (1502–1578), royal cosmographer, showed that a course of constant bearing is not the shortest path but a spiral towards the pole, the **rhumb line**. His work fed directly into the problem Mercator's map solved.
Most online street maps use a version of Mercator, called Web Mercator. At street scale the distortion is tiny, and keeping angles right means streets meet at true corners.
Every flat map of the round Earth lies about something; choose the map whose lie doesn't matter for your purpose.

cards.title: Fractais
cards.text: Os fractais repetem o seu padrão em todas as escalas: litorais, samambaias, brócolis e raios. Dê um zoom e você vê a mesma forma de novo.

deep.x: A **fractal** is a shape that shows similar detail however far you zoom in. A fern frond is made of smaller fronds, each made of smaller fronds still. The word was coined by Benoit Mandelbrot in 1975.
The coastline problem

In 1967 Mandelbrot asked: "How long is the coast of Britain?" The answer depends on your ruler. A 100 km ruler skips every bay; a 1 m ruler follows every rock. The shorter the ruler, the longer the coast, without settling down. Published figures for Portugal's coastline differ widely for the same reason.
The Koch snowflake
Start with a triangle. On the middle third of every side, add a smaller triangle. Repeat forever.
Yet the area never exceeds 8/5 of the starting triangle. An infinitely long edge can wrap a limited area.
Fractals at work

x: Your lungs and blood vessels branch fractally, packing a huge surface into a small space
Phone antennas with fractal shapes pick up several frequency bands
Film-makers generate mountains and coastlines with fractal rules
Romanesco broccoli is a near-perfect natural example, though real fractals stop after a few levels

deep.x: The Mandelbrot set is drawn from one short rule, z → z² + c, yet its edge contains endless detail.
Fractals repeat their pattern at every scale, which is why some lengths depend on how closely you look.

quiz.q: Qual é a hipotenusa de um triângulo com catetos 3 e 4?
Dobre o tamanho de um cubo: o volume aumenta…

lessons.title: Estatística
lessons.summary: Números que informam e que enganam.

cards.title: Média, mediana e moda
cards.text: A média é o valor médio; a mediana é o valor do meio; a moda é o mais frequente. Elas podem ser bem diferentes.

deep.x: Three different ideas all get called "the average". Each answers a different question.

items.b: add up, divide by how many

deep.x: Three very different answers from the same seven numbers. The single large value, 40, pulls the mean up, while the median ignores how big it is.
When to use which

x: **Mean**: when values are fairly symmetric, like temperatures or exam marks. It uses every value.
**Median**: when a few extreme values distort things, like house prices, salaries or waiting times.
**Mode**: for categories you can't average, like the most popular shoe size or favourite colour.

deep.x: For an even number of values, the median is halfway between the middle two: for 4, 6, 9, 12 it's 7.5.
Almost everyone has more legs than the average person. A few people have fewer than two, so the mean is just under 2, while the median and mode are both 2.

deep.w: "Average" always means the mean
deep.r: In everyday speech it can mean any of the three. Ask which.

deep.x: The mean, median and mode answer different questions; always check which "average" you're being given.

cards.title: Quando a média engana
cards.text: Se um bilionário entra num café, a riqueza média dos clientes dispara, mas a mediana quase não se mexe. Os salários são mais bem descritos pela mediana.

deep.x: The mean is sensitive to extreme values because it adds them in at full size. One huge number can drag it far from what's typical.

x: a billionaire walks in with €1 billion

deep.x: Skewed data is everywhere

A **skewed** distribution has a long tail on one side. Incomes, house prices, company sizes, city populations and social-media followers all have a small number of very large values. In each case the mean sits well above what most people experience.

items: Incomes: a few earn hugely more

deep.x: That's why statistics offices, including Portugal's INE and Eurostat, usually report **median** household income. In most countries more than half of workers earn less than the mean wage.
Use both
When the mean is well above the median, the data has a long upper tail. The gap itself tells you something about inequality.

deep.w: The mean salary is what a typical worker earns
deep.r: With skewed pay, most workers earn less than the mean.

deep.x: When a few values are huge, the median describes the typical case far better than the mean.

cards.title: Dispersão
cards.text: Duas turmas podem ter a mesma média, mas dispersões muito diferentes. O desvio padrão mede o quanto os valores costumam se afastar da média.

deep.x: Averages hide a lot. Two sets of numbers can have the same mean and look completely different.
Measuring spread

x: **Range**: largest minus smallest. Simple, but one odd value changes it a lot.
**Interquartile range**: the spread of the middle half, ignoring the extremes.
**Standard deviation**: roughly, the typical distance of values from the mean.

deep.x: Calculating a standard deviation
s.d. = √(average of the squared distances from the mean)
Squaring stops negative and positive distances from cancelling out; the square root brings the answer back to the original units.
Why spread matters

For investments, spread means risk: two funds with the same average return can differ wildly year to year. For a bus, a reliable 10-minute wait beats one that's 10 minutes on average but sometimes 30.
Always ask about spread as well as average: same mean, very different stories.

cards.title: A curva em sino
cards.text: Muitas medidas, como a altura, se agrupam em torno de uma média, formando um sino. Cerca de 68% dos valores ficam a até um desvio padrão e 95% a até dois.

deep.x: Measure the heights of thousands of adults of the same sex and plot how many fall at each height. You get a symmetrical hump, high in the middle and tailing off on both sides. This shape is the **normal distribution**, or bell curve, studied by Abraham de Moivre in 1733 and later Carl Friedrich Gauss.
The 68–95–99.7 rule
Why it appears so often

When something is the sum of many small, independent influences (lots of genes, nutrition, chance), the result tends towards a bell shape. This is the **central limit theorem**. You can watch it in a Galton board, where balls bounce left or right off many pins and pile up in a bell.
When it doesn't apply

Not everything is bell-shaped. Incomes, earthquake sizes and city populations have long tails, where extreme values are far more common than a bell curve predicts. Using a bell curve for financial crashes badly underestimated them before 2008.

deep.w: Everything in nature follows a bell curve
deep.r: Many things do roughly, but anything driven by multiplying effects or rare extremes often doesn't.

deep.x: When many small random effects add up, values cluster in a bell shape, and the standard deviation tells you how wide it is.

cards.title: Amostras
cards.text: Uma amostra aleatória bem escolhida de 1,000 pessoas pode representar milhões. Uma amostra grande, mas enviesada, não: quem você pergunta importa mais do que quantos.

deep.x: You don't have to drink the whole pot to know if the soup needs salt. One spoonful is enough, as long as the pot is well stirred. A **random sample** is the statistical version of stirring: everyone has the same chance of being picked.
Size helps, bias doesn't go away
A bigger sample reduces random wobble. It does nothing about **bias**: a systematic tilt in who gets asked or who answers.

In the 1936 US election the *Literary Digest* magazine mailed millions of ballots, mostly to people from telephone directories and car registrations: better-off voters in the Depression. With 2.4 million replies it predicted a big win for Alf Landon. Franklin Roosevelt won in a landslide. George Gallup, with a far smaller but more representative sample, got it right.
Common sources of bias
Population size barely matters
Surprisingly, a random sample of 1,000 is about as accurate for Portugal's 10 million people as for the EU's 450 million. What matters is the sample size, not the share of the population asked.

x: the same whether the population is 10 million or 450 million

deep.x: Medical trials use randomisation for the same reason: tossing a coin to decide who gets the treatment stops anyone, even unconsciously, putting healthier patients in one group.
Who you ask matters more than how many: a small random sample beats a huge biased one.

cards.title: Margem de erro
cards.text: As pesquisas informam uma margem de erro. Com cerca de 1,000 pessoas, ela fica em torno de ±3 pontos percentuais, então 51% contra 49% pode ser um empate.

deep.x: A poll of 1,000 people won't hit the true figure exactly; a different 1,000 would give a slightly different result. The **margin of error** says how far off it could plausibly be, usually at 95% confidence: in 19 polls out of 20, the truth lies within that range.
Diminishing returns
To halve the margin you need four times as many people, because of the square root. That's why most national polls stop at about 1,000 to 2,000.
A gap has a bigger margin

If a poll shows 51% against 49%, each figure could be about 3 points off, and in opposite directions. The margin on the **gap** between them is nearly double, about ±6 points. A 2-point lead is a statistical tie.
What the margin doesn't cover

The margin of error only measures random sampling luck. It ignores people who refuse to answer, people who change their minds, and badly worded questions. Real polling errors are often bigger than the stated margin for these reasons.

deep.w: A bigger country needs a much bigger poll
deep.r: Accuracy depends on how many people you ask, not on how many people live there.

deep.x: A poll of 1,000 is good to about ±3 points; any lead smaller than that is too close to call.

cards.title: Gráficos enganosos

items.w: Barra de 98 a 100 parece o dobro
items.r: Confira o eixo: a diferença é de 2%

cards.text: Um eixo y que não começa no zero pode fazer uma pequena diferença parecer enorme. Sempre confira a escala.

deep.x: Charts persuade quickly, which is why they are easy to bend. Most tricks don't involve false numbers; they change how the numbers look.
The cut-off axis
Bar charts show size by length, so the bars should start at zero. Start the axis higher and small differences balloon.

x: axis from 49: bars of 1 and 3, so B looks 3 times bigger

deep.x: Line charts are different: they show change, so zooming in on the axis is often fine, as long as it is clearly labelled.
Other common tricks

x: **Scaled pictures**: draw a coin twice as tall to show "twice as much", and it's also twice as wide, so it looks four times bigger
**Cumulative totals**: a running total can only go up, hiding a fall in monthly figures
**Chosen time windows**: start a share-price chart at a low point and any rise looks dramatic

deep.x: The design writer Edward Tufte proposed a "lie factor": the size of the effect shown in the graphic divided by the size of the effect in the data. Honest charts score close to 1.
Before reading a chart's shape, read its axes: where they start, what units, and over what period.

cards.title: O paradoxo de Simpson
cards.text: Uma tendência que aparece em todos os grupos pode se inverter quando os grupos são combinados. Um tratamento pode parecer melhor em cada hospital, mas pior no total, se os hospitais tiverem perfis de pacientes diferentes.

deep.x: **Simpson's paradox** is when a pattern that holds in every group reverses when the groups are combined. It happens when the groups are different sizes and differ in some hidden way.
A real example: kidney stones
A 1986 study compared two operations for kidney stones.
What's going on

Doctors gave treatment A mostly to patients with **large** stones, the hard cases, and B mostly to easy, small stones. A's overall figure is dragged down by its tougher patients, not by being worse. The hidden factor, stone size, is called a **confounder**.

steps: Split by case: A is better

deep.x: Which answer is right?

Usually the split figures, when the hidden factor affects both who gets the treatment and how well they do. But the right choice depends on the cause-and-effect story, which data alone can't always tell you.

In 1973 the University of California, Berkeley, appeared to admit men at a higher rate than women. Department by department, women did as well or better: they had applied more to competitive departments with low admission rates.
A trend in every group can flip when groups of different sizes are lumped together; look for the hidden factor.

cards.title: Regressão à média

steps: Próxima vez: mais perto da média

cards.text: Depois de um resultado extremo, o seguinte tende a ficar mais perto da média. A temporada recorde de um astro do esporte costuma ser seguida por outra mais comum, sem maldição nenhuma.

deep.x: Any result is partly skill and partly luck. An extreme result usually needed extreme luck too, and luck doesn't repeat on demand. So next time, the result tends to be closer to average. That's **regression to the mean**.
Where the name comes from

In 1886 Francis Galton noticed that very tall parents tend to have children who are tall, but less extremely so; very short parents tend to have children who are short, but less so. He called it "regression towards mediocrity".
Mistaken causes
Because the drift is automatic, people invent explanations for it.
Daniel Kahneman described flight instructors who believed that praising a great landing made the next worse, and shouting at a bad one made the next better. Both were simply regression to the mean.

x: A road has 2 crashes a year on average
a freak year brings 8, so a camera goes up
some of that fall would have happened anyway

deep.x: How to spot real effects
Compare with a **control group** that had the same extreme start but no treatment. Clinical trials do exactly this.

deep.w: A bad year followed by a better one proves the fix worked
deep.r: Things often improve on their own after an extreme. Only a comparison group shows the true effect.

deep.x: After an extreme result, expect something more ordinary next time, curse or no curse.

cards.title: Como ler uma estatística no noticiário
cards.text: Faça quatro perguntas: em comparação com o quê? Em quantos? Quem foi medido? Quem pagou pelo estudo?

deep.x: A headline number is the start of a story, not the end. Four questions catch most problems.
Compared with what?
"10,000 cases this year" means little without last year's figure, the rate per person, or the normal seasonal level. A rise in the number of cyclists hurt may just reflect more people cycling.
Out of how many?
Who was measured?
A study of 40 students, or of mice, may not apply to you. Watch also for people who chose to take part: volunteers are often keener, healthier or richer than average.
Who paid?
Funding doesn't make a result wrong, but it's a reason to look for independent studies that agree.
Bonus: correlation is not causation
Ice-cream sales and drownings rise together in summer. Ice cream doesn't cause drowning; hot weather increases both. Only experiments, or very careful studies, can untangle cause.
A single study rarely settles anything. Scientists trust a finding when several independent teams get the same result.
Before believing a statistic, ask: compared with what, out of how many, measured on whom, and paid for by whom?

quiz.q: Qual média é melhor para descrever salários típicos?
quiz.explain: Alguns poucos salários muito altos puxam a média para cima.

quiz.q: Aproximadamente que proporção dos valores fica a até 1 desvio padrão numa curva em sino?

lessons.title: Lógica e enigmas
lessons.summary: Pensamento claro, dos paradoxos aos computadores.

cards.title: Verdadeiro e falso

items.b: verdadeiro se pelo menos um for

cards.text: A lógica trabalha com afirmações verdadeiras ou falsas e as combina com E, OU e NÃO. Todo chip de computador é construído com essas operações.

deep.x: In 1854 the English mathematician George Boole published *The Laws of Thought*, treating logic like algebra. Statements take one of two values, true or false, and three operations combine them. This is now called **Boolean algebra**.

items.b: true only if both are true
true if at least one is

deep.x: Truth tables
A truth table lists every combination of inputs and the result. With two inputs there are four rows.
From logic to chips

In 1937 Claude Shannon, a 21-year-old student at MIT, showed that electrical switches could carry out Boole's logic: switches in series behave like AND, switches side by side like OR. Every computer chip is built on that idea. A modern processor contains billions of transistors acting as tiny switches, wired into logic gates.
Everyday "or" is slippery
"Soup or salad comes with your meal" means one, not both: that's **exclusive or**. In logic, OR includes both. Search engines and spreadsheet filters use the logical version.
A single kind of gate, NAND ("not both"), is enough to build every other logic operation, and so in principle an entire computer.
AND, OR and NOT are enough to combine true and false into any logical rule, and into every computer.

cards.title: Se… então…
cards.text: "Se chove, o chão fica molhado" não quer dizer "se o chão está molhado, choveu": um irrigador poderia fazer isso. Confundir as duas coisas é um erro de lógica clássico.

deep.x: "If A, then B" is a one-way promise. It says that whenever A happens, B follows. It says nothing about what happens when A doesn't.
Two classic mistakes

x: **Affirming the consequent**: "The ground is wet, so it rained." A sprinkler or a burst pipe could be to blame.
**Denying the antecedent**: "It didn't rain, so the ground is dry." Same problem.

deep.x: The safe move is the **contrapositive**: if the ground is dry, it can't have rained. It always means the same as the original.
The Wason card test

In 1966 the psychologist Peter Wason showed people four cards, each with a letter on one side and a number on the other: E, K, 4, 7. The rule: "If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other." Which cards must you turn over to test it?

x: 4: irrelevant (the rule says nothing about evens)
7: must check (a vowel behind would break the rule)

deep.x: Fewer than 1 in 10 people usually choose E and 7. But reframe the puzzle as "if someone is drinking beer, they must be over 18", and most people get it right. We're better at spotting rule-breakers than abstract logic.

deep.w: "All dogs are mammals" means "all mammals are dogs"
deep.r: Reversing an if-then statement changes its meaning. Check the converse separately.

deep.x: "If A then B" doesn't mean "if B then A"; only "if not B then not A" follows.

cards.title: Prova por contradição
cards.text: Suponha o contrário do que você quer provar e mostre que isso leva a um absurdo. Foi assim que Euclides provou que existem infinitos números primos.

deep.x: To prove something by **contradiction**, assume it's false and follow the logic until something impossible appears. If an assumption leads to nonsense, the assumption was wrong, so the original statement must be true.
Euclid: primes never run out
Suppose there were a last prime, so all primes fit on a finite list. Multiply them all together and add 1. Call that N.

x: Dividing N by any prime on the list leaves remainder 1, so none of them divides it
But every whole number above 1 has at least one prime factor
So N has a prime factor that isn't on the list, which contradicts the list being complete
two new primes, not on the list

deep.x: N itself needn't be prime, as this shows. It just has to have a prime factor missing from the list.
The square root of 2 isn't a fraction

Assume √2 = a/b, simplified as far as possible. Then a² = 2b², so a² is even, which means a is even. Write a = 2c: then 4c² = 2b², so b² = 2c², and b is even too. Both even means the fraction could be simplified further, a contradiction.
Legend says Hippasus, a follower of Pythagoras, was drowned for revealing that √2 isn't a ratio of whole numbers. It's a story, not history, but it shows how unsettling the discovery was.
If assuming something leads to an impossibility, its opposite must be true.

cards.title: O paradoxo do mentiroso
cards.text: "Esta frase é falsa." Se for verdadeira, é falsa; se for falsa, é verdadeira. Paradoxos como esse abalaram os fundamentos da lógica no século XX.

deep.x: "This sentence is false." If it's true, then what it says holds, so it's false. If it's false, then it isn't false, so it's true. It can't consistently be either. Greek philosophers discussed versions of it, credited to Eubulides in the 4th century BCE.
Russell's paradox
In 1901 Bertrand Russell found a version inside mathematics itself. Consider the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. Does it contain itself? If yes, it shouldn't; if no, it should.
A popular version: a village barber shaves everyone who doesn't shave himself, and nobody else. Who shaves the barber?
Russell wrote to Gottlob Frege in 1902, just as Frege's great work on the foundations of arithmetic was going to print. The paradox showed his system was inconsistent.
How mathematics recovered

Mathematicians rebuilt set theory on carefully restricted rules, starting with Ernst Zermelo in 1908, so that troublesome collections like Russell's can't be formed. The logician Alfred Tarski later showed a related limit: a language can't fully define its own notion of "true" without running into the liar.
The "Pinocchio paradox" is a modern twist: what happens if Pinocchio says "My nose will grow now"?
Sentences that talk about their own truth can trap logic in a loop, and that loop forced mathematics to rebuild its foundations.

cards.title: A incompletude de Gödel

steps: Rico o bastante para a aritmética

cards.text: Em 1931, Kurt Gödel provou que qualquer sistema de regras consistente e rico o bastante para a aritmética tem afirmações verdadeiras que não consegue provar. A matemática nunca pode ser completa.

deep.x: Around 1900 David Hilbert hoped to put all of mathematics on a finite set of rules (axioms) that could prove every true statement and never a false one. In 1931 Kurt Gödel, a 25-year-old in Vienna, showed that this was impossible.

items.b: any system rich enough for arithmetic

deep.x: The idea behind it

Gödel found a way to turn statements about proofs into statements about numbers. That let him build a statement that says, in effect, "This statement cannot be proved within this system." It is the liar paradox with "false" replaced by "unprovable".

x: If the system could prove it, the system would prove something false, so it wouldn't be consistent
So, if the system is consistent, the statement can't be proved, which is exactly what it says. It's true.

deep.x: What it does and doesn't mean

Adding the unprovable statement as a new rule doesn't help: the new, bigger system has its own unprovable truths. But ordinary mathematics carries on fine. Most theorems mathematicians care about are provable. Since the 1970s, a few natural statements about whole numbers have been found that are true but unprovable in the standard rules of arithmetic.

deep.w: Gödel proved mathematics is unreliable, or that truth is relative
deep.r: He proved that no fixed set of rules can capture every truth. What is proved stays proved.

deep.x: In 1936 Alan Turing proved a cousin result for computers: no program can decide, for every program, whether it will eventually stop. This is the "halting problem".
No consistent set of rules for arithmetic can prove every true statement: mathematics always has more truth than any rulebook.

cards.title: Algoritmos
cards.text: Um algoritmo é uma receita precisa, passo a passo, para resolver um problema. A palavra vem do nome de al-Khwarizmi, um matemático de Bagdá do século IX.

deep.x: An **algorithm** is a finite list of precise steps that turns an input into an output, with no guesswork. A recipe is a loose example; a computer program is a strict one. The word comes from al-Khwarizmi, who worked at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad around 820 CE. His book on Indian numerals, translated into Latin, began "Algoritmi dixit": "al-Khwarizmi said".
One of the oldest: Euclid's algorithm
Euclid described, around 300 BCE, how to find the largest number dividing two others. It is still used today, including inside encryption software.
Why speed matters

Different algorithms for the same job can differ enormously. To find a name in a sorted list of a million, checking one by one may take a million steps. **Binary search**, opening in the middle and discarding the wrong half each time, takes at most 20.

x: so 20 halvings cover a million names

deep.x: Algorithms all around you

x: Your phone's route planner (Edsger Dijkstra's shortest-path method, 1956)
Search engine rankings and social-media feeds

deep.x: In 1843 Ada Lovelace published a step-by-step method for Charles Babbage's planned Analytical Engine to calculate Bernoulli numbers. It's often called the first computer program, a century before such machines existed.
An algorithm is a recipe so precise that a machine can follow it, and a clever recipe can be millions of times faster than a naive one.

cards.title: Binário
cards.text: Os computadores contam em base 2, usando só 0 e 1. Cada posição vale o dobro da que está à sua direita: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16…

deep.x: We count in base 10: each place is worth ten times the one to its right. Binary is base 2: each place is worth double, and the only digits are 0 and 1.
Why computers use it

A circuit only needs to tell two states apart, on or off, high voltage or low. That's far more reliable than distinguishing ten levels, especially with electrical noise and billions of components. Each 0 or 1 is a **bit**.
Powers of two everywhere
Memory sizes come in 8, 16, 32, 64… gigabytes, and every extra bit doubles what can be counted. That's why 8 bits give 2⁸ = 256 values, the number of shades in each colour channel of a typical image.
Gottfried Leibniz published an account of binary arithmetic in 1703, inspired partly by the patterns of the Chinese *I Ching*. It waited over two centuries to find its killer use.
Using fingers as bits, up or down, you can count to 1,023 on two hands.
Binary uses only 0 and 1, with each place worth double the last; that's all a switch needs to store a number.

cards.title: O paradoxo de Zenão
cards.text: Para atravessar uma sala, você precisa primeiro percorrer a metade, depois a metade do que falta, e assim para sempre. Zenão dizia que você nunca chegaria. A soma infinita 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … na verdade é igual a 1.

deep.x: Zeno of Elea, in the 5th century BCE, argued that motion is impossible. Before you cross a room you must reach the halfway point, then half the remaining distance, then half again, forever. An infinite number of tasks can never be finished, he said.
The sum that settles it
The distances form an endless list: 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16… Add them up step by step and watch the total.

x: gap left always halves: the total heads to exactly 1

v.unit: running total of the room crossed

deep.x: The total gets as close to 1 as you like and never passes it. Mathematicians say the infinite sum **equals** 1, its **limit**. Infinitely many pieces can add up to a finite amount.
Time halves too

At 1 m per second across a 1 m room, the first half takes 1/2 second, the next quarter 1/4 second, and so on. The infinitely many steps take 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … = 1 second in total. Nothing paradoxical happens.
a + ar + ar² + … = a ÷ (1 − r), when r is between −1 and 1
The same maths shows that 0.999… (nines forever) is exactly equal to 1. It's 9/10 + 9/100 + 9/1000 + …, and the sum is 1.
Making this fully rigorous took until the 1800s, when Augustin-Louis Cauchy and Karl Weierstrass gave limits a precise definition.
An endless list of shrinking pieces can add up to a finite total, so you do reach the other side of the room.

cards.title: Problemas sem solução
cards.text: Algumas perguntas que parecem simples continuam sem resposta, como a conjectura de Goldbach: todo número par maior que 2 é a soma de dois primos? Já foi testada até números enormes, mas nunca provada.

deep.x: Mathematics is full of questions a child can understand that nobody can answer. The most famous is **Goldbach's conjecture**, from a letter Christian Goldbach wrote to Leonhard Euler in 1742: every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes.
Bigger even numbers have more and more ways to be split, which makes a counterexample seem very unlikely. But "very unlikely" is not a proof.
The record check of Goldbach's conjecture, up to 4 × 10¹⁸, was led by Tomás Oliveira e Silva of the University of Aveiro in Portugal, completed in 2013.
Other open questions

items.b: easy to check = easy to solve?

deep.x: In 2000 the Clay Mathematics Institute offered US$1 million each for seven "Millennium Problems", including the Riemann hypothesis and P vs NP.
Some do fall

Fermat's Last Theorem took over 350 years. Grigori Perelman solved the Poincaré conjecture, a Millennium Problem, and turned down the prize money in 2010. Harald Helfgott proved in 2013 that every odd number above 5 is the sum of three primes, a weaker cousin of Goldbach.

deep.w: If a pattern holds for billions of cases, it's proved
deep.r: Some patterns fail only at enormous numbers. Only a proof covers every case.

deep.x: Simple-sounding questions can resist the best minds for centuries; testing builds confidence, but only proof settles it.

cards.title: A travessia do rio
cards.text: Um fazendeiro precisa atravessar um rio com um lobo, uma cabra e um repolho, levando um de cada vez. O lobo não pode ficar sozinho com a cabra, nem a cabra com o repolho. O truque: trazer a cabra de volta.

deep.x: This puzzle appears in a collection called *Problems to Sharpen the Young*, linked to Alcuin of York around 800 CE. The boat carries the farmer plus one item. Left alone, the wolf eats the goat and the goat eats the cabbage.
The solution: seven crossings

Step 4 is the one people miss: moving something backwards feels like going the wrong way. Taking the cabbage at step 3 and then bringing the goat back works just as well, so there are two seven-step solutions.
Why the goat is the key
The goat is the only item that conflicts with both others. So it must never be left with either, and the only way to manage that is to keep it with you or alone.
Thinking in states

Computer scientists solve puzzles like this by listing every **state**: who is on which bank. There are only 16 possible arrangements, some forbidden. Draw them as dots, connect the legal moves, and the answer is the shortest path from start to finish. The same method plans robot moves, solves Rubik's cubes and finds routes.
Variants include the "missionaries and cannibals" puzzle, which became a standard example in early artificial-intelligence research.
Sometimes the way forward includes a step back: undoing a move can unlock the solution.

quiz.q: Quanto é 101 em binário como número comum?
"Se chove, o chão fica molhado. O chão está molhado." Então choveu?

cards.title: O que é uma porcentagem
cards.text: "Por cento" quer dizer "em cada 100". 25% são 25 em cada 100, ou um quarto. Para calcular a porcentagem de um número, multiplique pela porcentagem e divida por 100.

deep.x: "Per cent" comes from the Latin *per centum*, "for each hundred". A percentage is a fraction with 100 on the bottom, which makes different fractions easy to compare.
percentage of a number = number × percentage ÷ 100
Comparing on the same scale
Which is better: 18 out of 25 or 34 out of 50? Turn both into "out of 100".
More than 100%
A percentage can exceed 100 when you compare with a starting amount. If a town's population goes from 2,000 to 5,000, the new figure is 250% of the old one: an increase of 150%.
Converting

x: Fraction to percentage: divide, then multiply by 100: 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%

deep.x: The % sign evolved from Italian merchants abbreviating "per cento". Over centuries the scribbled abbreviation shrank to a small circle, a slash and another circle.
A percentage is just a fraction out of 100, which puts everything on the same scale.

cards.title: Truques rápidos
cards.text: 10% é fácil: mova a vírgula decimal uma casa para a esquerda. A partir daí, 5% é a metade disso e 20% é o dobro.

deep.x: Most percentages can be built from a few easy pieces. Find 10% first, then combine.

items.b: move the decimal point left once

deep.x: Building awkward percentages
Any percentage is a sum of easy pieces.
Subtracting instead
For big percentages, it's often easier to take away the small remainder.
Quick checks

50% is half; 25% is half of half; 75% is 50% + 25%. 33% is about a third. Knowing these anchors helps you spot a wrong answer fast: 23% of €80 must be a bit under a quarter of €80, so a bit under €20.
Portugal's standard VAT rate on the mainland is 23%; the intermediate rate is 13% and the reduced rate 6%. The 20% + 3% trick works for 23% wherever you shop.
Find 10%, then halve, double and add your way to any percentage.

cards.title: Porcentagens se invertem
cards.text: 8% de 25 é igual a 25% de 8, porque a multiplicação funciona nos dois sentidos. Use a forma mais fácil: 4% de 75 é 75% de 4, que dá 3.

deep.x: x% of y is always the same as y% of x. Both equal x × y ÷ 100, and multiplication doesn't care about order.
x% of y = y% of x
Why it helps
One version is usually much friendlier, because 50%, 25%, 20% and 10% are easy to take.
Seeing why it works
When to look for it

x: One number is 10, 20, 25, 50 or a multiple of 100
You're dealing with small percentages of awkward numbers: 2% of 350 = 350% of 2 = 7
Checking a calculator: do it both ways round

deep.x: This flip is the same symmetry that makes 6 × 7 = 7 × 6. It's called the **commutative** property of multiplication.
When one way round is hard, swap the numbers: x% of y equals y% of x.

cards.title: Sobe e desce
cards.text: Um aumento de 50% seguido de uma queda de 50% não leva você de volta ao início. €100 viram €150 e depois €75.

deep.x: A percentage change is always measured from the **current** amount, which changes after every step. So equal percentage rises and falls don't cancel out.
The fall is bigger in euros because it's a percentage of a bigger number. Turn changes into multipliers and the effect is clear.
overall change = 1.5 × 0.5 = 0.75, so 25% down
Smaller changes still leave a dent
The order doesn't matter: down 50% then up 50% also ends at €75.
Recovering from a loss
After a fall, you need a bigger percentage rise to get back.

v.unit: % rise needed to recover a loss

x: to get back to €100 it must double

deep.x: That's why investors fear big losses: a 50% fall followed by a 50% rise leaves you 25% down.
Two investments can have the same average yearly return but end with very different amounts. The steadier one usually comes out ahead, an effect called **volatility drag**.
Percentage changes multiply rather than add, so a fall needs a bigger rise to undo it.

cards.title: Pontos percentuais
cards.text: Se os juros passam de 2% para 3%, isso é uma alta de 1 ponto percentual, mas um aumento de 50% na taxa. As manchetes muitas vezes confundem os dois.

deep.x: When the thing being measured is itself a percentage, there are two ways to describe a change.
Why it matters for your mortgage
Many Portuguese mortgages have variable rates tied to Euribor. If your rate goes from 2% to 3%, it sounds like a small change, but the interest part of your payment rises by half.
Basis points
Bankers use **basis points**: one basis point is 0.01 percentage points. When the European Central Bank raises rates by "25 basis points", it means a quarter of a percentage point.
In politics and the economy

If a party's vote goes from 20% to 25%, it gained 5 points, but its vote share rose 25%. If unemployment goes from 6% to 6.5%, that's half a point, or an 8% rise in the rate. Both descriptions are true; they answer different questions.

deep.w: "Unemployment rose 8%" means 8% more of the workforce lost their jobs
deep.r: It may mean the rate rose from 6% to 6.5%, just half a percentage point.

deep.x: When percentages change, ask whether it's percentage points or per cent: the difference can be huge.

cards.title: Porcentagem reversa
cards.text: Um preço com 23% de IVA incluído é €123. O preço antes do IVA não é €123 menos 23%; é €123 ÷ 1,23 = €100.

deep.x: A price that **includes** VAT is the original price × 1.23. To go back, divide by 1.23. Subtracting 23% doesn't work, because the 23% was calculated on the smaller, original price.
The same idea for discounts
If you paid €64 in a 20% sale, you paid 80% of the original. So the original was €64 ÷ 0.8.
Other rates
In Portugal, many restaurant meals carry 13% VAT and many basic foods 6%.
The VAT inside a price is a smaller share than the rate. At 23%, VAT is 23/123, about 18.7% of what you pay.
To undo a percentage change, divide by the multiplier; don't subtract the same percentage.

cards.title: Descontos se acumulam de um jeito estranho
cards.text: "30% de desconto, mais 20% extra" não é 50% de desconto. É 0,7 × 0,8 = 0,56 do preço: um desconto de 44%.

deep.x: Each discount applies to the price **after** the previous one, so later discounts work on a smaller amount. Multiply what you keep, not what you take off.
Order doesn't matter
0.8 × 0.7 is also 0.56. Twenty then thirty gives the same result as thirty then twenty.
Two halves don't make free
Comparing multi-buy offers
These only save you money if you wanted that many items. "Buy 3 for 2" is 33% off when you need three; it's a 100% increase in spending if you only wanted one.

deep.w: "Up to 70% off" means 70% off
deep.r: It means at most 70% off, usually on a few items. Most may be far less.

deep.x: Stacked discounts multiply: 30% then 20% is 44% off, not 50%.

cards.title: Variação percentual
cards.text: Variação ÷ valor original × 100. De 80 para 100 é uma alta de 25%; de 100 de volta para 80 é uma queda de 20%. O ponto de partida faz diferença.

deep.x: The rule is always the same: divide the change by where you started.
% change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100
The change is the same size, 20, but the starting points differ, so the percentages do too.
Everyday uses
Pay rises and inflation
To see whether you're better off, compare your pay rise with inflation. If pay rises 5% while prices rise 7%, you can buy about 2% less, even though you earn more.
Common slips

x: Dividing by the new value instead of the old
Mixing up a change of 25% with a final value of 25%
Forgetting that "tripled" is a 200% rise, not 300%

deep.x: Doubling is a 100% increase, but halving is only a 50% decrease, which is why rises and falls sound lopsided.
Percentage change is always measured from the starting value, so the same jump up and down gives different percentages.

cards.title: Gorjetas e divisão da conta
cards.text: Para dividir uma conta de €60 com 10% de gorjeta entre quatro pessoas: €60 × 1,1 = €66, dividido por 4 = €16,50 para cada um.

deep.x: Turn the tip into a multiplier, then divide. Or divide first and then add the tip: multiplication and division can be done in either order.
Other tip sizes
Tipping in Portugal

In Portugal tips aren't included or expected the way they are in the US. Service is part of the price, and people often round up or leave around 5–10% for good service in restaurants. In the US 15–20% is normal because tips make up much of a waiter's pay.
Fair splits
When one person ordered much more, an even split isn't fair. Add up each person's share and scale up by the same tip.
Many card machines suggest tips as percentages of the total including tax, which makes the tip slightly larger than you might think.
Turn the tip into a multiplier like 1.1, then split: the order doesn't change the answer.

cards.title: Porcentagens enganosas
cards.text: "Vendas sobem 200%!" de 1 para 3 unidades parece dramático, mas quer dizer pouco. Sempre peça os números reais por trás de uma porcentagem.

deep.x: A percentage hides the size of the numbers behind it. That can make tiny changes sound dramatic, and huge ones sound small.
Small bases inflate percentages
The smaller the starting figure, the more dramatic the percentage. A new product, a rare crime or a tiny town can show huge percentage changes from a handful of cases.
Other tricks

x: **The flattering frame**: "95% fat-free" sounds better than "5% fat", though they're the same
**Tiny samples**: "90% of users agree" may mean 9 out of 10 people asked
**Hidden bases**: "crime fell 20%" in which area, since when, compared with what?
**Percentages of percentages**: a rise in interest rates "of 50%" may be one percentage point

deep.x: What to ask for
Always ask for the counts: how many before, how many after, out of how many in total. With those three numbers you can judge any percentage yourself.

deep.w: A bigger percentage always means a bigger change
deep.r: 200% of 1 is tiny; 10% of a million is 100,000.

deep.x: A percentage without the numbers behind it can tell almost any story; always ask "out of how many?"

quiz.q: Um item de €100 sobe 50% e depois cai 50%. Quanto custa?
Um preço com 23% de IVA é €123. Qual é o preço sem IVA?
"30% de desconto e depois mais 20%" equivale a um desconto de…

cards.title: Frações são divisões
cards.text: 3/4 quer dizer 3 dividido por 4: três de quatro partes iguais, ou 0,75. O número de baixo diz em quantas partes se divide; o de cima, quantas você pega.

deep.x: A fraction is a division waiting to happen. The line between the numbers literally means "divided by", so 3/4 is the same instruction as 3 ÷ 4. That's why the same fraction can be read as a share, a point on the number line, or a decimal.
Two ways to see 3/4

x: Cut one pizza into 4 equal slices and take 3 of them
Share 3 pizzas equally between 4 people: each gets 3/4 of a pizza

deep.x: Both give the same amount, which is the whole point: "3 out of 4 parts" and "3 shared by 4" are the same number.
When the decimal never ends
Some fractions give tidy decimals and some repeat forever. A simplified fraction ends neatly only when its bottom number is built from 2s and 5s, the factors of 10.
A fraction can also be bigger than 1. 7/4 means 7 ÷ 4 = 1.75, also written 1¾. The one thing a fraction can't have is 0 on the bottom: dividing into zero parts has no meaning.
The horizontal fraction bar is usually credited to Arab mathematicians around the 12th century. Fibonacci helped spread it in Europe with his book *Liber Abaci* in 1202.
Read the fraction line as "divided by" and fractions, decimals and percentages become one idea.

cards.title: Frações equivalentes
cards.text: Multiplicar o numerador e o denominador pelo mesmo número não muda a fração: 1/2 = 2/4 = 50/100. Para simplificar, divida os dois por um fator comum.

deep.x: Multiplying top and bottom by the same number is the same as multiplying by 2/2 or 5/5, and those are just 1 in disguise. Multiplying by 1 changes how a number looks, never what it is.
Simplifying

To simplify, divide top and bottom by their **greatest common factor**, the biggest number that goes into both. You can also do it in small steps, dividing by 2, then 3, until nothing else divides both.
A fraction is in its **simplest form** when the only number dividing top and bottom is 1. 3/4 is; 6/8 isn't.
Comparing fractions
Equivalent fractions let you compare. Rewrite both with the same bottom number, or use the shortcut of cross-multiplying.
Where you meet it
Percentages are equivalent fractions with 100 on the bottom: 3/4 = 75/100 = 75%. Exam marks work the same way: 18 out of 24 is the same score as 3 out of 4.

deep.w: Bigger numbers mean a bigger fraction
deep.r: 50/100 is exactly the same size as 1/2. Only the ratio of top to bottom matters.

deep.x: Multiplying top and bottom by the same number is multiplying by 1: the value never changes.

cards.title: Somar frações
cards.text: Para somar frações, primeiro deixe-as com o mesmo denominador: 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.

deep.x: You can only add things that are counted in the same units. Thirds and halves are different-sized pieces, so you first cut both into a common size. Sixths work because both a half and a third can be cut into sixths exactly.
Finding the common bottom
The neatest choice is the **lowest common multiple**: the smallest number both bottoms divide into. Multiplying the two bottoms together always works, but may give a bigger number to simplify later.
Subtraction follows exactly the same steps.
Mixed numbers
With whole numbers involved, add the wholes and the fractions separately, then tidy up.

deep.w: Add the tops and add the bottoms
deep.r: That gives 2/5, which is smaller than the 1/2 you started with. Adding a positive amount can't make a total shrink.

deep.x: "Tops plus tops, bottoms plus bottoms" is right in one setting: combining scores. 1 goal from 2 shots plus 1 from 3 shots is 2 goals from 5 shots. That's a combined rate, not a sum of fractions.
Fractions can only be added once they are cut into same-sized pieces.

cards.title: Multiplicar frações
cards.text: Multiplique os numeradores entre si e os denominadores entre si. A metade de três quartos é 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8. "De" significa multiplicar.

deep.x: Multiplying fractions is the easiest operation: top times top, bottom times bottom. The tricky part is intuition, because multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes things smaller.
Picture it as an area
Draw a square. Shade 3/4 of it with vertical lines, then shade 1/2 of it with horizontal lines. The overlap covers 3 of the 8 small rectangles: 3/8.
Cancel first
You can simplify before multiplying, by cancelling any top with any bottom. It keeps the numbers small.
"Of" means multiply
"Two-thirds of 600" is 2/3 × 600 = 400. The same rule hides inside shop discounts, which is where people go wrong.

deep.w: Multiplying always makes a number bigger
deep.r: Multiplying by anything between 0 and 1 makes it smaller. 1/2 × 8 is 4.

deep.x: Multiplying by a fraction means taking that fraction of something, so "of" means "×".

cards.title: Dividir por uma fração

items.r: 3 ÷ ½ = 6, pois seis metades fazem três

cards.text: Dividir por uma fração é multiplicar pela fração invertida. 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6: quantas metades cabem em 3? Seis.

deep.x: Division asks "how many of these fit into that?" 3 ÷ 1/2 asks how many halves fit into 3. Each whole holds two halves, so 3 holds 6. That's why dividing by 1/2 is the same as multiplying by 2.
Why the flip works

The flipped fraction is called the **reciprocal**. Dividing by a number and multiplying by its reciprocal always give the same answer, because a number times its reciprocal is 1. Dividing by 4 is multiplying by 1/4; dividing by 1/4 is multiplying by 4.
Check by multiplying back
Every division can be checked with a multiplication. If 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6, then 6 × 1/2 should give 3 again, and it does.
In the kitchen
A 2-litre bottle poured into 1/4-litre glasses fills 2 ÷ 1/4 = 8 glasses. A 3/4 kg block of cheese cut into 1/8 kg portions gives 6.

deep.w: Division always makes numbers smaller
deep.r: Dividing by anything between 0 and 1 makes the answer bigger, because many small pieces fit.

deep.x: Dividing by a fraction asks how many of those pieces fit, and that means multiplying by its flip.

cards.title: Razões
cards.text: Uma razão compara quantidades. Uma mistura de cimento e areia na razão 2:3 tem 2 partes de cimento para cada 3 de areia: 2/5 da mistura é cimento.

deep.x: A ratio compares parts with parts. A fraction compares a part with the whole. In a 2:3 cement-to-sand mix there are 5 parts in total, so cement is 2/5 of the mix and sand is 3/5.
Sharing in a ratio
Add the parts, find the value of one part, then multiply.
Ratios can have more than two parts. A common concrete mix is about 1:2:3 of cement, sand and gravel: 6 parts, so 1/6 of the dry mix is cement.
Simplifying ratios
Like fractions, ratios simplify by dividing every part by a common factor. 12:18 becomes 2:3. The order matters: 2:3 cement to sand is a very different mix from 3:2.
Ratios all around you
A4 paper is 210 × 297 mm, a ratio of 1 : √2. Fold it in half and the new sheet (A5) has exactly the same shape. That's why the European ISO paper sizes scale so neatly.

deep.w: A 2:3 mix means 2/3 is cement
deep.r: Cement is 2 parts out of 5 in total, so 2/5.

deep.x: A ratio compares parts with each other; add the parts to get the whole.

cards.title: Adaptar receitas
cards.text: Uma receita para 4 pessoas leva 300 g de farinha. Para 6 pessoas, multiplique por 6/4 = 1,5: 450 g.

deep.x: Every scaling problem uses one number, the **scale factor**: new amount ÷ old amount. For 6 people from a recipe for 4, it's 6/4 = 1.5. Multiply every ingredient by it and the proportions stay the same.

x: Recipe for 4: 300 g flour, 2 eggs, 200 ml milk
beat 2 eggs and use about three-quarters

deep.x: What doesn't scale simply

x: **Eggs** come in whole units, so round sensibly or weigh them (a medium egg is about 50 g without the shell)
**Cooking time** depends on thickness, not total amount: two cakes take about as long as one
**Salt and spices** are often scaled a little less, then adjusted by taste

deep.x: Tins and trays
A tin's capacity depends on its area, and area grows with the square of the diameter. Going from a 20 cm to a 24 cm round tin is only 20% wider but needs much more batter.
Bakers often write recipes as "baker's percentages", with flour as 100% and everything else as a share of it. A bread with 65% water means 650 g of water per kilo of flour, for any size of batch.
Find one scale factor and multiply everything by it; then think about what doesn't scale.

cards.title: Preço por unidade
cards.text: Compare ofertas pelo preço por unidade. 500 g por €2,40 dá €4,80/kg; 750 g por €3,30 dá €4,40/kg. Aqui o pacote maior sai mais barato, mas nem sempre é assim.

deep.x: A unit rate turns two prices for two sizes into a fair comparison: euros per kilo, per litre or per wash. Divide the price by the amount.
The shelf label does it for you

Under an EU directive from 1998, shops must show the **unit price** (price per kilo or litre) next to the selling price for most goods. In Portugal it's on the shelf label as "preço por kg" or "por litro". It's the quickest way to compare brands and pack sizes.
Traps to watch for

x: **Multibuys**: "3 for 2" means each item costs 2/3 of the price, 33% off, but only if you'll use all three
**Shrinkflation**: same price, smaller pack, so the unit price quietly rises
**Big isn't always cheaper**: promotions on small packs often beat the family size

items: Use the same unit for both
Compare per kg or per litre

deep.x: Rates beyond the shop
Fuel use is a unit rate too. Europe quotes litres per 100 km, so lower is better.

deep.w: The bigger pack is always better value
deep.r: Often true, but not always. Only the unit price tells you.

deep.x: Divide price by quantity to compare like with like.

cards.title: Escalas de mapas
cards.text: Num mapa em escala 1:25,000, 1 cm equivale a 25,000 cm, ou seja, 250 m no terreno. Mapas de trilha costumam usar essa escala.

deep.x: A map scale is a ratio. 1:25,000 means one unit on paper is 25,000 of the same units on the ground, whatever the unit. Turning centimetres into metres is the only fiddly step: 25,000 cm is 250 m.

x: A path measures 7.4 cm on a 1:25,000 map

deep.x: Large scale, small scale

A **large-scale** map shows a small area in big detail (1:10,000). A **small-scale** map shows a big area with little detail (1:1,000,000). It sounds backwards, but 1/10,000 is a bigger fraction than 1/1,000,000.
Areas scale by the square
Lengths shrink by 25,000, but areas shrink by 25,000 × 25,000. One square centimetre on a 1:25,000 map covers 250 m × 250 m.
Portugal's classic walking map, the Carta Militar, is published at 1:25,000 by the army's geospatial centre. Britain's Ordnance Survey Explorer maps use the same scale.

deep.w: A large-scale map covers a large area
deep.r: It's the opposite: large scale means a zoomed-in map of a small area.

deep.x: A map scale is a ratio: multiply map distances by it, and remember areas scale by its square.

cards.title: Proporção direta e inversa

items: um dobra, o outro cai à metade

cards.text: O dobro de horas com o mesmo pagamento dá o dobro de dinheiro: proporção direta. O dobro de trabalhadores numa tarefa leva mais ou menos à metade do tempo: proporção inversa.

deep.x: In **direct proportion**, two quantities rise together at a fixed ratio: double one, double the other. In **inverse proportion**, their product stays fixed: double one, halve the other.
Spotting which is which

For direct proportion, the ratio y ÷ x is the same every time, and the graph is a straight line through zero. For inverse proportion, x × y is the same every time, and the graph is a curve that never touches the axes.
Worker-days
Jobs are often measured as a fixed amount of work. If 4 painters need 6 days, the job is 24 painter-days. 8 painters should need 3 days.
Why "roughly"
Real teams don't divide perfectly. People get in each other's way, have to coordinate, and some tasks can't be split at all: nine people can't make a baby in one month.
In his 1975 book *The Mythical Man-Month*, the software engineer Fred Brooks argued that adding people to a late software project makes it later. It's now known as Brooks's law.
Direct: the ratio stays fixed. Inverse: the product stays fixed.

quiz.q: Quanto é 1/2 + 1/3?
Quanto é 3 ÷ ½?

cards.title: Arredonde e ajuste
cards.text: Para somar 298 + 157, some 300 e tire 2: 457 − 2 = 455. Arredondar para números redondos deixa muitas contas fáceis.

deep.x: The trick works because addition can be done in any order. 157 + 298 is the same as 157 + 300 − 2. You swap one awkward sum for an easy one plus a small correction.
It works for subtraction too
Taking away a number that's just under a round one means taking away too much, so you add the extra back.

x: you took 2 too many, so add 2

deep.x: The direction of the correction
This is where mistakes creep in. Ask: did I add or take away too much?
At the shops
Prices ending in 99 cents are made for this method. Round every item up to the next euro, add, then subtract a cent per item.
Shops use 99-cent prices because shoppers notice the first digit most: €4.99 feels closer to €4 than to €5. Researchers call it the **left-digit effect**. Rounding up undoes the illusion.

deep.w: Mental maths is about memorising lots of facts
deep.r: Mostly it's about reshaping numbers into easier ones.

deep.x: Round to a friendly number, do the easy sum, then correct by the difference.

cards.title: Multiplicar por 5
cards.text: Para multiplicar por 5, multiplique por 10 e divida por 2. 5 × 48 = 480 ÷ 2 = 240.

deep.x: Five is half of ten, so multiplying by 5 is multiplying by 10 and halving. Multiplying by 10 is easy in our number system: just shift the digits one place.
For even numbers you can halve first: 5 × 48 = 24 × 10 = 240.
The same idea for 25 and 50

x: × 25: multiply by 100 and divide by 4 (halve twice)

deep.x: Dividing by 5
Reverse it: double, then divide by 10.
Percentages and tips
Ten per cent is easy: move the decimal point. Five per cent is half of that.
Euro coins and notes come in 1s, 2s and 5s (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50…), so counting money by fives and tens is something you already do every day.
Five is ten halved: shift the digits, then halve.

cards.title: Multiplicar por 11
cards.text: Para um número de dois algarismos, some os algarismos e coloque a soma no meio: 11 × 36 = 3(3+6)6 = 396. Se a soma der 10 ou mais, vai um.

deep.x: Multiplying by 11 means multiplying by 10 and adding the number once more. For a two-digit number, that lines the digits up so the middle digit is their sum.
When the digits add to 10 or more
Write down the units digit of the sum, and add 1 to the left-hand digit.

x: write 5 in the middle, carry 1 to the 7

deep.x: Longer numbers
The same pattern works for any length: keep the end digits, and in between add each neighbouring pair.
Testing for 11
There's a matching check. Alternately add and subtract the digits. If the result is 0 or a multiple of 11, so is the number.
Powers of 11 copy rows of Pascal's triangle: 11² = 121, 11³ = 1,331, 11⁴ = 14,641. From 11⁵ onwards the carries spoil the pattern.
To multiply a two-digit number by 11, put the sum of its digits in the middle.

cards.title: Quadrados terminados em 5
cards.text: Para elevar ao quadrado um número terminado em 5, multiplique a primeira parte pelo número seguinte e acrescente 25 no final: 35² = (3 × 4) e depois 25 = 1,225.

deep.x: The trick comes straight from algebra. A number ending in 5 can be written as 10a + 5, where a is the part before the 5. Squaring it gives 100 × a × (a + 1) + 25. So the answer is always "a times the next number up", followed by 25.
Halves work too
For a number ending in .5, the ending becomes .25.
A wider family
The same idea works for any pair with the same tens digit whose units add to 10.
45² = 2,025, so 2025 was a perfect square year. The next one is 2116, which is 46².
A number ending in 5, squared, is "n times n + 1" followed by 25.

cards.title: Dobrar e dividir ao meio
cards.text: Divida um número por 2 e dobre o outro: o produto não muda. 16 × 25 = 8 × 50 = 4 × 100 = 400.

deep.x: A product doesn't change if you multiply one number by 2 and divide the other by 2: the 2s cancel. Keep going until one number becomes friendly, such as 10, 50 or 100.
Not just 2
Any factor works, as long as you divide one number by what you multiply the other by.
An ancient method

**Russian peasant multiplication**, also used in ancient Egypt, is built entirely on doubling and halving. Halve the left column (dropping remainders), double the right, then add the right-hand numbers next to odd left-hand ones.
It works because it's secretly writing 13 in binary (8 + 4 + 1), the same base-2 system computers use to multiply.

deep.w: Changing both numbers changes the answer
deep.r: If one number is doubled and the other halved, the product is exactly the same.

deep.x: Halve one number and double the other; the product stays the same.

cards.title: Decomponha
cards.text: Separe multiplicações difíceis: 7 × 48 = 7 × 50 − 7 × 2 = 350 − 14 = 336.

deep.x: Multiplication spreads over addition and subtraction: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c. This is called the **distributive law**, and it's the engine behind almost every mental multiplication.
Split up or split down
The grid method
Many schools teach this as the grid or box method. Split both numbers into tens and units, multiply each pair, then add the boxes.
The long multiplication you learned at school is the same idea, just written in columns.

deep.w: Split both numbers and multiply the pieces: (20 + 3)(10 + 2) = 200 + 6
deep.r: You need all four cross-products: 200 + 40 + 30 + 6 = 276.

deep.x: Split an awkward number into friendly parts, multiply each part, and add the results.

cards.title: Critérios de divisibilidade
cards.text: Um número é divisível por 3 se a soma dos seus algarismos for múltiplo de 3; por 9 se for múltiplo de 9; por 4 se os dois últimos algarismos formarem um múltiplo de 4.

deep.x: These tests work because of how 10 behaves. 10 is one more than 9, so 10, 100, 1,000 all leave a remainder of 1 when divided by 9 (or by 3). That means a number leaves the same remainder as the sum of its digits.

x: 18 is a multiple of 9, so 7,236 ÷ 9 works (804)
last two digits 36 ÷ 4 = 9, so it divides by 4 too

deep.x: Why the last two digits for 4?
100 is a multiple of 4, so all the hundreds divide by 4 anyway. Only the last two digits can spoil it. The same logic gives the test for 8: 1,000 divides by 8, so check the last three digits.
Casting out nines
Digit sums can also check a calculation. Reduce each number to a single digit by adding its digits, then do the same sum on those.
It catches most slips, though not a swap of two digits, which leaves the digit sum unchanged.

Check digits use the same idea. The last digit of a Portuguese NIF (tax number) is calculated with a remainder test on division by 11, so most typing errors are caught automatically. IBANs use division by 97.
Our number system is built on 10, so remainders by 3, 9, 2, 4 and 5 can be read from the digits.

cards.title: Estime primeiro
cards.text: Antes de calcular, faça uma estimativa. 49 × 21 dá cerca de 50 × 20 = 1,000; se a sua resposta for 10,290, algo deu errado.

deep.x: An estimate is a quick answer you can trust roughly, made by rounding numbers to one or two significant figures. Its job isn't to be exact. Its job is to catch answers that are wildly wrong.
What estimates catch

x: **Decimal point slips**: €3.95 × 12 should be about €4 × 12 = €48 (exact: €47.40), not €474
**Wrong button on the calculator**: 230 ÷ 5 is about 50, so 1,150 means you pressed ×
**Unit mix-ups**: grams versus kilos, cents versus euros

deep.x: Rounding up and down
Rounding one number up and the other down often cancels the error, as in 49 × 21. Rounding both the same way gives a deliberately high or low answer, which is useful for budgets.
Fermi estimates

The physicist Enrico Fermi was famous for rough answers to big questions. How many heartbeats in a day? About 70 a minute × 60 × 24 ≈ 100,000. The exact product is 100,800, so the estimate lands within 1%.
In 1999 NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one team used imperial units and another metric. A quick sanity check of the numbers could have caught it.
Estimate before you calculate, so a wrong answer looks wrong.

cards.title: Contar para cima para dar o troco
cards.text: Os comerciantes dão o troco contando para cima. Pagando €20 por €13,65: até €14 são 35 centavos, até €20 são €6, então €6,35.

deep.x: Subtraction and "how much do I need to add?" are the same question. Counting up from the smaller number avoids borrowing, which is where most subtraction mistakes happen.
Use landmark numbers
Jump to the next round number, then to the next, and add up the jumps.
This is often called the **shopkeeper's method**, and it's how many people taught themselves arithmetic behind a till.
Fewest coins
To give change with as few coins as possible, take the biggest coin that fits, then repeat. With euro coins (1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 cents, €1 and €2) this simple rule always gives the minimum.

Several euro countries, including Finland, the Netherlands, Belgium and Ireland, round cash totals to the nearest 5 cents, so 1- and 2-cent coins are rarely needed there. Card payments are still charged to the exact cent.

deep.w: Subtraction has to be done right to left with borrowing
deep.r: Counting up from the smaller number gives the same answer, often with fewer slips.

deep.x: To subtract, count up from the smaller number in easy jumps.

cards.title: Converter temperaturas
cards.text: De Celsius para Fahrenheit, aproximadamente: dobre e some 30. 20 °C ≈ 70 °F (exatamente 68). Para o valor exato, multiplique por 1,8 e some 32.

deep.x: The exact rule is °F = °C × 1.8 + 32. The two scales disagree in two ways: a Celsius degree is 1.8 times bigger, and their zeros are in different places (water freezes at 0 °C but 32 °F).
How good is "double and add 30"?
Doubling slightly overdoes the 1.8, and 30 slightly underdoes the 32. The two errors cancel exactly at 10 °C, and the gap grows the further you go.
The other way
Reverse each step: subtract 32, then divide by 1.8. Roughly: subtract 30 and halve.
Landmarks worth knowing
Anders Celsius's original 1742 scale ran backwards: 0 was boiling and 100 was freezing. It was flipped soon after his death.
Exact: multiply by 1.8 and add 32. Rough: double and add 30, best near 10 °C.
