Quanto é 45²?

cards.title: O que é álgebra
cards.text: A álgebra usa letras para números que ainda não conhecemos. "Um número mais 5 é 12" vira x + 5 = 12, então x = 7.

deep.x: Algebra is arithmetic with a placeholder. A letter stands for a number you don't know yet, or for any number at all. Once it has a name, you can reason about it with the same rules you already use for 3s and 7s.
Unknowns and variables

In x + 5 = 12, x is an **unknown**: one particular number to find. In a formula like cost = 2 × n, n is a **variable**: it can be anything, and the cost follows. The same letter does both jobs in different settings.
Why bother with letters?
Letters let you prove something works for every number, not just the ones you tried. Take the classic party trick.
Whatever number someone picks, the answer is 5. Trying examples suggests it; the algebra proves it.
Writing it the short way

x: Numbers go in front of letters: 3x, not x3
Letters next to each other multiply: ab means a × b

deep.x: The habit of using x, y and z for unknowns comes from René Descartes's book *La Géométrie* in 1637. He used a, b and c for known quantities.

deep.w: Algebra is a different kind of maths
deep.r: It's ordinary arithmetic with names for numbers you haven't pinned down yet.

deep.x: A letter is just a number that hasn't been revealed yet, and it obeys all the usual rules.

cards.title: Mantenha o equilíbrio
cards.text: Uma equação é uma balança: o que você fizer de um lado, faça também do outro. Subtraia 5 dos dois lados de x + 5 = 12 para obter x = 7.

deep.x: Picture a pair of kitchen scales with x + 5 on one pan and 12 on the other, perfectly level. Take 5 off one side and it tips, unless you take 5 off the other too. That's the only rule of solving equations.
What you're allowed to do

x: Add or subtract the same amount on both sides
Multiply or divide both sides by the same number
Never divide by zero: that is how fake "proofs" that 1 = 2 are built

deep.x: Always check
Put your answer back into the original equation. If both sides match, you're right.
"Move it across and change the sign"

Many people learn this shortcut. It works, but it hides the reason. Moving +5 across to become −5 is really subtracting 5 from both sides in one go. Knowing that stops you from "moving" things that can't be moved, like half a bracket.

items.r: do the same to both sides

deep.x: The equals sign was invented by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557. He chose two parallel lines because "no two things can be more equal".
An equation stays true as long as you do the same thing to both sides.

cards.title: Equações de dois passos
cards.text: 3x + 4 = 19: subtraia 4 dos dois lados (3x = 15) e depois divida ambos por 3 (x = 5). Desfaça as operações na ordem inversa.

deep.x: Think of the equation as a recipe done to x: multiply by 3, then add 4, and you get 19. To get back to x, undo each step in the reverse order, just as you take off shoes before socks.
Unknowns on both sides
First gather the x terms on one side, then solve as usual. Moving the smaller x term avoids negatives.
Why the order matters
If you divide by 3 first, you must divide everything, including the 4. It still works, but you get fractions: x + 4/3 = 19/3. Undoing the last operation first keeps the numbers clean.

deep.w: Do the operations in the order you see them
deep.r: Undo them in reverse: the last thing done to x is the first thing you remove.

deep.x: Undo operations in reverse order, doing each to both sides.

cards.title: De onde ela veio
cards.text: A palavra "álgebra" vem de *al-jabr*, "restauração", no título do livro de al-Khwarizmi, escrito em Bagdá no século IX. As letras para as incógnitas vieram depois, com François Viète, na década de 1590.

deep.x: Around 820 in Baghdad, at a scholarly centre known as the House of Wisdom, Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on solving equations "by completion and balancing". **Al-jabr**, "restoring", meant moving a subtracted amount to the other side to make it positive. **Al-muqabala**, "balancing", meant cancelling equal amounts on both sides.
Algebra in words

Al-Khwarizmi wrote everything in sentences, with no symbols at all. A problem like x² + 10x = 39 was written out as "a square and ten roots equal thirty-nine". He solved it geometrically, by completing a square.
Earlier and later

Babylonian scribes solved similar problems on clay tablets nearly 4,000 years ago. Around the 3rd century, Diophantus of Alexandria used abbreviations. Full symbolic algebra took until the 1590s, when François Viète used letters for both unknowns and knowns.
A Portuguese chapter
The Portuguese mathematician Pedro Nunes, royal cosmographer and a pioneer of navigation, published a *Book of Algebra* in 1567, one of the important algebra texts of 16th-century Europe.
In old Spanish an *algebrista* was a bone-setter, someone who "restored" broken bones. The word appears with that meaning in *Don Quixote*.
Algebra began as a method for balancing and restoring equations, written in words long before letters took over.

cards.title: Fórmulas são álgebra
cards.text: Toda fórmula é álgebra: área = comprimento × largura, velocidade = distância ÷ tempo. Reorganizá-las permite descobrir qualquer parte que esteja faltando.

deep.x: A formula is an equation that links several quantities. Know all but one, and algebra gives you the last. Rearranging uses exactly the same balance rule as solving.

x: A room is 4.5 m wide with an area of 18 m²

deep.x: Rearranging step by step
To make one letter the subject, undo what's been done to it, both sides at a time.
Formulas at home
European mains electricity is 230 volts, so a 2,200-watt kettle draws about 9.6 amps. That's why a kettle and a heater on one extension lead can trip a fuse.
Check the units
Units obey algebra too. km ÷ km/h leaves hours; m² ÷ m leaves metres. If the units come out wrong, the formula is upside down.

deep.w: A formula only works one way round
deep.r: Any letter can be made the subject, as long as you do the same to both sides.

deep.x: Every formula is an equation, so you can rearrange it to find whichever piece is missing.

cards.title: Eliminar parênteses
cards.text: Multiplique tudo o que está dentro pelo que está fora: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12. Também ajuda no cálculo mental: 3 × 104 = 300 + 12.

deep.x: A bracket means "treat this as one number". Multiplying it by 3 means three lots of everything inside, so every term gets multiplied. This is the distributive law again.
Mental maths with brackets
Two brackets
With two brackets, every term in the first multiplies every term in the second: four products in all. Picture a rectangle split into four smaller ones.
A special case is worth knowing: (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b², because the middle terms cancel.
Going backwards: factorising
Taking a common factor out is the reverse. 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3). Factorising is a key step in solving harder equations.

deep.w: (a + b)² is just a² + b²
deep.r: Try 3 and 4: (3 + 4)² = 49, but 9 + 16 = 25. The missing 24 is the 2ab.

deep.x: Multiply every term inside the bracket by what's outside, and every term by every term with two brackets.

cards.title: Duas incógnitas
cards.text: Dois cafés e um bolo custam €5; um café e um bolo custam €3,50. Subtraia: um café custa €1,50, então o bolo custa €2. Isso é um sistema de equações.

deep.x: One equation with two unknowns has endless answers. A second, different equation pins them down. The coffee example uses **elimination**: subtracting one equation from the other removes the cake.
Substitution
The other method: rearrange one equation for one letter, and put it into the other.

x: Adult and child tickets: a + c = 11 and 2a + 3c = 27

deep.x: The picture behind it
Each equation with two unknowns is a straight line on a graph. The solution is where the lines cross.
The general rule
You usually need as many independent equations as unknowns. Three unknowns need three equations, and so on.
Your phone's GPS solves a system of equations. It needs signals from at least four satellites to find four unknowns: your three position coordinates and the exact time.
To find two unknowns you need two equations; combine them to eliminate one.

cards.title: Sinais negativos
cards.text: Subtrair um número negativo é somar: 5 − (−3) = 8. Multiplicar dois negativos dá um positivo: (−2) × (−3) = 6.

deep.x: A number line makes negatives concrete. Adding moves right, subtracting moves left. A negative number reverses the direction. So subtracting −3 is moving left in reverse, which means moving right by 3.
Think of money: cancelling a €3 debt leaves you €3 better off. Taking away a negative is adding.
Why negative × negative is positive
Follow the pattern. Each step down, the answer goes up by 2, and the pattern only continues if (−1) × (−2) = 2.
The calculator trap
Order of operations matters. −3² means −(3²) = −9, but (−3)² = 9. Many calculators and spreadsheets treat these differently, so use brackets.
A slow acceptance

In 628 CE the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote rules for "fortunes" and "debts", including that a debt times a debt is a fortune. Many European mathematicians distrusted negative numbers until the 1600s and 1700s.
Chinese counting rods used red for positive and black for negative, the opposite of Western bookkeeping, where being "in the red" means owing money.
Subtracting a negative adds, and two negatives multiplied give a positive.

cards.title: Sequências como fórmulas
cards.text: Em 3, 5, 7, 9…, cada termo é 2n + 1. Ache o 100º termo sem listar todos: 2 × 100 + 1 = 201.

deep.x: A sequence that goes up by the same amount each time is an **arithmetic sequence**. Its formula always has the form (step) × n + (adjustment), where n is the position.
Finding the formula
The difference between terms gives the number in front of n. Then adjust to make the first term right.

x: n = 1 gives 4, but we need 7: add 3

deep.x: Adding them up
A story says the young Carl Friedrich Gauss added 1 to 100 in moments. Pair the first and last, the second and second-last: each pair makes 101, and there are 50 pairs.
Not every sequence is arithmetic
The square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16… have differences 3, 5, 7, which themselves go up by 2: a sign of n². Doubling sequences like 1, 2, 4, 8 multiply rather than add.

deep.w: You need to list terms to find a far-off one
deep.r: A formula jumps straight to the 100th or the millionth term.

deep.x: Find the rule linking position to value, and any term is one calculation away.

cards.title: Um problema real
cards.text: Um plano de celular custa €10 por mês mais €0,05 por MB. Com €15 por mês, quantos MB você pode usar? 10 + 0,05m = 15, então m = 100 MB.

deep.x: Word problems follow a routine. Name the unknown, turn the words into an equation, solve, then check the answer makes sense in the real situation.
Fixed cost plus a rate

Many bills have this shape: a fixed charge plus a price per unit. Taxis, electricity, gym memberships and phone plans all do. On a graph it's a straight line: the fixed charge is where it starts, the rate is how steeply it climbs.
Comparing two plans
Suppose Plan B is €20 a month, unlimited. Where do the plans cost the same?

x: below 200 MB Plan A is cheaper, above it Plan B wins

deep.x: This **break-even point** is the question behind most "which deal is better?" decisions.
"At most" means an inequality
With a €15 budget, you can use up to 100 MB, not exactly 100: 10 + 0.05m ≤ 15 gives m ≤ 100. Inequalities are solved the same way as equations.
Flipping an inequality needs care: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the sign. −2m < 6 becomes m > −3.
Name the unknown, translate the words into an equation, solve, then check it makes sense.

quiz.q: Resolva 3x + 4 = 19.
Quanto é 5 − (−3)?

cards.title: Linear versus exponencial
cards.text: O crescimento linear soma a mesma quantidade a cada passo; o exponencial multiplica. O exponencial começa devagar e depois explode.

deep.x: Linear growth adds a fixed amount each step. Exponential growth multiplies by a fixed factor. Early on, adding can look faster. But a multiplier works on an ever-bigger base, so it always overtakes in the end.
Money grows exponentially
Simple interest is linear. Compound interest, where you earn interest on interest, is exponential.
The rule of 70
To find how long something growing at a steady percentage takes to double, divide 70 by the percentage.
The same rule works for inflation: at 3% a year, prices double in about 23 years.

deep.w: Steady percentage growth is steady growth
deep.r: A fixed percentage adds more each year, because it's a share of a growing amount.

deep.x: Linear adds the same each step; exponential multiplies, and multiplying always wins in the end.

cards.title: A lenda do tabuleiro de xadrez
cards.text: Coloque 1 grão de arroz na primeira casa, 2 na seguinte, depois 4, 8… Na casa 64, você precisaria de cerca de 18 quintilhões de grãos, muito mais do que todo o arroz já cultivado.

deep.x: The legend, told in many versions, has a king offering the inventor of chess any reward. The inventor asks for rice: one grain on the first square, doubling on each square after. The king laughs at such a modest request, until the grain stores run out.
The numbers
Square n holds 2 to the power (n − 1) grains. Add them all and you get one less than the next power of 2.
How much rice is that?
The world grows roughly 500 million tonnes of milled rice a year. The board would need several centuries of today's entire harvest.
Each square beats all before it
Every square holds one more grain than all the previous squares combined. Square 10 has 512 grains; squares 1 to 9 hold 511 between them. This is why doubling feels so sudden.

The phrase "the second half of the chessboard" was popularised by the inventor Ray Kurzweil for the point when exponential technology growth becomes enormous. The first half holds about 4 billion grains, roughly 100 tonnes; the second half holds the rest.
With repeated doubling, each step is bigger than everything that came before it combined.

cards.title: O lago das vitórias-régias
cards.text: As plantas dobram a cada dia e cobrem um lago no dia 30. Quando ele estava coberto pela metade? No dia 29. Problemas exponenciais parecem pequenos até o finalzinho.

deep.x: The answer, day 29, feels wrong because our instincts are linear. Halfway in coverage is not halfway in time. With doubling, the pond is only half full one day before the end.
Why it matters

On day 25, a glance at the pond shows almost open water. Someone might say there's plenty of time. In fact, only five days are left. Many real problems, from debts to outbreaks, look the same way: tiny for a long time, then suddenly overwhelming.
Buying more time doesn't buy much
Suppose you discover three more ponds just as big. Four ponds is four times the space, but doubling fills that in just two more days.
The riddle is often told as a French children's puzzle. It was made famous by the 1972 report *The Limits to Growth*, which used it to warn about resource use.

deep.w: If something's small now, there's lots of time
deep.r: With doubling, "small" can be one or two steps from "everything".

deep.x: With doubling, the last step is as big as all the steps before it.

cards.title: Potências
cards.text: 2⁵ significa 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. As potências são uma forma abreviada de multiplicação repetida. Qualquer número elevado a 0 é 1.

deep.x: A power has a **base** (the number being multiplied) and an **exponent** (how many times it's used). In 2⁵ the base is 2 and the exponent is 5.
The rules come from counting

x: Power of a power: (2³)² = 2⁶, so multiply them

deep.x: Why anything to the power 0 is 1
Go down the pattern: each step divides by 2. The rules demand it too: 2³ ÷ 2³ = 2⁰, and anything divided by itself is 1.
Scientific notation
Powers of 10 tame huge and tiny numbers. The Earth is about 1.5 × 10⁸ km from the Sun; a hydrogen atom is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m across. The exponent tells you how many places to move the decimal point.
0⁰ is a genuine puzzle. Most mathematicians and calculators treat it as 1 because that keeps formulas tidy, but some say it should stay undefined.

deep.w: A negative power gives a negative number
deep.r: 2⁻³ = 1/8, a small positive number. The minus means "divide", not "below zero".

deep.x: A power is repeated multiplication, and its rules all follow from counting the factors.

cards.title: Logaritmos
cards.text: Um logaritmo pergunta: "qual expoente?" log₁₀ 1,000 = 3, porque 10³ = 1,000. Os logaritmos transformam multiplicações enormes em somas simples.

deep.x: A logarithm undoes a power. Since 10³ = 1,000, log₁₀ 1,000 = 3. For whole powers of 10, the log is just the number of zeros. For any number, it's roughly "how many digits, minus a bit".
Multiplying by adding
Because 10ᵃ × 10ᵇ = 10ᵃ⁺ᵇ, the log of a product is the sum of the logs. Before calculators, this turned slow multiplication into fast addition with a table.
Other bases

x: **Base 2** counts doublings: log₂ 1,024 = 10. Reaching a million takes about 20 doublings.
**Base e** (about 2.718), the "natural log", appears wherever growth is continuous, from interest to radioactive decay

deep.x: A centuries-old shortcut

The Scottish mathematician John Napier published logarithms in 1614. Astronomers, navigators and engineers relied on log tables and slide rules for over 350 years, including for the Apollo Moon missions.
The French mathematician Laplace is said to have remarked that logarithms, by shortening months of calculation into days, effectively doubled astronomers' working lives.
A logarithm asks "what power?", and it turns multiplying into adding.

cards.title: Escalas logarítmicas ao nosso redor
cards.text: A escala de terremotos do tipo Richter, os decibéis e o pH usam logaritmos. Cada grau a mais de magnitude significa cerca de 32 vezes mais energia liberada.

deep.x: A log scale goes up by multiplying, not adding. Each step means "times 10" (or another factor). It's the natural choice for things that vary over enormous ranges, from a whisper to a jet engine.
Earthquakes

Seismologists now use the **moment magnitude** scale, which replaced Charles Richter's 1935 scale but feels the same. Each whole step is about 10 times the ground shaking and about 32 times the energy (10 to the power 1.5).
The 1755 Lisbon earthquake is estimated at about magnitude 8.5 to 9; no instruments existed then. The largest ever recorded was in Chile in 1960, at 9.5.
Sound
Decibels compress sound into a manageable range. About +3 dB doubles the sound energy, but your ears judge something as "twice as loud" only at about +10 dB.

deep.w: A magnitude 8 is twice as strong as a magnitude 4
deep.r: Four steps is about 32⁴, roughly a million times more energy.

deep.x: Musical pitch is a log scale too. The A above middle C is 440 Hz; each octave higher doubles it, to 880 Hz and then 1,760 Hz.
On a log scale each step multiplies, so small differences in the number hide huge differences in reality.

cards.title: Como os vírus se espalham
cards.text: Se cada pessoa infectada contamina outras 2 a cada poucos dias, os casos dobram. Trazer esse número para baixo de 1 faz a epidemia encolher.

deep.x: The key number is **R**, the average number of people each infected person goes on to infect. If R is above 1, each "generation" of cases is bigger than the last. If it's below 1, each is smaller, and the outbreak fades.
A small change in R makes a huge difference over time, because it is compounded every generation.
What drives R

x: How many people an infected person meets
How likely each contact is to pass it on
How many people are already immune

deep.x: Herd immunity
If a fraction of people are immune, fewer contacts can be infected. Once at least 1 − 1/R₀ of the population is immune (R₀ is the starting R), the epidemic can't grow.
Measles is among the most contagious diseases known. That's why vaccination coverage of about 95% is the usual target for it.
Keep R below 1 and an epidemic shrinks; above 1, it grows exponentially.

cards.title: A lei de Moore
cards.text: Em 1965, Gordon Moore percebeu que o número de transistores nos chips dobrava mais ou menos a cada dois anos. Isso se manteve por décadas e impulsionou a revolução digital.

deep.x: In a 1965 article, Gordon Moore, who later co-founded Intel, predicted that the number of components on a chip would double every year. In 1975 he revised it to about every two years. It's not a law of nature, but an observation that the industry turned into a target.
Checking the maths
Doubling every two years for 50 years is 25 doublings.

x: close to the biggest real chips of the early 2020s

deep.x: Why it's slowing

x: Transistor features are now only tens of atoms across
Each new factory costs tens of billions of euros
Chips now gain more from clever design and stacking than from shrinking alone

deep.x: A European link
The most advanced chips are patterned with extreme ultraviolet light, using machines made by ASML in the Netherlands, the only company that makes them. Each machine costs well over €100 million.
Gordon Moore lived to see his observation hold for more than half a century. He died in 2023, aged 94.

deep.w: Moore's law is a law of physics
deep.r: It's an industry trend that held for decades because companies worked hard to keep it going.

deep.x: Doubling every two years for half a century turned thousands of transistors into tens of billions.

cards.title: Meia-vida
cards.text: As substâncias radioativas decaem de forma exponencial. Depois de uma meia-vida, resta a metade; depois de duas, um quarto. A meia-vida de 5,730 anos do carbono-14 permite datar restos antigos.

deep.x: Exponential decay is growth in reverse: instead of doubling at a steady rate, the amount halves. Each atom has a fixed chance of decaying in a given time, so the total shrinks by the same fraction in each half-life.
How carbon dating works
Living things take in carbon-14 at a steady level while alive. When they die, it decays without being replaced. Measuring what's left gives the time since death.

x: A bone has 25% of its original carbon-14

deep.x: After about 50,000 years less than 0.3% remains, which is too little to measure reliably. Older things are dated by other methods. Willard Libby developed the technique and won the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Half-lives vary enormously

deep.w: After two half-lives it's all gone
deep.r: Each half-life halves what's left: after two, a quarter remains; after ten, about 0.1%.

deep.x: You can't predict when a single atom will decay. The half-life is a statement about huge numbers of atoms, which is why it's so reliable.
Each half-life removes half of whatever is left, so the amount shrinks but never jumps to zero.

cards.title: Dobrar papel
cards.text: Uma folha de papel com cerca de 0,1 mm de espessura, dobrada 42 vezes, teria mais de 400,000 km de espessura, passando da Lua. Na prática, não dá para dobrar papel mais do que umas 7 vezes à mão.

deep.x: Each fold doubles the thickness. That's 2 to the power of the number of folds, multiplied by the thickness of one sheet.

x: the Moon is about 384,000 km away

items.b: about 840 m, taller than any tower

deep.x: Why you can't actually do it

Each fold halves the area while doubling the thickness. Soon the paper is a tiny, stiff block, far thicker than it is wide. The curve at each fold also uses up paper, and that loss grows with every layer.
The record

In 2002 Britney Gallivan, an American high-school student, worked out a formula for how long a strip of paper must be to fold it in half n times. Then she did it: 12 folds, using a strip of thin paper about a kilometre long.
51 folds would take the stack about 225 million km, beyond the Sun, which is about 150 million km away.

deep.w: Each fold adds a little thickness
deep.r: Each fold doubles all the thickness so far, which is why the numbers explode.

deep.x: Doubling a tiny amount just 42 times gets you to the Moon.

quiz.q: Um lago fica totalmente coberto no dia 30, e a cobertura dobra a cada dia. Quando estava coberto pela metade?
Quanto é log₁₀ 1,000?

lessons.title: Gráficos e funções
lessons.summary: Ver relações num piscar de olhos.

cards.title: O que é uma função
cards.text: Uma função é uma regra que transforma cada entrada em exatamente uma saída, como uma máquina: coloque 3, e a regra "multiplique por 2" dá 6.

deep.x: A function is a promise of predictability. Give it the same input and it always gives the same output. That is what lets you trust a recipe, a tax table or a currency converter: the rule never changes its mind.
The one-output rule

A rule can send many inputs to the same output, but never one input to several outputs. "Square it" sends both 2 and −2 to 4, and that's fine. "Give me a number whose square is 4" is not a function, because it has two answers.
Writing it down
Mathematicians write f(x) = 2x, read "f of x". The notation was popularised by Leonhard Euler in the 1730s. The set of allowed inputs is the **domain**; the outputs it can produce are the **range**.
On a graph, a function passes the "vertical line test": any vertical line hits the curve at most once, because each x has only one y.

deep.w: A function must use a formula
deep.r: Any rule that gives exactly one output counts, even a lookup table or a list of birthdays

deep.x: A function is a reliable machine: same input in, same output out, every time.

cards.title: Coordenadas
cards.text: A ideia de Descartes: descrever qualquer ponto com dois números, (x, y): quanto para o lado e quanto para cima. Isso uniu a álgebra e a geometria.

deep.x: Before coordinates, algebra (equations) and geometry (shapes) were separate subjects. René Descartes, in his 1637 book *La Géométrie*, showed that every point could be named by two numbers. Suddenly a circle became an equation and an equation became a picture.
Four quadrants

Negative numbers let you go left of and below the origin, so the plane splits into four quarters. The point (−2, 3) is two steps left and three up. Order matters: (3, −2) is a completely different place.
Coordinates everywhere

x: GPS uses latitude and longitude: Lisbon is about 38.7° N, 9.1° W
A phone screen locates every pixel by (x, y), though y usually counts downwards from the top
Board games like chess (e4, d5) and Battleship use a coordinate grid
Spreadsheet cells like C7 are column-and-row coordinates

deep.x: A popular story says Descartes got the idea watching a fly crawl on his ceiling and wondering how to describe its position. It's probably a legend, but it captures the idea perfectly.
Two numbers can pin down any point on a flat surface, and that turns shapes into algebra.

cards.title: Retas
cards.text: y = mx + c desenha uma reta: m é a inclinação (o quanto ela sobe), c é onde ela corta o eixo y.

deep.x: In y = mx + c, every value of x gives one y, and all those points line up perfectly. The two numbers m and c are all you need to know about the line: its tilt and its starting height.
What the slope says

x: m positive: the line climbs from left to right
m = 0: it's flat, a horizontal line
Same m, different c: parallel lines that never meet

deep.x: A road sign showing 10% means a slope of 0.1: you rise 10 m for every 100 m travelled horizontally. Portugal's steepest streets, like some in Lisbon's Alfama, go well beyond 15%.
Finding a line from two points
Two points are enough to fix a straight line. Work out the slope first, then the crossing point.

deep.w: A steeper line has a bigger c
deep.r: Steepness is m; c only slides the line up or down

deep.x: Slope tells you how steep, intercept tells you where it starts: two numbers describe every straight line.

cards.title: A corrida de táxi
cards.text: Um táxi cobra €3,50 de bandeirada mais €1,20 por km. Tarifa = 1,2 × km + 3,5: uma reta. 10 km custam €15,50.

deep.x: The taxi fare is a perfect real-life straight line. The €3.50 is the intercept: you pay it even for zero kilometres. The €1.20 per km is the slope: each extra kilometre adds the same amount.
Comparing two offers
Suppose a ride app charges €2.00 to start but €1.50 per km. Which is cheaper? Set the two lines equal and solve.

x: k = 5 km: below 5 km the app wins, above it the taxi wins

deep.x: Why the start fee matters

The fixed charge makes short trips expensive per kilometre. A 1 km ride costs €4.70, which is €4.70 per km; a 20 km ride costs €27.50, only about €1.38 per km. The longer you go, the closer the average gets to the slope.

items.b: where two offers cost the same

deep.x: Real taxi meters also charge for waiting time and night rates, so the true graph is made of several straight pieces.
Fixed cost plus cost per unit is a straight line, and comparing deals means finding where the lines cross.

cards.title: Inclinação é taxa
cards.text: A inclinação é uma taxa de variação: euros por km, km por hora, graus por minuto. Retas mais inclinadas significam mudanças mais rápidas.

deep.x: A slope always has units: the y-units divided by the x-units. On a distance–time graph the slope is km per hour, which is speed. On a cost graph it's euros per item. Reading the units tells you what the slope means.

x: A train covers 120 km in 1.5 h

deep.x: Negative and zero slopes

A falling line has a negative slope: something decreasing. A phone battery going from 100% to 60% in 8 hours has a slope of −5% per hour. A flat line means no change at all, like a parked car on a distance–time graph.
Average versus instant

The slope between two points is an average rate. If you drove Porto to Lisbon (about 310 km) in 3 hours, your average was about 103 km/h, even though you stopped for coffee and sped up on the motorway. The rate at a single instant needs calculus.

deep.w: A steeper line on any graph means faster
deep.r: Only if both graphs use the same scales; stretch an axis and any line looks steep

deep.x: Every slope is a rate: something per something, read straight off the units.

cards.title: Curvas
cards.text: y = x² forma uma curva em U chamada parábola. Uma bola jogada para o alto segue uma, e as antenas parabólicas usam essa forma para concentrar os sinais.

deep.x: In y = x², doubling x makes y four times bigger. That's why the parabola starts gently and then shoots upwards. It's symmetric: the left arm mirrors the right, meeting at the lowest point, the **vertex**.
Thrown balls
Galileo showed around 1638 that a thrown object follows a parabola, if you ignore air resistance. Gravity pulls it down at a steady rate while it moves sideways at a steady speed.

x: Ball thrown straight up at 20 m/s
peak at t ≈ 2.0 s, h ≈ 20.4 m

deep.x: Satellite dishes and headlights

A parabola has a special point, the **focus**. Signals arriving parallel to the dish's axis all bounce to the focus, so a dish collects a weak signal from a huge area into one receiver. Car headlights and torches work in reverse: a bulb at the focus sends out a parallel beam.
Squares in everyday life
Braking distance grows roughly with the square of speed. Driving at 100 km/h instead of 50 km/h doubles your speed but roughly quadruples the braking distance.

deep.w: A hanging chain makes a parabola
deep.r: It makes a catenary, a slightly different curve; Galileo got this one wrong

deep.x: Squaring makes change accelerate, and that U-shape shows up from football kicks to satellite dishes.

cards.title: Como ler gráficos

items: O que há em cada eixo?

cards.text: Antes de ler um gráfico, confira o que cada eixo mostra, as unidades e a escala. Depois observe a forma geral antes dos detalhes.

deep.x: A graph is an argument in picture form, and pictures can mislead. Spending ten seconds on the axes, units and scale protects you from most tricks.
Common traps

x: **Truncated axis**: a bar chart starting at 95 instead of 0 makes 97 look twice as tall as 96
**Log scale**: each step is ×10, so a straight line means steady percentage growth, not steady growth
**Two y-axes**: you can make any two trends appear to move together by stretching one
**Cumulative totals**: they can only go up, which can hide that things are slowing down
an axis starting at €95k makes it look like tripling

deep.x: Shape before detail

Ask first: is it going up, down or flat? Steady or speeding up? Are there jumps or outliers? Only then pick out individual values. Remember too that two lines moving together doesn't prove one causes the other.
Florence Nightingale used a circular chart in 1858 to show that more British soldiers in the Crimean War died of preventable disease than of battle wounds. It helped change army hospital policy.
Read the axes before you read the story.

cards.title: Formas de mudança
cards.text: Retas mostram mudança constante; curvas que sobem cada vez mais mostram aceleração; curvas que se achatam mostram saturação, como a bateria de um celular carregando.

deep.x: The shape of a graph tells you what kind of process you're looking at, often before you know any numbers. Four shapes cover a surprising amount of real life.
Examples

x: Steady: a tap filling a bath at 10 litres a minute
Accelerating: money with compound interest, or an early epidemic doubling every few days
Saturating: a cup of coffee cooling towards room temperature
S-curve: smartphone ownership, which crept up, then exploded, then levelled off as nearly everyone had one

deep.x: Why phones charge that way

Lithium-ion batteries charge quickly at first with a constant current. Near the top the charger switches to constant voltage and the current tapers off to protect the battery. That's why 0–50% can take 20–30 minutes on many phones, while the last 20% feels slow.

deep.w: Growth that is speeding up will keep speeding up
deep.r: Most real growth hits a limit and bends into an S-curve

deep.x: Learn to recognise the shape and you know what kind of change you're dealing with.

cards.title: Relações inversas
cards.text: Algumas grandezas andam em sentidos opostos: o tempo de viagem cai quando a velocidade sobe. O gráfico desce em curva sem nunca chegar a zero.

deep.x: In an inverse relationship, two quantities multiply to a constant. Distance = speed × time, so for a fixed journey, double the speed and you halve the time.
speed × time = distance (fixed), so time = distance ÷ speed
Why the curve never touches zero

However fast you go, the time can shrink towards zero but never reach it. And as speed approaches zero, time grows without limit. The graph, called a **hyperbola**, hugs both axes without touching them.
Diminishing returns
Because of this shape, the same speed increase saves very different amounts of time.

x: saves 5 min, and a cyclist from 15 to 20 km/h saves 10 min

items: Workers and days to finish a job
Pressure and volume of a gas

deep.x: Robert Boyle found in 1662 that squeezing a gas to half its volume doubles its pressure: another inverse relationship.

deep.w: Inverse means one goes up when the other goes down
deep.r: Not quite: many pairs do that; inverse means their product stays constant

deep.x: When two things multiply to a constant, doubling one halves the other.

cards.title: Funções no código
cards.text: Planilhas e programas estão cheios de funções: =SOMA(), =MÉDIA(). Cada uma recebe entradas e devolve uma saída, exatamente como na matemática.

deep.x: A spreadsheet formula is a function in action. =SUM(A1:A10) takes ten numbers as input and returns exactly one output. Change an input cell and the output updates, just as f(x) changes when x does.
Building bigger functions
Functions can be fed into each other, which mathematicians call **composition**. =ROUND(AVERAGE(B2:B30), 1) first averages, then rounds. In maths you'd write g(f(x)).
In programming

In Python you write `def double(x): return 2 * x`, which is the "double it" machine in four words. Programmers prize **pure functions**: ones that, like maths functions, give the same output for the same input and change nothing else. They're easier to test and to trust.
=RAND() and =NOW() are not functions in the mathematical sense: call them twice with the same (empty) input and you get different outputs.

deep.w: Programming functions and maths functions are unrelated
deep.r: Programming borrowed the idea directly from maths; the pure ones match it exactly

deep.x: Every formula you type into a spreadsheet is a little mathematical function.

Que forma tem o gráfico de y = x²?
options: Uma parábola em forma de U

cards.title: O que a teoria dos jogos estuda
cards.text: A teoria dos jogos estuda decisões em que a sua melhor escolha depende do que os outros fazem: negócios, política, biologia, até atravessar a rua.

deep.x: A "game" here is any situation with several decision-makers whose results depend on each other's choices. The players can be people, companies, countries, or even genes. Game theory asks: what's the smart move when everyone else is also thinking?
Where it came from

John von Neumann proved a key theorem in 1928, and in 1944 he and economist Oskar Morgenstern published *Theory of Games and Economic Behavior*. The field grew during the Cold War, then spread into economics, biology and computer science.
Everyday games

x: Choosing a price when a rival café across the street might undercut you
Deciding whether to step into the road when a driver might not stop
Bidding on a house against unknown buyers
Two countries deciding whether to cut emissions

deep.x: The key difference from ordinary decisions is that you must model what others will do, and they're modelling you.
Around a dozen Nobel prizes in economics have gone to game theorists, including John Nash in 1994 and the auction designers Paul Milgrom and Robert Wilson in 2020.

deep.w: Game theory is about games like chess and poker
deep.r: It's about any strategic interaction, from pricing to evolution

deep.x: Game theory is the maths of decisions that depend on other people's decisions.

cards.title: O dilema do prisioneiro
cards.text: Dois suspeitos podem ficar calados ou trair um ao outro. Trair é melhor para cada um individualmente, mas, se os dois traírem, ambos acabam pior do que se tivessem ficado calados.

deep.x: The dilemma was devised in 1950 by Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher at the RAND Corporation; Albert Tucker gave it the prison story. Two suspects are questioned in separate rooms and can't talk to each other.
Why betraying wins for each

Think as one prisoner. If the other stays silent, betraying gets you 0 years instead of 1. If the other betrays, betraying gets you 3 instead of 5. Whatever they do, betraying is better: it's a **dominant strategy**.

x: Total if both betray: 3 + 3 = 6, three times worse

deep.x: Why it matters
Each person's sensible choice leads to an outcome both dislike. The same structure appears whenever individual and group interests clash:
Escaping the dilemma needs something outside the game: contracts, laws, reputation, or the chance to meet again.

deep.w: The prisoners betray because they're selfish or stupid
deep.r: Betraying is the logical choice for each; the trap is in the structure, not the people

deep.x: Individually rational choices can add up to a collectively bad result.

cards.title: Equilíbrio de Nash
cards.text: Um equilíbrio de Nash é uma situação em que ninguém ganha mudando sozinho a sua escolha. John Nash, retratado em *Uma Mente Brilhante*, o definiu em 1950.

deep.x: At a Nash equilibrium, each player's choice is their best response to what everyone else is doing. No one can do better by changing alone, so nobody has a reason to move. It's a resting point, not necessarily a good one.

steps: Do the same for every player

deep.x: Examples

x: In the prisoner's dilemma, both betraying is the only equilibrium, even though both would prefer mutual silence
Driving on the right is an equilibrium in Portugal; so is driving on the left in the UK. Neither driver gains by switching alone
In rock-paper-scissors there's no stable pure choice; the equilibrium is to play each one a third of the time at random

deep.x: Nash's result

John Nash proved in his 1950 PhD thesis, about 27 pages long, that every game with a finite number of players and choices has at least one equilibrium, if players are allowed to randomise. He shared the 1994 Nobel prize in economics and won the Abel Prize in 2015.
Studies of professional football penalties found that kickers and goalkeepers mix their left and right choices remarkably close to what Nash equilibrium predicts.

deep.w: A Nash equilibrium is the best possible outcome
deep.r: It's only stable; everyone can be stuck in a worse place

deep.x: At a Nash equilibrium, no one can improve by changing their move alone.

cards.title: Jogos repetidos
cards.text: Quando o jogo se repete, a cooperação pode vencer. Nos torneios de computador de Robert Axelrod, nos anos 1980, o "olho por olho" (cooperar primeiro e depois copiar o outro) se saiu muito bem.

deep.x: A one-off prisoner's dilemma favours betrayal. But most relationships repeat: neighbours, colleagues, trading partners. When there's a tomorrow, today's betrayal can be punished, and cooperation becomes worth it. Axelrod called this "the shadow of the future".
Axelrod's tournaments

Political scientist Robert Axelrod invited experts to submit computer programs to play repeated prisoner's dilemmas against each other. The first tournament, in 1980, had 14 entries; the second had over 60. Both times, the winner was the shortest program: **tit for tat**, submitted by Anatol Rapoport.
Why it worked
Tit for tat never beats its partner in a single match; it can only tie or lose narrowly. It won by doing well with everyone, encouraging cooperation instead of exploiting.
In the trenches of World War I, opposing units sometimes settled into "live and let live": not shooting at meal times, answering any attack in kind. Axelrod used it as a real example of tit for tat.
With mistakes and misunderstandings, pure tit for tat can spiral into endless revenge. A "generous" version that sometimes forgives does better in noisy worlds.
When you'll meet again, being nice, firm and forgiving pays.

cards.title: Jogos de soma zero
cards.text: Nos jogos de soma zero, o ganho de um jogador é exatamente a perda do outro, como no pôquer ou no xadrez. A maior parte da vida, incluindo o comércio, não é de soma zero: os dois lados podem ganhar.

deep.x: In a zero-sum game the total prize is fixed, so the payoffs always add up to zero: my +10 is your −10. Pure competition, with no room for joint gains.
Von Neumann's minimax

In 1928 John von Neumann proved that every two-player zero-sum game with finite choices has a "value": a strategy that guarantees each side a certain result whatever the opponent does. You minimise your maximum possible loss.
Football isn't zero-sum

x: A win gives 3 + 0 = 3 points in total
so a league's total points depend on how many games are drawn

deep.x: That rule, introduced in England in 1981 and by FIFA for the 1994 World Cup, deliberately makes winning worth more than two draws.
Trade creates value

David Ricardo's 1817 example used Portugal and England. Portugal could make both wine and cloth with less labour, yet both countries gained when Portugal specialised in wine and England in cloth and they traded. This is **comparative advantage**.

deep.w: Every deal has a winner and a loser
deep.r: A voluntary trade usually happens because both sides expect to gain

deep.x: Most of life isn't a fixed pie; the best deals make the pie bigger.

cards.title: O jogo do covarde
cards.text: Dois motoristas aceleram um em direção ao outro; quem desviar perde a moral, mas, se nenhum desviar, os dois batem. O jogo serve de modelo para impasses entre países ou empresas.

deep.x: Chicken flips the prisoner's dilemma. Here the worst outcome is mutual toughness: a crash. Each driver wants the other to swerve, but would rather swerve than die.
Two equilibria
There are two stable outcomes, each with one driver swerving. The fight is over which one happens. That's why the game is about signals, reputation and nerve.
Commitment wins

The counter-intuitive move is to remove your own options. Visibly throw your steering wheel out of the window and the other driver must swerve. Strategist Herman Kahn used this image in the nuclear age; Thomas Schelling built a theory of commitment around it.

steps: Rival sees you can't back down

deep.x: Real stand-offs

x: The 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, which Bertrand Russell and others compared to chicken
Strikes, where both sides lose money each day
Two companies each refusing to leave a market that can only support one

deep.w: The bravest player always wins chicken
deep.r: The player whose commitment is most believable wins; if both commit, both crash

deep.x: In chicken, the strongest move can be making it impossible for yourself to back down.

cards.title: Vantagem de quem sai na frente
cards.text: Em alguns jogos, ser o primeiro a agir permite se comprometer e moldar o resultado. Em outros, esperar permite aprender com os erros de quem vai na frente.

deep.x: Some games are played in turns. Moving first means you act before others, but also without seeing what they'll do. Whether that helps depends on the game.
When leading helps

Economist Heinrich von Stackelberg showed in 1934 that a firm committing first to a large output can force rivals to produce less. Building the first factory, the first network or the first standard can lock others out. In chess, White moves first and scores slightly more than Black at top level.
When following helps
Google was not the first search engine, and Facebook was not the first social network. They learned from AltaVista, Yahoo, Friendster and MySpace. Followers avoid the pioneer's costs and mistakes.
Thinking backwards
For turn-based games, the trick is **backward induction**: start from the end and ask what the last player will do, then the one before, and so on.
In 1519 Hernán Cortés scuttled most of his ships after landing in Mexico, a classic example of commitment: with no way home, retreat was no longer an option for his men.
Ask whether the advantage comes from committing first or from learning second.

cards.title: Leilões
cards.text: A teoria dos jogos é usada para desenhar leilões de espectro de rádio que valem bilhões. Num leilão fechado de segundo preço, a melhor estratégia é oferecer exatamente o que aquilo vale para você.

deep.x: Auction rules change how people bid. Game theory works out the best bid under each rule, which helps sellers raise money and buyers avoid overpaying.
Why bid your true value?

In a second-price (Vickrey) auction, your bid only decides whether you win; the price is set by someone else. Bidding lower risks losing something you'd happily have paid for. Bidding higher risks winning at a price above your value.

x: Painting worth €500 to you, rival bids €400

deep.x: William Vickrey analysed this in 1961 and shared the 1996 Nobel prize. Online auction "proxy bidding", where the site bids for you up to your maximum, works much the same way.
Spectrum auctions

Governments sell radio frequencies for mobile networks this way. The UK's 3G auction in 2000 raised £22.5 billion. Portugal's 5G auction, run by ANACOM, ended in 2021 after about 10 months and raised around €566 million.
The "winner's curse": when many bid for something of uncertain value, like an oil field, the winner is often the one who overestimated it most.
In a second-price auction, honesty is the best strategy: bid exactly what it's worth to you.

cards.title: A evolução como jogo
cards.text: Os animais "jogam" estratégias moldadas pela evolução: os falcões brigam, as pombas dividem. Uma mistura dos dois pode ser estável numa população.

deep.x: Animals don't calculate payoffs, but natural selection does it for them. Strategies that leave more offspring spread; those that don't, fade. In 1973 John Maynard Smith and George Price used game theory to explain why most animal fights are ritual displays rather than fights to the death.
Hawks and doves
If everyone is a dove, a hawk does brilliantly. If everyone is a hawk, injuries are constant and a dove that simply avoids fights does better. Neither pure strategy is stable.
The stable mix
The population settles where hawks and doves do equally well: an **evolutionarily stable strategy**. If the prize is worth V and an injury costs C (more than V), the stable share of hawks is V ÷ C.
hawk share = V ÷ C
Male side-blotched lizards in California come in three throat colours whose mating strategies beat each other in a circle, like rock-paper-scissors; their numbers cycle over the years.
Evolution plays games too, and the winning strategy is often a balanced mix.

cards.title: Dividir a conta
cards.text: Quando um grupo divide a conta do restaurante em partes iguais, todo mundo fica tentado a pedir mais, já que os outros dividem o custo. No fim, todos pagam mais: uma pequena tragédia dos comuns.

deep.x: When four friends split the bill equally, each extra euro you spend costs you only 25 cents. That makes treats look cheap. But everyone faces the same temptation.

x: splitting four ways you pay €2 for €4 of pleasure: order it
each pays €8 for €4 of pleasure: €4 worse off

deep.x: Tragedy of the commons

Garrett Hardin popularised the term in 1968 using shared grazing land: each herder adds one more cow because they get the benefit while the cost of overgrazing is shared. Fisheries, traffic jams and shared office fridges work the same way.
Evidence

In an experiment in Israel, economists Uri Gneezy, Ernan Haruvy and Hadas Yafe had students dine in groups (the study was published in 2004). Those who split the bill ordered noticeably more than those who paid individually.
Fixes

x: Pay for what you order (a "conta separada")
Agree a shared budget in advance
Friendships are repeated games, so reputation keeps most groups in check

deep.w: Splitting equally is always the fairest way
deep.r: It's simple, but it rewards whoever orders most

deep.x: When costs are shared and benefits are personal, everyone takes a little too much.

quiz.q: No dilema do prisioneiro, o que costuma acontecer?
options: Os dois traem e saem perdendo
quiz.explain: A lógica individual vence o bem coletivo.

lessons.title: Códigos e criptografia
lessons.summary: Mensagens secretas, de César ao seu celular.

cards.title: A cifra de César
cards.text: Júlio César deslocava cada letra três posições: A vira D, B vira E. Fácil de usar e fácil de quebrar.

deep.x: The Roman historian Suetonius records that Julius Caesar wrote private letters with each letter replaced by the one three places later in the alphabet. At the end you wrap round: X becomes A, Y becomes B, Z becomes C.
Why it's weak

The whole secret is a single number, the shift. With 26 letters there are only 25 useful shifts, so an enemy can simply try them all, a method called **brute force**. Writing out 25 lines takes a few minutes.
Still around

x: ROT13, a shift of 13, was used online to hide spoilers and puzzle answers; doing it twice gets you back the original
Children's decoder rings use the same idea
In 2006 the Sicilian Mafia boss Bernardo Provenzano was reported to use a Caesar-style number code in his notes, and investigators read them

deep.x: The Caesar cipher's key is so small that you can break it by hand faster than you could make a cup of coffee.

deep.w: A cipher is safe as long as the method is secret
deep.r: Once the method leaks, a tiny key falls at once; real security needs a huge number of possible keys

deep.x: A code with only 25 possible keys is a puzzle, not a secret.

cards.title: Quebrar códigos pela frequência
cards.text: Em inglês, o E é a letra mais comum, seguida do T e do A. Conte as letras de uma mensagem cifrada e você consegue adivinhar a substituição. Al-Kindi descreveu isso no século IX.

deep.x: In a simple substitution cipher every letter is swapped for another, in any jumbled order. That gives 26! (about 4 × 10²⁶) possible keys, far too many to try one by one. Yet it falls quickly, because language is lopsided.

v.unit: share of letters in English text, %

deep.x: Al-Kindi's method

Around 850 CE, the Baghdad scholar al-Kindi described the technique in his treatise on deciphering messages. Count how often each symbol appears in the coded text, then match the most common symbols to the most common letters of the language.
Different languages, different fingerprints
In Portuguese the top letters are A (about 14–15%), E and O, so a codebreaker must know the language first. Short words help too: in English look for THE and AND; in Portuguese, QUE, NÃO, DE and A.
In 1587 Mary, Queen of Scots, was executed partly because Thomas Phelippes used frequency analysis to read her encrypted letters plotting against Elizabeth I.

deep.w: More possible keys always means a safer cipher
deep.r: A substitution cipher has 400 million billion billion keys, and frequency analysis still breaks it in an afternoon

deep.x: A cipher that keeps the pattern of the language can be broken by counting.

cards.title: Vigenère

steps: Cada letra se desloca de um jeito

cards.text: A cifra de Vigenère usa uma palavra-chave para deslocar cada letra uma quantidade diferente, driblando a simples contagem de frequências. Foi chamada de "a cifra indecifrável" durante 300 anos.

deep.x: Vigenère beats frequency analysis by using several Caesar shifts in turn, chosen by a keyword. With the key LEMON, the first letter shifts by L (11 places), the second by E (4), and so on, repeating the keyword.
Notice the two T's in ATTACK become X and F: the same letter is disguised differently each time, so letter counts flatten out.
How it fell

The method was described by Giovan Battista Bellaso in 1553 and later wrongly credited to Blaise de Vigenère. Charles Babbage broke it in the 1850s but didn't publish; Friedrich Kasiski published a method in 1863.
If the key is 5 letters long, every 5th letter uses the same shift. Split the text into five groups and each one is just a Caesar cipher, open to frequency analysis.
If the key is truly random, as long as the message and never reused, Vigenère becomes a **one-time pad**, which is mathematically unbreakable.
Repeating the key is what gives Vigenère away.

cards.title: Enigma
cards.text: A máquina Enigma, da Alemanha, usava rotores para mudar a cifra a cada tecla pressionada. Matemáticos poloneses foram os primeiros a decifrá-la; a equipe de Alan Turing em Bletchley Park a quebrou em grande escala.

deep.x: Enigma looked like a typewriter. Press a key and an electric current ran through three (later four) rotors and a plugboard, lighting up the coded letter. Then a rotor stepped on, so the next press used a different substitution.
A huge number of settings
With three rotors chosen from five and ten plugboard cables, the army Enigma had about 159 quintillion (1.59 × 10²⁰) starting settings, changed every day.
Who broke it

Polish mathematicians Marian Rejewski, Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski used group theory to reconstruct the machine's wiring in 1932. In July 1939 they handed their work to Britain and France. At Bletchley Park, Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman designed the Bombe, an electromechanical machine to test settings quickly.
The flaws

x: Enigma never encoded a letter as itself, which ruled out many guesses
Messages often began with predictable words like weather reports, called "cribs"
Operators were lazy with settings and repeated messages

deep.x: About 10,000 people worked at Bletchley Park by 1945, and roughly three quarters of them were women.
Enigma fell not to brute force but to maths, machines and human habits.

cards.title: Chaves
cards.text: A criptografia moderna é pública: o método é conhecido, e a segurança vem inteiramente de uma chave secreta. Uma chave de 128 bits tem trilhões de vezes mais combinações do que existem grãos de areia na Terra.

deep.x: The principle comes from Auguste Kerckhoffs in 1883: assume the enemy knows how your system works. Then security doesn't depend on hiding the method; it depends only on the key, which is easy to change if stolen.
How big is 128 bits?
Each bit doubles the number of possible keys, so 128 bits give 2¹²⁸ keys: about 3.4 × 10³⁸.

x: about 10¹⁹ years, a billion times the age of the universe

deep.x: The standard today

**AES** (Advanced Encryption Standard), chosen in 2001 from a public competition and designed by two Belgians, Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen, encrypts your Wi-Fi, phone storage and banking sessions. Openly published methods are trusted precisely because experts worldwide have tried and failed to break them.

deep.w: Secret, home-made algorithms are safer
deep.r: Unreviewed algorithms usually have hidden flaws; trust comes from public scrutiny

deep.x: Where attacks really happen
Nobody guesses AES keys. Attackers steal them instead: through phishing, malware, weak passwords or careless storage.
Keep the key secret and make it long; the method can be shouted from the rooftops.

cards.title: Criptografia de chave pública
cards.text: O seu celular usa duas chaves: uma pública, que qualquer pessoa pode usar para trancar uma mensagem, e uma privada, que só você tem, para destrancá-la. Foi inventada nos anos 1970.

deep.x: Older ciphers had a chicken-and-egg problem: to send a secret message, you first had to share a secret key securely. Public-key cryptography removes that. Your public key can be posted anywhere; only your private key unlocks what it locks.
Who invented it
The maths trick: one-way functions
RSA relies on the fact that multiplying two large primes is easy, but splitting the result back into its primes is extraordinarily hard. Real keys use numbers over 600 digits long.
Here "mod 33" means "take the remainder after dividing by 33".
Where you use it

x: The padlock in your browser (HTTPS) sets up each connection this way
Digital signatures: the private key signs, anyone checks with the public key
Portugal's Cartão de Cidadão chip holds keys for legally valid digital signatures

deep.x: In practice, public-key maths is slow, so it's used just to agree a fresh shared key, then fast AES does the bulk of the work.
A public key lets strangers send you secrets without ever meeting.

cards.title: A analogia do cadeado
cards.text: Mande um cadeado aberto para alguém: a pessoa tranca uma caixa com ele, e só você tem a chave. Ninguém precisou combinar um segredo antes.

deep.x: Imagine you want a friend in Faro to send you a valuable item by post, but you can't trust the postal workers. You post them an open padlock, keeping the only key. They put the item in a box, snap your padlock shut and post it back. Anyone can see the padlock; nobody but you can open it.
Mapping the analogy
The paint-mixing version

Diffie–Hellman key exchange is often explained with paint. You both agree on a common colour in public. Each adds a secret colour, swaps the mixtures, then adds their own secret again. Both end with the same final colour; an eavesdropper sees only mixtures and can't "unmix" them.
Where the analogy breaks

A thief could intercept your padlock and send your friend their own instead. This is a **man-in-the-middle** attack. That's why browsers rely on certificates, signed by trusted authorities, to prove that a public key really belongs to your bank.

deep.w: Encryption alone proves who you're talking to
deep.r: You also need authentication, such as certificates, or you may be locking the box for an impostor

deep.x: A padlock anyone can close but only you can open is the heart of secure messaging.

cards.title: Hashes
cards.text: Um hash transforma quaisquer dados numa impressão digital de tamanho fixo. Mude uma letra e o hash muda completamente. Os sites guardam hashes das senhas, e não as senhas.

deep.x: A hash function takes any input, a word, a film or a whole hard drive, and squeezes it into a short, fixed-length code. SHA-256, the most widely used, always produces 256 bits, written as 64 hexadecimal characters.

items: Hard to find two with one hash

deep.x: Passwords

A website stores the hash of your password. When you log in, it hashes what you type and compares. If hackers steal the database, they get hashes, not passwords. Good sites add a random **salt** to each password first and use deliberately slow hashes such as bcrypt or Argon2, so guessing takes much longer.
Other uses

x: Checking a downloaded file hasn't been tampered with
Git, the tool programmers use, names every version by its hash
Bitcoin mining is a race to find hashes starting with many zeros

deep.x: Collisions, two inputs with the same hash, must exist (there are more possible files than hashes), but for SHA-256 nobody has ever found one. The older SHA-1 fell in 2017 when researchers produced two different PDFs with the same hash.
A hash is a fingerprint: easy to take, impossible to turn back into the hand.

cards.title: Senhas fortes

items.r: quatro palavras aleatórias e um gerenciador de senhas

cards.text: Comprimento vale mais do que complexidade. Quatro palavras aleatórias são mais fáceis de lembrar e mais difíceis de quebrar do que "P@ssw0rd1". Use um gerenciador de senhas e autenticação em dois fatores.

deep.x: Attackers don't guess randomly. They start with leaked passwords, dictionary words and common tricks like @ for a and 0 for o. "P@ssw0rd1" looks complex but sits near the top of every cracking list. What counts is how many guesses a password really needs.
Length wins

x: 5 random words from a 7,776-word list: 7,776⁵ ≈ 2.8 × 10¹⁹, about 4,000 times more

deep.x: The words must be chosen randomly, for example with dice, not a famous phrase or song line.
The three habits that matter most

items: A password manager to store them

deep.x: Why reuse is the real danger
When one site is breached, criminals try the same email and password on banks, email and shopping sites, an attack called **credential stuffing**. A unique password limits the damage to one account.

deep.w: Changing your password every month makes it safer
deep.r: Experts no longer recommend forced regular changes; change it when there's a breach

deep.x: A long, unique, random password beats a short clever one.

cards.title: A ameaça quântica
cards.text: Computadores quânticos grandes poderão um dia quebrar os sistemas de chave pública atuais. Novos algoritmos "pós-quânticos" foram padronizados em 2024 para nos prepararmos.

deep.x: Quantum computers use qubits, which exploit superposition and interference to solve certain problems dramatically faster. In 1994 Peter Shor showed that a big enough quantum computer could factor large numbers and solve related problems quickly, which would break RSA and the elliptic-curve systems that protect today's internet.
How close is it?

Breaking RSA-2048 is estimated to need on the order of a million error-prone physical qubits running for days. Today's machines have hundreds to a few thousand, with high error rates. Nobody knows the date, but the risk is taken seriously.
Harvest now, decrypt later
Spies can record encrypted traffic today and wait. Secrets that must stay safe for 20 years, such as medical or state records, need protection now.
The new standards

The US standards body NIST published these in August 2024 after an eight-year public competition. They rely on lattice problems and hash functions that quantum computers aren't known to crack. Browsers and messaging apps like Chrome and Signal already use hybrid schemes that combine old and new.
The EU has set a roadmap asking member states to start the switch by 2026 and to protect high-risk systems by around 2030.
The quantum threat isn't here yet, but the locks are being changed before the burglar arrives.

lessons.title: Grandes matemáticos
lessons.summary: As pessoas por trás das ideias.

cards.title: Euclides
cards.text: Por volta de 300 a.C., Euclides escreveu *Os Elementos*, construindo a geometria a partir de alguns axiomas básicos. A obra foi usada como livro didático por mais de 2,000 anos.

deep.x: Almost nothing is known about Euclid himself, except that he taught in Alexandria around 300 BCE. His *Elements* gathered the best Greek mathematics into 13 books and roughly 465 propositions, each proved step by step from what came before.
The axiomatic method

Euclid started with five postulates, things accepted without proof, such as "a straight line can be drawn between any two points". Everything else had to be deduced. This way of building knowledge, from a few assumptions to a tower of certain results, became the model for all of mathematics.
Not just geometry

x: Book IX proves there are infinitely many prime numbers
Book VII gives Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor, still used in computers today

deep.x: The fifth postulate

The fifth, about parallel lines, always looked less obvious than the rest. In the 1820s and 1830s, Lobachevsky and Bolyai showed you could replace it and get consistent, curved geometries. Einstein's theory of gravity uses one.
*Elements* is often said to have had more editions than any book except the Bible.
Euclid showed how to build certain knowledge from a handful of simple assumptions.

cards.title: Arquimedes
cards.text: Arquimedes estimou o π, calculou volumes de esferas, explicou as alavancas e a flutuação e, dizem, gritou "Eureca!" no banho.

deep.x: Archimedes (c. 287–212 BCE) lived in Syracuse, Sicily, and is widely regarded as the greatest mathematician of the ancient world. He combined pure geometry with practical engineering.
Squeezing π
He drew polygons inside and outside a circle and doubled their sides up to 96. The circle's perimeter had to lie between the two polygons' perimeters.
His favourite result

He showed that a sphere has exactly two thirds the volume of the smallest cylinder that contains it, and asked for this to be carved on his tomb. Cicero reported finding the tomb, with sphere and cylinder, about 140 years later.
The bath story

The architect Vitruvius, writing two centuries later, tells how Archimedes realised in his bath that a crown's volume could be measured by the water it displaced, revealing whether the goldsmith had mixed in cheaper silver. Historians suspect the details are embellished.
A lost Archimedes text, *The Method*, was found in 1906 hidden under a medieval prayer book; the parchment had been scraped and reused. It shows him using ideas close to calculus.
He was killed by a Roman soldier when Syracuse fell in 212 BCE, reportedly while working on a geometry problem.
Archimedes trapped π between two polygons, an idea of squeezing that calculus would later build on.

cards.title: Hipátia
cards.text: Hipátia de Alexandria (c. 360–415 d.C.) foi matemática, astrônoma e professora, uma das primeiras mulheres da matemática que conhecemos pelo nome.

deep.x: Hypatia worked in Alexandria, then still a great centre of learning under Roman rule. She was the daughter of the mathematician Theon, and she became more famous than her father, leading a school of philosophy that drew students from across the Mediterranean.
Her work
None of her writings survive under her own name, so we know her through others. Ancient sources credit her with commentaries on:
Commentaries mattered: they explained and corrected difficult texts, and copies of the books themselves survived partly through such teaching editions.
Teacher and inventor

Letters from her student Synesius, later a bishop, ask her advice about building an astrolabe, an instrument for measuring the positions of stars, and a hydrometer for measuring the density of liquids.
Her death
In 415 CE, amid a violent political struggle between Alexandria's bishop Cyril and its Roman governor Orestes, whom she advised, Hypatia was murdered by a Christian mob.

deep.w: Hypatia's death marked the end of ancient science
deep.r: Mathematics continued in Alexandria and elsewhere for centuries; her story became a symbol later on

deep.x: The Spanish director Alejandro Amenábar told her story in the 2009 film *Agora*, starring Rachel Weisz.
Hypatia kept the great Greek texts alive by teaching and explaining them.

cards.title: Fibonacci
cards.text: Leonardo de Pisa, conhecido como Fibonacci, popularizou os algarismos indo-arábicos na Europa em 1202 com o seu *Liber Abaci*, um livro para comerciantes.

deep.x: Leonardo was born in Pisa around 1170. His father was a merchant's official in Bugia, in what is now Algeria, and there the boy learned the "Indian" numerals from Arab teachers. He saw at once how much easier they were than Roman numerals.
Liber Abaci (1202)

His "Book of Calculation" taught merchants how to convert currencies, weights and measures, share profits and compute interest using the new digits. It was revised in 1228 and spread through Italian trading cities.
The rabbits

One puzzle asked how many pairs of rabbits you'd have if every pair produced a new pair each month from its second month. The answer gives 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13…, each number the sum of the two before.
The sequence was known in India centuries earlier, in the study of poetic rhythms; and the nickname "Fibonacci" (son of Bonacci) was only popularised in the 19th century.
Resistance was real: in 1299 Florence's bankers' guild banned the new numerals in official accounts, partly because a written 0 could easily be changed into a 6 or 9.
Fibonacci's real gift to Europe was not rabbits but the digits we count with.

cards.title: Descartes e Fermat
cards.text: No século XVII, os dois ligaram a álgebra e a geometria por meio das coordenadas. Fermat também deixou um famoso "último teorema", que ficou sem prova por 358 anos.

deep.x: René Descartes and Pierre de Fermat, both French, discovered coordinate geometry independently in the 1630s. Descartes published his in *La Géométrie*, an appendix to his 1637 *Discourse on the Method*, the same book that contains "I think, therefore I am".
An amateur genius

Fermat was a magistrate who did maths in his spare time, rarely publishing. With Blaise Pascal he founded probability theory in letters exchanged in 1654, about how to split stakes in an unfinished game.
The last theorem
Around 1637 Fermat wrote in the margin of his copy of Diophantus that he had a marvellous proof, but the margin was too small to hold it. Nobody found one for centuries.
Fermat's "little theorem", a different and proven result from 1640, is at the heart of RSA encryption on your phone.
Coordinates married algebra and geometry, and an amateur's margin note kept mathematicians busy for 358 years.

cards.title: Newton e Leibniz
cards.text: Os dois inventaram o cálculo de forma independente no fim do século XVII e brigaram amargamente sobre quem tinha sido o primeiro. Hoje usamos a notação de Leibniz.

deep.x: Isaac Newton developed his "method of fluxions" in 1665–66, when Cambridge closed because of plague and he worked at home in Lincolnshire. But he didn't publish it. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, in Germany, developed calculus around 1675 and published first, in 1684.
The bitter dispute

Newton's supporters accused Leibniz of plagiarism. In 1712 the Royal Society, of which Newton was president, issued a report backing Newton; Newton secretly wrote much of it himself. Historians now agree both discovered calculus independently.
Notation matters

Leibniz's dy/dx reads like a fraction, "a tiny change in y over a tiny change in x", which makes many rules feel natural. British mathematicians loyal to Newton's dots are often said to have fallen behind the continent for about a century.
Beyond calculus

x: Newton: laws of motion and gravity (*Principia*, 1687), optics and the reflecting telescope
Leibniz: binary arithmetic, a calculating machine, and philosophy

deep.x: Leibniz saw binary numbers, using just 0 and 1, as having deep meaning, centuries before computers made them essential.
Calculus was discovered twice, and good notation turned out to matter as much as the idea.

cards.title: Euler
cards.text: Leonhard Euler foi o matemático mais prolífico de todos os tempos, escrevendo mais de 800 artigos, mesmo depois de ficar cego. A sua identidade e^iπ + 1 = 0 liga cinco números fundamentais.

deep.x: Leonhard Euler (1707–1783) was born in Basel, Switzerland, and worked in St Petersburg and Berlin. His collected works fill more than 80 large volumes, and the edition has taken over a century to complete.
Blindness didn't stop him
He lost most of the sight in his right eye in 1738 and became nearly blind in 1766. He kept working by dictation and phenomenal memory, and about half of his output came after that.
Notation he gave us
His famous identity
It connects five fundamental numbers: 0 and 1 (arithmetic), π (geometry), e (growth) and i (imaginary numbers), using one addition, one multiplication and one power.
Other firsts

x: Founded graph theory with the Königsberg bridges in 1736
Showed that for a solid like a cube, vertices − edges + faces = 2

deep.x: In a 1988 poll of readers of *The Mathematical Intelligencer*, Euler's identity was voted the most beautiful theorem in mathematics.
Euler wrote so much, and so clearly, that much of the notation in every maths book is his.

cards.title: Gauss
cards.text: Quando menino, Gauss teria somado os números de 1 a 100 em segundos: juntou 1+100, 2+99… em 50 pares que somam 101, o que dá 5,050.

deep.x: Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855), from Brunswick in Germany, is often called the "prince of mathematicians". The schoolroom story comes from a biography published after his death, so the details may be polished, but the trick is real.
A teenage breakthrough

At 18 he showed that a regular 17-sided polygon can be constructed with just a ruler and compass, something nobody had managed since the Greeks. He was so pleased he decided to become a mathematician.
Finding a lost planet

The dwarf planet Ceres was discovered in January 1801 and then lost behind the Sun. Using only a few observations and his new methods, Gauss predicted where it would reappear, and astronomers found it there in December.
Everyday legacy
The bell-shaped **Gaussian** (normal) curve describes heights, measurement errors and exam marks. His method of least squares underpins every "line of best fit" in a spreadsheet.
Germany's 10-Deutsche-Mark banknote showed Gauss next to his bell curve.
Look for structure before calculating: pairing turns 100 additions into one multiplication.

cards.title: Ada Lovelace
cards.text: Em 1843, Ada Lovelace escreveu o que é considerado o primeiro programa de computador, para a Máquina Analítica de Babbage, e previu que os computadores fariam música.

deep.x: Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace (1815–1852), was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron. Her mother had her tutored in mathematics, and at 17 she met Charles Babbage, who was designing calculating machines.
The Analytical Engine

Babbage's Analytical Engine, designed from 1837, was a general-purpose mechanical computer: it had a "store" (memory), a "mill" (processor) and would read instructions from punched cards, an idea borrowed from Jacquard weaving looms. It was never built.
The Notes

In 1843 she translated an Italian engineer's article about the Engine and added notes nearly three times as long. Note G laid out step by step how the Engine could compute Bernoulli numbers, a tricky sequence. This is widely called the first published computer program.
Seeing further

She grasped that the Engine could manipulate any symbols, not just numbers, and suggested it might compose elaborate music. She also argued it could not originate ideas of its own; Alan Turing answered this "Lady Lovelace's objection" in 1950.

deep.w: Ada Lovelace built the first computer
deep.r: Babbage designed it, nobody built it, and Ada wrote about how it could be programmed

deep.x: The programming language Ada, created for the US defence department around 1980, is named after her, and Ada Lovelace Day is celebrated on the second Tuesday of October.
Lovelace saw that a calculating machine could become a general symbol machine, a century before computers existed.

cards.title: Grandes nomes modernos
cards.text: Emmy Noether ligou a simetria às leis de conservação; Ramanujan encontrou fórmulas surpreendentes com pouca formação acadêmica; Maryam Mirzakhani foi a primeira mulher a ganhar a Medalha Fields, em 2014.

deep.x: Mathematics in the last century has been shaped by people from every background. Three stories show its range.
Emmy Noether (1882–1935)

Noether proved in 1915 that every symmetry in physics comes with a conserved quantity. If the laws are the same tomorrow as today, energy is conserved; if they're the same here as there, momentum is conserved. Göttingen University long refused to pay her as a woman, and as a Jew she fled the Nazis in 1933. Einstein called her a creative mathematical genius.
Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887–1920)

A clerk in Madras, India, he sent pages of astonishing formulas to G. H. Hardy in Cambridge in 1913. Hardy invited him to England, where he did remarkable work before dying at 32. He left nearly 4,000 results in all.

x: = 9³ + 10³, the smallest number that's a sum of two cubes in two ways

deep.x: Maryam Mirzakhani (1977–2017)

Born in Tehran, she worked at Stanford on the geometry and dynamics of curved surfaces. In 2014 she became the first woman to win the Fields Medal, given every four years to mathematicians under 40. She died of cancer aged 40.
In 2014 the Brazilian Artur Avila also won the Fields Medal, the first for a mathematician trained in Latin America; in 2022 Ukrainian Maryna Viazovska became the second woman to win it.
Great mathematics comes from everywhere: a German lecturer barred from pay, an Indian clerk, an Iranian schoolgirl.
