cards.title: Duas grandes perguntas
cards.text: O cálculo responde a duas perguntas: com que rapidez algo está mudando neste instante (derivadas) e quanto se acumulou ao longo do tempo (integrais).

deep.x: Algebra handles things that stay put. Calculus handles things that change: a car speeding up, a tank filling, a population growing. It splits into two halves that answer opposite questions.
A car journey

Your dashboard shows both. The speedometer gives the rate of change of distance at this instant: a derivative. The odometer adds up all the little distances travelled: an integral. From either one, you could in principle reconstruct the other.
Why "calculus"?
*Calculus* is Latin for a small pebble, the kind once used for counting. Today "the calculus" means specifically this mathematics of change, developed in the 17th century.
The key tool

Both halves use the same trick: chop things into tiny pieces. For a derivative you look at a tiny change in time; for an integral you add up a huge number of tiny slices. Making the pieces smaller and smaller, in the limit, gives exact answers.

x: Electricity: a 2 kW heater for 3 hours
total energy = 6 kWh (an integral of a constant rate)

deep.w: Calculus is only for physicists and engineers
deep.r: It's behind economics, medicine dosing models, weather forecasts and AI

deep.x: Derivatives ask "how fast?", integrals ask "how much?", and calculus links the two.

cards.title: Velocidade instantânea
cards.text: O velocímetro do carro mostra a velocidade num instante, não uma média. O cálculo a define medindo em intervalos de tempo cada vez menores.

deep.x: Speed is distance divided by time. But at a single instant, no time passes and no distance is covered: 0 ÷ 0, which means nothing. Calculus gets round this by measuring over ever shorter intervals and watching where the answers settle.
Watching it settle
A dropped stone falls about 5t² metres in t seconds. How fast is it going at exactly 2 seconds?
How cars measure it
A speedometer doesn't do calculus; it counts wheel rotations over a short time, which is already a very good average. GPS speed works similarly, comparing positions a fraction of a second apart.
Speed cameras

Portugal uses both fixed radar cameras, which measure an instant speed, and average-speed sections, which divide distance by the time between two cameras. You can slow down for a radar; you can't fool an average.
Speedometers in Europe are required never to show less than your true speed, so most read a few km/h high.
Instant speed is what average speed approaches as the time interval shrinks towards zero.

cards.title: A inclinação de uma curva
cards.text: Uma derivada é a inclinação de uma curva num ponto: amplie o bastante e qualquer curva suave parece uma reta.

deep.x: A straight line has one slope everywhere. A curve's steepness keeps changing. The derivative gives the slope at each single point: the slope of the **tangent**, the straight line that just touches the curve there.
Zoom in
Zoom in on a smooth curve and it straightens out. The Earth looks flat from where you stand for the same reason. The slope of that almost-straight piece is the derivative.

steps: Pick a point on the curve

deep.x: A rule appears

Do this at every x for y = x² and a pattern pops out: the slope is always 2x. At x = 1 it's 2; at x = 5 it's 10. A whole family of shortcut rules like this lets you find derivatives without zooming at all.

deep.w: Every curve has a slope at every point
deep.r: A sharp corner, like the tip of a V, has no single tangent, so no derivative there

deep.x: Zoom in far enough and a smooth curve becomes a straight line, whose slope is the derivative.

cards.title: A área sob uma curva
cards.text: Uma integral soma fatias minúsculas. Num gráfico de velocidade–tempo, a área sob a curva é a distância percorrida.

deep.x: If you drive at a steady 30 m/s for 60 s, you cover 30 × 60 = 1,800 m. On a speed–time graph that's a rectangle 30 high and 60 wide. When speed changes, the shape isn't a rectangle any more, but the distance is still the area.

x: A car speeds up evenly from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s
the area is a triangle: ½ × 10 × 20

deep.x: Slicing
For a curved shape, cut the area into thin vertical strips, treat each as a rectangle, and add them up. Thinner strips mean a better fit.

x: Area under y = x² from 0 to 1

v.unit: estimate of area under y = x² (true: 0.333)

deep.x: The integral sign ∫ is a stretched S, for "sum", chosen by Leibniz.
Areas with real meaning
Your electricity meter is an integrator: it adds up power, moment by moment, into kilowatt-hours on your bill.
An integral adds up infinitely many thin slices, and the area it finds can be distance, energy or money.

cards.title: Opostos
cards.text: A derivação e a integração desfazem uma à outra: é o teorema fundamental do cálculo. Distância → velocidade → aceleração, e de volta.

deep.x: Differentiation turns a total into a rate; integration turns a rate back into a total. Doing one then the other gets you back where you started, just as adding 5 then subtracting 5 does.
Read down for derivatives; read up for integrals. That chain is how a phone's motion sensor, which only feels acceleration, can estimate how far it has moved.
A worked chain
Why it's "fundamental"

The fundamental theorem says: to find the area under a curve between two points, find any function whose derivative is that curve and subtract its values at the ends. This turns the endless adding of slices into a two-line calculation.

x: Area under y = x² from 0 to 1

deep.x: Newton's teacher Isaac Barrow proved a geometric version of this link, but it was Newton and Leibniz who saw it as the engine of a whole method.
Rates and totals are two sides of one coin: differentiation and integration undo each other.

cards.title: Máximos e mínimos
cards.text: Onde uma curva atinge um pico ou um vale, a inclinação é zero. É assim que os engenheiros encontram a viga mais resistente ou o projeto mais barato.

deep.x: At the very top of a hill, the ground is momentarily flat. The same is true of any smooth graph: at a peak or a dip, the tangent is horizontal. So to find the best value, find where the derivative equals zero.

steps: Write the quantity as a function
Solve, then check it's a max or min

deep.x: A thrown ball
The best fence
You have 40 m of fencing for a rectangular garden. Which shape encloses the most area?

v.unit: area with 40 m of fence, m²

deep.x: In the real world

x: Drinks cans are shaped to use little metal for their volume, though handling and stacking matter too
Airlines set prices to maximise revenue
Engineers shape beams for the most strength per kilogram
Nature does it too: light takes the quickest path, which explains why it bends entering water

deep.w: Zero slope always means a maximum
deep.r: It can be a minimum, or a flat step that's neither; you have to check

deep.x: The best value hides where the slope is zero.

cards.title: A maior caixa
cards.text: Corte quadrados dos cantos de um cartão de 30 cm e dobre para fazer uma caixa. O cálculo mostra que quadrados de 5 cm dão o maior volume: 2,000 cm³.

deep.x: Take a 30 cm × 30 cm square of card. Cut an x cm square from each corner and fold up the sides. The base is (30 − 2x) on each side and the height is x.
Trying values
Small cuts give a wide but shallow tray; big cuts give a tall but narrow tower. Somewhere in between is the best.
The calculus way

x: zero at x = 5 (x = 15 leaves no base)

steps: Write V in terms of x

deep.x: A general rule
For any square sheet of side L, the best cut is always L ÷ 6. A 60 cm sheet needs 10 cm squares and gives 16,000 cm³, eight times as much, because volume grows with the cube of size.
Notice the flat top: cutting 4 or 6 cm instead of 5 cm loses only about 3% of the volume. Near a maximum, small errors barely matter, which is good news for engineers.
Write the quantity as a formula, find where its slope is zero, and you've found the best design.

cards.title: Mudança por toda parte
cards.text: O cálculo modela o crescimento populacional, o aquecimento e o resfriamento, os juros, as trajetórias de foguetes e o aprendizado de máquina, que usa derivadas para ajustar seus pesos.

deep.x: Whenever a quantity's rate of change depends on the quantity itself, you get a **differential equation**. These are the language of science and much of economics.
Interest and the number e
Compound interest more and more often and you approach a limit involving e ≈ 2.718.

x: compounded daily: €1,051.27, close to the limit of €1,051.27

deep.x: Machine learning

An AI model has millions or billions of adjustable numbers, called weights. Training measures the error, then uses derivatives to find which direction to nudge each weight so the error falls. This is **gradient descent**: walking downhill on an error landscape, one small step at a time.
Forecasting

Weather models solve calculus equations for air pressure, temperature and wind on a 3D grid around the planet, stepping forward a few minutes at a time. Portugal's IPMA and the European centre ECMWF both rely on such models.
Every time a chatbot is trained, derivatives are calculated trillions of times, using an automatic method called backpropagation.
Wherever something changes in proportion to something else, calculus writes the rule.

cards.title: Limites
cards.text: O cálculo se apoia nos limites: o valor do qual algo se aproxima quando uma grandeza fica muito pequena. 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8… se aproxima de 1, embora nenhum passo chegue lá.

deep.x: A limit is the value something gets closer and closer to, as close as you like, without necessarily reaching it. It's the careful idea that makes "infinitely small" safe to use.

x: + 1/16 = 0.9375: the gap to 1 halves each time

deep.x: Zeno's paradox

Around 450 BCE Zeno argued that a runner can never finish a race: first she must run half, then half of what's left, and so on forever. Limits answer him: infinitely many steps can add up to a finite distance, covered in a finite time.
Making it rigorous

Newton and Leibniz used "infinitely small" quantities that critics mocked; the philosopher George Berkeley called them "ghosts of departed quantities" in 1734. In the 1800s Augustin-Louis Cauchy and Karl Weierstrass gave limits a precise definition: you can get within any distance you choose, however tiny.

deep.w: An infinite sum must be infinite
deep.r: Infinitely many terms can add to a finite total, as long as they shrink fast enough

deep.x: Not every shrinking series settles: 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4… grows forever, just very slowly.
A limit is where a process is heading, even if no single step gets there.

cards.title: Quem o inventou?
cards.text: Newton e Leibniz desenvolveram o cálculo de forma independente entre as décadas de 1660 e 1680, embora Arquimedes e outros tivessem usado ideias parecidas séculos antes.

deep.x: Newton and Leibniz built calculus into a general method with rules anyone could use. But the core ideas, slicing areas, finding tangents, summing infinite series, had been explored for two thousand years.
The forerunners

x: **Archimedes** found the area of a parabolic segment as exactly 4/3 of a triangle, by filling it with ever smaller triangles
**Madhava of Sangamagrama** in Kerala, India (c. 1340–1425), found infinite series for π and for sine and cosine, ideas Europe rediscovered centuries later
**Fermat** found maxima and tangents with a method very close to differentiation
**Bonaventura Cavalieri** (1635) used "indivisibles", thin slices, to compute volumes

deep.x: What Newton and Leibniz added
They saw that derivatives and integrals were inverse operations, and turned scattered tricks into one system. That made calculus a tool any trained person could apply.
Gottfried Leibniz rediscovered Madhava's series for π independently in 1673, almost 300 years later.
Calculus has many parents; Newton and Leibniz gave it a single, usable form.

cards.title: As pontes de Königsberg

steps: Conte as linhas em cada ponto

cards.text: Em 1736, Euler provou que não era possível atravessar todas as sete pontes de Königsberg exatamente uma vez. Para resolver o problema, ele reduziu a cidade a pontos e linhas: nascia a teoria dos grafos.

deep.x: Königsberg (now Kaliningrad, Russia) sat on the river Pregel, with two islands joined to the banks and each other by seven bridges. Residents liked to wonder whether you could walk through the city crossing each bridge exactly once.
Euler's leap

In 1736 Leonhard Euler realised that the shapes, distances and street layout didn't matter at all. Only which land areas were connected to which, and how many times. That abstraction is the birth of **graph theory** and the beginning of topology.
Counting the lines

Every time you walk through a land area you use two bridges, one in and one out. So any area you pass through must have an even number of bridges, except possibly where you start and finish. All four areas had an odd number, so the walk was impossible.

x: = 2 × 7 bridges, since each bridge has two ends

deep.x: Bombing in 1944 destroyed some of the bridges. With today's bridges, a walk crossing each one once is possible, though you can't end where you started.

deep.w: Euler found the walk by trying routes
deep.r: He proved no walk exists, without trying a single route, by counting

deep.x: Euler solved a city puzzle by throwing away everything except what connects to what.

cards.title: Nós e arestas
cards.text: Um grafo é um conjunto de nós (pontos) ligados por arestas (linhas). Cidades e estradas, pessoas e amizades, páginas da web e links: tudo isso são grafos.

deep.x: A graph in this sense isn't a chart. It's a network: a set of things (nodes, or vertices) and connections between them (edges). It's one of the most flexible ideas in mathematics.
Kinds of edges
A Facebook friendship goes both ways; following someone on Instagram doesn't, so it's a directed edge. A road map adds weights: distances or travel times.
The degree

The number of edges at a node is its **degree**. Adding up all the degrees always gives exactly twice the number of edges, because every edge has two ends. This "handshake lemma" means the number of odd-degree nodes is always even.
Why abstraction helps
Once you've drawn the graph, the same algorithm that finds a route on the Lisbon Metro can trace a disease, rank web pages or suggest friends. Different worlds, same maths.
Lisbon's Metro has four lines and about 50 stations; as a graph it's small enough to draw on a napkin, yet it already shows hubs like Marquês de Pombal where lines meet.
Strip away the details, keep the dots and the lines, and wildly different problems become the same problem.

cards.title: A regra de Euler
cards.text: Só é possível percorrer uma rede usando cada aresta uma única vez se zero ou dois nós tiverem um número ímpar de arestas. Königsberg tinha quatro nós ímpares.

deep.x: An **Euler path** uses every edge exactly once. Whether one exists depends only on how many nodes have an odd degree (an odd number of edges).

items.b: path: start at one, end at other

deep.x: Why

Every time a walk passes through a node, it uses two edges: in and out. So a node visited in the middle of a walk always "spends" its edges in pairs. Only the start and end can have a leftover single edge.
Test it yourself

The classic "house" drawing, a square with a cross and a triangular roof, can be drawn without lifting your pen. Count the degrees: the two bottom corners have 3 each, everything else is even. Start at one bottom corner and you'll finish at the other.

x: path possible, starting at a bottom corner

deep.x: Finding the route

Knowing a path exists is one thing; Fleury's algorithm (1883) gives a simple rule for tracing it: never cross a bridge that would cut you off from edges you haven't used yet, unless you have no choice.
Biologists use Euler paths to assemble genomes: overlapping fragments of DNA are turned into a graph, and an Euler path through it spells out the sequence.
Count the odd nodes: zero or two, and you can trace every line once.

cards.title: Caminhos mais curtos

steps: Explore o mais próximo não visitado

cards.text: O seu aplicativo de mapas encontra a rota mais rápida com algoritmos como o de Dijkstra (1956), que explora a partir do ponto de partida, sempre estendendo o caminho mais curto encontrado até então.

deep.x: Edsger Dijkstra, a Dutch computer scientist, designed his algorithm in 1956, by his own account in about twenty minutes while sitting at a café terrace in Amsterdam. Variations of it now run billions of times a day.
How it works
The algorithm grows a "frontier" of known shortest routes, always extending from the closest unsettled point. When the destination is reached, its distance is guaranteed to be the shortest.
A small example
Roads: A–B 4 km, A–C 2 km, C–B 1 km, B–D 5 km, C–D 8 km. What's the shortest way from A to D?

x: via C, B costs 2 + 1 = 3, better than 4

v.unit: route length A to D, km

deep.x: Notice the shortest route uses the indirect path through C: going "the wrong way" first can pay off.
In your phone

Map apps weight roads by expected travel time, not distance, using live traffic. To answer instantly on a continent-sized map, they use faster cousins of Dijkstra, such as A* (which aims towards the goal) and precomputed shortcuts between major roads.
Internet routers run a version of Dijkstra's algorithm, in a protocol called OSPF, to decide where to send each packet of data.
Always extend the shortest known route, and you're guaranteed to find the shortest one overall.

cards.title: O caixeiro-viajante
cards.text: Encontre a rota mais curta que passa por todas as cidades uma vez. É fácil com 5 cidades, mas as possibilidades explodem: 20 cidades têm mais de 60 quatrilhões de rotas.

deep.x: Finding the shortest path between two points is easy. Finding the shortest round trip through many points is famously hard, because the number of possible routes grows factorially.
routes = (n − 1)! ÷ 2 for n cities
Hard, but not hopeless

No known method guarantees the best tour quickly for every case. It's in a class of problems called **NP-hard**: if anyone found a fast general method, it would solve thousands of other hard problems too, and win a $1 million prize.

In practice, clever methods do brilliantly. In 2006 a program called Concorde proved the optimal tour through 85,900 points, from a circuit-board design. Quick heuristics routinely find routes within 1–2% of the best.

deep.w: Faster computers will solve it by checking every route
deep.r: At 20 cities a billion routes per second still takes about two years; at 30, longer than the age of the universe

deep.x: Some problems explode so fast that cleverness, not computing power, is the only way through.

cards.title: Seis graus de separação

steps: Qualquer pessoa, em uns seis passos

cards.text: O experimento de Stanley Milgram, de 1967, sugeriu que quaisquer dois americanos estão ligados por cerca de seis conhecidos. Dados do Facebook encontraram depois uma média de cerca de 3,5 passos.

deep.x: In 1967 social psychologist Stanley Milgram asked people in Nebraska and Kansas to get a letter to a stranger in Boston, passing it only to someone they knew personally. Most chains fizzled out, but those that arrived took about five to six steps on average.
Why so few steps?
Friend networks explode outward. If everyone has around 150 friends, two steps reach thousands and four reach hundreds of millions, even after allowing for lots of shared friends.
Small worlds

In 1998 Duncan Watts and Steven Strogatz showed why: most links are local (neighbours, colleagues), but a few long-range links, a cousin in Brazil or a classmate who moved to Berlin, act as shortcuts across the whole network.
Facebook's numbers
In 2016 Facebook calculated that its users were separated by an average of 3.57 people in between. Online networks are more connected than the letter-passing world of 1967.

deep.w: Six degrees is a proven law
deep.r: It's an average from experiments; chains vary, and Milgram's own data was patchy

deep.x: A few long-distance links are enough to make a huge world small.

cards.title: Hubs
cards.text: Em muitas redes, alguns poucos hubs têm um número enorme de ligações: grandes aeroportos, sites populares, influenciadores. Ataque os hubs e a rede se rompe.

deep.x: In a random network, most nodes have roughly the same number of links. Real networks are different: a few hubs have enormous numbers, while most nodes have only a handful. Albert-László Barabási and Réka Albert described such **scale-free** networks in 1999.
Rich get richer

New nodes tend to link to nodes that are already popular. A new website links to Wikipedia, not to an obscure blog; a new airline route connects to a big airport. This **preferential attachment** makes hubs grow ever larger.
Robust and fragile at once

Randomly remove nodes and you'll mostly hit small ones; the network barely notices. Target the hubs and it can shatter into disconnected pieces. One closed hub airport, like Frankfurt or Lisbon for TAP's network, disrupts flights across continents.
Everyday hubs

x: A few accounts with millions of followers
Proteins that interact with hundreds of others in a cell

deep.x: The friendship paradox: on average, your friends have more friends than you do, because popular people appear in many people's friend lists.
Networks with hubs shrug off random damage but are vulnerable to targeted attacks.

cards.title: Quatro cores
cards.text: Qualquer mapa pode ser colorido com apenas quatro cores sem que regiões vizinhas fiquem iguais. Provado em 1976, foi a primeira grande demonstração que dependeu de um computador.

deep.x: Colour a map so that neighbouring regions, ones sharing a border line, always differ. Francis Guthrie noticed in 1852, while colouring the counties of England, that four colours always seemed enough. Proving it took 124 years.
Why three isn't enough
Luxembourg touches Belgium, France and Germany, and those three all touch each other. Four regions all touching one another need four colours.
The controversial proof

Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken showed every map can be reduced to one of 1,936 basic configurations, then had a computer check each one, using about 1,200 hours of computing time. Many mathematicians were uneasy: no human could check it all by hand.
In 2005 Georges Gonthier verified the whole proof in Coq, software that checks every logical step.
Not really about maps

Map-makers never worried about it; real atlases use extra colours for clarity. The ideas matter instead for scheduling exams so no student has a clash, and assigning radio frequencies so neighbouring masts don't interfere.

deep.w: A map with many regions needs many colours
deep.r: Even a map of thousands of regions never needs more than four

deep.x: Four colours are always enough, and proving it changed what counts as a proof.

cards.title: PageRank

steps: Páginas apontam umas para as outras
Votos de páginas importantes valem mais

cards.text: A ideia original do Google: uma página é importante se páginas importantes apontam para ela. A web é tratada como um gigantesco grafo de votos.

deep.x: In the 1990s search engines mostly ranked pages by how often your search words appeared, which was easy to cheat. Larry Page and Sergey Brin, PhD students at Stanford, used the web's link structure instead. Google was founded in 1998.
Votes that count unequally

A link from page A to page B is a vote for B. But a vote from an important page counts more, and it's shared out among all the pages it links to. So importance is defined in terms of itself, and solved by repeating the calculation until it settles.
The random surfer

Picture someone clicking random links forever, but now and then jumping to a random page instead. PageRank is the share of time they'd spend on each page. Google's original paper used a 15% chance of jumping, written as a "damping factor" of 0.85.
Beyond search
The same maths ranks scientific papers by citations, finds key species in food webs and important proteins in cells. Modern Google uses hundreds of signals, but link analysis remains part of it.
The name PageRank is a pun: it ranks web pages, and it's named after Larry Page.

deep.w: More incoming links always means higher PageRank
deep.r: A single link from a very important page can outweigh hundreds from obscure ones

deep.x: A page matters if pages that matter point to it.

cards.title: Epidemias em redes
cards.text: As doenças se espalham pelas redes de contato. Vacinar os hubs bem conectados, como os profissionais de saúde, pode proteger muito mais gente do que a vacinação aleatória.

deep.x: An infection can only travel along contacts. That means the shape of the contact network, not just how infectious a disease is, decides how it spreads. A few people with many contacts, often called superspreaders, can drive most transmission.
The basic number
The **reproduction number** R is the average number of people each case infects. If R stays above 1, an outbreak grows; below 1 it dies away. Immunity cuts R by removing links.
herd immunity threshold ≈ 1 − 1/R₀
Targeting hubs
Removing a hub breaks many paths at once. That's why healthcare workers, who meet many vulnerable people, are often vaccinated first.
The friend trick

How do you find hubs if you can't see the network? Pick random people and vaccinate one of their friends instead. Thanks to the friendship paradox, friends are on average better connected. Simulations by Reuven Cohen and colleagues in 2003 showed this "acquaintance immunisation" works far better than random choice.
Portugal reached one of the world's highest COVID-19 vaccination rates in 2021, with well over 85% of the population fully vaccinated.
In a network, who you protect matters as much as how many.

cards.title: Problemas de Fermi
cards.text: O físico Enrico Fermi adorava perguntas como "quantos afinadores de piano há em Chicago?". Divida-as em partes que você consegue chutar, multiplique, e muitas vezes você vai errar por um fator de no máximo umas poucas vezes.

deep.x: Enrico Fermi (1901–1954) won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics and led the team that built the first nuclear reactor, in Chicago in 1942. He was famous for producing rough numbers fast, and he set his students questions that seemed impossible to answer without looking anything up.
The piano tuner method

x: 1 in 10 owns a piano: 100,000 pianos, each tuned once a year
a tuner manages 4 a day × 250 working days = 1,000 a year

deep.x: Nobody needs the true figure to see that the answer is "about a hundred", not ten or ten thousand. That is usually all a decision needs: is it worth opening a piano shop in this city?
Why it works

Each guess may be off, but you are rarely wildly wrong about everyday things such as how often people tune pianos. Splitting one hard question into several easy ones turns pure ignorance into a chain of assumptions you can inspect, argue about and improve one at a time.

At the first atomic bomb test in 1945, Fermi dropped scraps of paper as the blast wave passed and, from how far they drifted, estimated the yield at about 10 kilotons of TNT. The measured value was roughly twice that: within a factor of two, using a handful of paper.

deep.w: Fermi questions in job interviews have one right answer
deep.r: They test your reasoning; a well-argued 100 beats an unexplained 87

deep.x: Break a question you can't answer into several you can, then multiply.

cards.title: Postos de gasolina em Portugal
cards.text: Cerca de 10 milhões de pessoas, uns 5 milhões de carros, cada um abastecendo uma vez por semana: 5 milhões de abastecimentos por semana. Se um posto atende cerca de 3,000 por semana, são uns 1,700 postos; o número real é de alguns milhares.

deep.x: This estimate has only three moving parts: how many cars there are, how often they fill up, and how many fills one station can handle. The first two are easy to pin down; the third is a real guess.
Test the weakest guess
Is 3,000 fills a week realistic? Turn it into something you can picture.

That sounds like a busy motorway service area, not a village pump. Many stations in the interior, from Bragança to Alentejo, might see 100 cars a day. They exist because people need fuel within reach, not because they are full.

x: Same sum with 1,000 fills per station a week

deep.x: The real figure is roughly 3,000. Both versions land in the right order of magnitude, and the truth sits between them.
The answer is most sensitive to the guess you know least about. When refining an estimate, improve that one first instead of polishing the population figure.
A good estimate gets the order of magnitude right; fixing the shakiest assumption gets you closer.

cards.title: Ordens de grandeza
cards.text: Muitas vezes, a potência de 10 importa mais do que o valor exato. São centenas, milhares ou milhões? Acerte isso primeiro.

deep.x: An **order of magnitude** is a power of 10. Three thousand and seven thousand differ by more than double, but both are "thousands". Being out by a factor of 2 is a small miss; being out by a factor of 10 means you've misjudged the whole scale.
Scientific notation
Writing 3,000 as 3 × 10³ makes the order of magnitude obvious: it is the power. Scientists use it because the first digit is often uncertain, while the power of ten is the part they're sure of.

x: Lisbon to Porto ≈ 300 km, around the Earth ≈ 40,000 km
about two orders of magnitude apart

deep.x: Logarithmic scales

Several everyday scales count orders of magnitude directly. Each step on the pH scale is ×10 in acidity, and every 10 decibels is ×10 in sound intensity. A small-looking change on those scales is a big change in reality.
The 1977 short film *Powers of Ten* by Charles and Ray Eames zooms out by a factor of 10 every 10 seconds, from a picnic blanket to the edge of the known universe.

deep.w: Being out by a factor of 2 means the estimate failed
deep.r: For rough estimates, within ×2–3 is good; ×10 is the real miss

deep.x: Get the power of ten right before you worry about the first digit.

cards.title: Referências úteis
cards.text: Memorize alguns números de referência e você consegue estimar quase qualquer coisa.

deep.x: Estimation is not magic; it runs on a small stock of known numbers. With a dozen reference points, most questions become a short chain of multiplications rather than a wild guess.
People
Space and time

x: Around the Earth: 40,000 km (the metre was originally defined to make this so)
Mainland Portugal, north to south: about 560 km; Lisbon to Porto about 300 km
Walking pace about 5 km/h; a car on the motorway about 120 km/h
A day has 86,400 seconds; a year about 31.5 million

deep.x: Stuff
One litre of water weighs 1 kg, so a cubic metre weighs a tonne. Air is lighter but not nothing: about 1.2 kg per cubic metre.

x: How heavy is the air in a room 4 m × 5 m × 2.5 m?
50 × 1.2 ≈ 60 kg, about the mass of an adult

deep.x: A year is almost exactly π × 10 million seconds: 365 × 86,400 = 31,536,000, while π × 10⁷ ≈ 31,415,927. Physicists use this as a handy shortcut.
A dozen memorised numbers turn guessing into reasoning.

cards.title: Arredonde sem medo
cards.text: Arredonde para números fáceis de multiplicar. 47 × 213 ≈ 50 × 200 = 10,000. A resposta real é 10,011.

deep.x: The goal of rounding for an estimate is not accuracy at each step; it is arithmetic you can do in your head. Round each number to one significant figure, or to a friendly value like 25, 50 or 200, and multiply.
Round in opposite directions
That example was accurate because one number went up and the other went down by a similar share, so the errors cancelled. Round both the same way and the errors pile up.
Dividing
For division, round towards numbers that divide neatly, rather than to the nearest round number.

x: 23% ≈ a quarter, minus a bit: 80 + 20 = 100, minus a little

deep.w: Rounding to easy numbers is sloppy
deep.r: Engineers and accountants do it constantly to check results before trusting a calculator

deep.x: Round to numbers you can multiply in your head, and round in opposite directions when you can.

cards.title: Erros para mais e para menos se anulam
cards.text: Em estimativas de várias etapas, os erros de arredondamento em sentidos diferentes tendem a se anular, então a resposta final muitas vezes é melhor do que qualquer palpite isolado.

deep.x: A multi-step estimate multiplies several guesses, so their percentage errors multiply too. That sounds dangerous, but if the errors are independent, some guesses run high and others run low, and they partly cancel.

x: Petrol stations: cars guessed 20% too high, fills per week 15% too low

deep.x: Doing the odds
Suppose each of four guesses is either twice too big or half too small, at random. Being ×16 out needs all four to go the same way, which is unlikely.
In general, independent errors grow roughly with the square root of the number of steps, not in proportion to it. Nine steps are typically only about three times as wobbly as one.
When it doesn't work
Cancelling needs independence. A shared bias pushes every guess the same way: if you picture busy Lisbon every time you think about "Portugal", all your guesses will run high together.

In 1906 Francis Galton studied about 800 guesses of an ox's weight at a fair in Plymouth. The median guess, about 547 kg, was within 1% of the true 543 kg: individual errors cancelled across the crowd.
Independent errors tend to cancel; shared biases add up.

cards.title: Testes de bom senso
cards.text: Estimar ajuda a pegar erros. Se uma planilha diz que um café usa 40 toneladas de café por dia, uma estimativa rápida mostra que tem algo errado.

deep.x: A quick estimate is the cheapest error detector there is. It won't give you the answer, but it tells you the answer you've been given is impossible.

x: A busy café: 500 coffees a day × 7 g of ground coffee
40 tonnes is over 10,000 times too much

deep.x: Forty tonnes would make about 5.7 million espressos a day, more than one for every second person in Portugal. Almost certainly a unit or decimal slip: kilograms read as tonnes, or a misplaced point.
The usual suspects

items: One zero too many or too few

deep.x: Portugal writes 1.500 € for one thousand five hundred euros; in the UK, 1.500 means one and a half. Copy numbers between spreadsheets set up for different countries and that ×1,000 error appears silently.
A habit worth having

steps: Big gap? Hunt for the error

deep.x: If the precise result and your rough one disagree by more than a factor of 3 or so, don't trust either until you know why. Sometimes the estimate was wrong, which is also worth learning.

deep.w: Computers don't make mistakes
deep.r: They do exactly what they're told, including wrong units and misplaced decimals

deep.x: Always have a rough answer in mind before you trust a precise one.

cards.title: Estimar multidões
cards.text: Conte as pessoas numa área pequena e multiplique por quantas áreas como essa a multidão ocupa. A polícia e os organizadores muitas vezes discordam por um fator de dois.

deep.x: The standard method is named after Herbert Jacobs, a journalism lecturer at Berkeley who in the 1960s watched student protests from his office window. He noticed the plaza was marked out in a grid and counted people per square.
Typical densities

At about one person per square metre you can walk freely. At two, people stand close but don't touch. Above about five per square metre, crowds become dangerous, which is why event safety planners count carefully too.

x: Same square, loose crowd at 1 per m²
≈ 8,000 people: the density guess alone changes the answer ×2

deep.x: Why the numbers differ

For a march, people join and leave all day, so a single snapshot undercounts the total who took part. Today aerial photos, drones, phone-location data and image-counting software help, but density and turnover still involve judgement.
At World Youth Day in Lisbon in 2023, organisers reported about 1.5 million people at the final Mass in Parque Tejo. Figures that large are very hard to check independently.
Crowd size is area × density, and the density guess is where most disagreements hide.

cards.title: Quanto tempo dura um bilhão de segundos?
cards.text: Um milhão de segundos são cerca de 11,5 dias. Um bilhão de segundos são cerca de 32 anos. Números grandes são muito diferentes, mesmo que soem parecidos.

deep.x: "Million" and "billion" differ by one letter but by a factor of 1,000. Converting to time makes the gap obvious, because we have a feel for days and years that we don't have for big numbers.

x: back into the last Ice Age

deep.x: In money
Earning €1,000 every single day, you'd have a million euros in under three years. A billion would take about 2,740 years: you'd have needed to start before the Romans arrived in Iberia.
Mind the language

European Portuguese uses the "long scale", where *um bilião* is a million million. English and Brazilian Portuguese use the "short scale". A news story translated carelessly can be wrong by a factor of 1,000.
Your billionth second arrives when you are about 31 years and 8 months old. Some people celebrate it as a "gigabirthday".
Each step from thousand to million to billion is a jump of a thousand times, not a small step up.

cards.title: Intervalos de confiança
cards.text: Bons estimadores dão intervalos: "entre 2,000 e 4,000". Um intervalo do qual você tem 90% de certeza é mais honesto do que um único número com cara de preciso.

deep.x: A single number such as "3,000" hides how sure you are. A range with a confidence level, such as "90% sure it's between 2,000 and 4,000", tells the listener exactly how much to rely on it.
Most people's ranges are too narrow

Experiments since the 1970s ask people for 90% ranges on general-knowledge questions. If people were well **calibrated**, about 9 in 10 ranges would contain the truth. In practice it is often only around half: we are reliably overconfident.
Making a better range

x: Start wide, then narrow until you'd be genuinely surprised to be outside it
Think of reasons you might be wrong in each direction
Check your record: of your past "90%" ranges, how many caught the truth?

deep.x: The middle of a range
For multiplicative estimates, the best single guess is the geometric middle, not the halfway point.

x: 1,000 is ×10 from each end, a fairer central guess

deep.x: Weather forecasts are tested for calibration: on all the days a forecaster says "70% chance of rain", it should rain on about 70% of them.

deep.w: A precise number sounds more expert
deep.r: False precision hides uncertainty; a range shows how far to trust you

deep.x: Say how sure you are: a range with a confidence level is an honest estimate.

quiz.q: Quanto tempo dura um bilhão de segundos?
quiz.explain: Um milhão de segundos são cerca de 11,5 dias.

quiz.q: O que é um problema de Fermi?
options: Um problema de matemática sem solução
Uma estimativa aproximada feita a partir de palpites simples

cards.title: Progressões aritméticas
cards.text: Some o mesmo número a cada vez: 3, 7, 11, 15… (some 4). O termo de ordem n é fácil de achar: 4n − 1.

deep.x: An arithmetic sequence has a **common difference**: the same amount is added each time. Plot it and the points lie on a straight line, because steady adding is steady growth.
Jumping straight to any term
nth term = first term + (n − 1) × difference
The number in front of n is always the difference. That's a quick way to read the rule off: a difference of 4 means "4n, then adjust".
Adding them up

The story goes that the young Carl Friedrich Gauss was told to add 1 to 100 and answered at once by pairing the ends. Whether or not it happened exactly so, the trick works for any arithmetic sequence.
In everyday life
Saving €50 a month, a taxi fare with a fixed start charge plus a price per kilometre, seat numbers along rows in a theatre: all arithmetic.
Leap years form an arithmetic sequence with difference 4 (2024, 2028, 2032…), with one twist: century years not divisible by 400 are skipped, so 2100 won't be a leap year.
A constant difference means straight-line growth, with an nth term of the form dn + c.

cards.title: Progressões geométricas
cards.text: Multiplique pelo mesmo número a cada vez: 2, 6, 18, 54… (×3). Elas crescem muito mais rápido do que as progressões aritméticas.

deep.x: A geometric sequence has a **common ratio**: each term is the last one multiplied by the same number. For 2, 6, 18, 54… the ratio is 3.
nth term = first term × ratio^(n − 1)
Folding paper
Paper is about 0.1 mm thick. Each fold doubles the thickness.

x: ≈ 440,000 km, further than the Moon (about 384,000 km)

deep.x: In practice you can't fold paper more than about seven or eight times by hand, but the arithmetic shows why doubling outruns intuition.
Ratios above and below 1
Money at 3% a year is a geometric sequence with ratio 1.03. The "rule of 72" says it doubles in about 72 ÷ 3 = 24 years; the exact answer is about 23.4.

deep.w: Exponential just means very fast
deep.r: It means a constant growth factor; early on it can look slow, then suddenly isn't

deep.x: Constant ratio means each step multiplies, so geometric growth eventually beats any amount of adding.

cards.title: Números triangulares
cards.text: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15: o número de pontos em triângulos cada vez maiores, como os pinos de boliche. O de ordem n é n(n + 1)/2.

deep.x: Triangular numbers count dots arranged in a triangle: one row of 1, then 2, then 3, and so on. Ten-pin bowling uses the 4th (10 pins); the 15 red balls in snooker form the 5th.
Why n(n + 1)/2?
Two copies of the same triangle fit together into a rectangle n dots tall and n + 1 wide. The triangle is exactly half of it.
Hidden connections

x: Two neighbouring triangular numbers make a square: 10 + 15 = 25, 15 + 21 = 36
The handshakes among n + 1 people form the nth triangular number
Multiply any triangular number by 8 and add 1: always a square (8 × 6 + 1 = 49)

deep.x: On 10 July 1796, the 18-year-old Gauss wrote in his diary "Eureka! num = Δ + Δ + Δ": every whole number is the sum of at most three triangular numbers.
Two triangles make a rectangle, which is why the formula halves n(n + 1).

cards.title: Fibonacci na natureza
cards.text: Muitos girassóis têm 34 e 55 espirais; as pinhas mostram 8 e 13. Esses números de Fibonacci permitem arrumar as sementes de forma eficiente.

deep.x: The sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… is named after Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, who used it in his 1202 book *Liber Abaci* for a puzzle about breeding rabbits. Indian scholars had met the same numbers centuries earlier, counting rhythms in poetry.

x: Each term is the sum of the two before

deep.x: How plants make the spirals
A growing flower head adds new seeds at its centre, one at a time. Each one appears at a fixed turn from the last, about **137.5°**, called the golden angle. Older seeds get pushed outwards.

That angle leaves no gaps and no straight lines of seeds, so the head packs in as many as possible. The spirals our eyes pick out, running clockwise and anticlockwise, come out in neighbouring Fibonacci numbers as a side-effect.
Not a law of nature

Alan Turing was studying these patterns before his death in 1954. A 2016 citizen-science project in his honour counted spirals on several hundred sunflowers and found roughly one in five didn't fit the Fibonacci pattern neatly.

deep.w: Every plant follows Fibonacci
deep.r: Many do, plenty don't; it's a strong tendency from how growth works, not a rule

deep.x: The golden angle is 360° divided by φ², about 137.5°, which links these spirals to the golden ratio.
Turning by the golden angle packs seeds evenly, and Fibonacci spirals are the visible side-effect.

cards.title: A razão áurea
cards.text: Divida cada número de Fibonacci pelo anterior e você se aproxima de 1,618…, a razão áurea φ.

deep.x: Divide each Fibonacci number by the one before it and the answers swing above and below a single value, getting closer each time.
Strange properties
A golden rectangle has sides in the ratio φ : 1. Cut a square off it and the leftover rectangle is golden again, forever. Like π, φ is irrational: its decimals never repeat.
Myths and real uses

The architect Le Corbusier deliberately built his 1940s "Modulor" system of proportions on φ. Most claims about older works are weaker: with enough measurements to choose from, you can find 1.6 almost anywhere.

deep.w: The Parthenon and the Mona Lisa were designed on the golden ratio
deep.r: The evidence is weak; such claims usually rely on picking convenient measurements

deep.x: Neighbouring Fibonacci numbers convert miles to kilometres, because 1.609 is close to 1.618: 5 miles ≈ 8 km, 8 miles ≈ 13 km (really 12.9).
Fibonacci ratios zigzag towards φ ≈ 1.618, a number with genuinely unusual properties, but fewer mystical ones than claimed.

cards.title: O triângulo de Pascal
cards.text: Cada número é a soma dos dois que estão acima dele. O triângulo esconde os números naturais, os números triangulares, as potências de 2 e as probabilidades de lançamentos de moeda.

deep.x: Start with 1 at the top. Each number below is the sum of the two above it, with 1s down the edges.
What it's counting

Each entry is the number of ways to choose some items from a set. In row 4, the 6 means there are 6 ways to choose 2 things from 4. That's why it predicts coin tosses: choosing which 2 of 4 tosses come up heads.
Patterns inside

x: Diagonals: 1s, then counting numbers, then triangular numbers (1, 3, 6, 10…)
Colour the odd numbers and a fractal appears: the Sierpiński triangle

deep.x: Not really Pascal's
Blaise Pascal wrote the classic study in 1654, while working out problems of chance with Pierre de Fermat. In China it is still called Yang Hui's triangle.
Each entry counts ways of choosing, which is why one adding rule hides so much.

cards.title: Os primos resistem aos padrões
cards.text: Os primos vão ficando mais raros, mas nunca acabam, e nenhuma fórmula simples gera todos eles. Prevê-los é um dos problemas em aberto mais profundos da matemática.

deep.x: A prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Around 300 BC, Euclid proved there is no largest prime. Multiply all the primes you know and add 1: the result is not divisible by any of them, so a new prime must divide it.

x: but 59 and 509 are new primes, as Euclid predicted

deep.x: Thinning out
The **prime number theorem**, proved in 1896, says that near a number N roughly 1 in every ln N numbers is prime, where ln is the natural logarithm.
So on average primes are predictable. One by one, they are not.
Formulas that fail
Euler noticed that n² + n + 41 gives primes for every n from 0 to 39. At n = 40 it gives 1,681 = 41 × 41.
Open questions

The Riemann hypothesis carries a US$1 million prize from the Clay Mathematics Institute. Prime puzzles matter in practice too: much internet encryption relies on how hard it is to split huge numbers into their prime factors.
The largest known prime, found in 2024, is 2^136,279,841 − 1. Written out it has over 41 million digits.
Primes thin out predictably on average but refuse any simple formula one by one.

cards.title: Sequências traiçoeiras
cards.text: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16… parece óbvio, mas corte um círculo com retas ligando pontos e você obtém 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 e depois 31. Padrões precisam de prova.

deep.x: Put points on a circle, join every pair with straight lines, and count the regions inside. With 1 to 5 points you get 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and it looks like doubling. The sixth point gives 31.
The true rule (known as Moser's circle problem) involves counting groups of 4 points and pairs of points. It continues 57, 99… nothing like 32, 64.
Many rules fit the same start

"1, 2, 4, 7, 11" is the most pieces you can cut a pancake into with 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 straight cuts. Any finite list of numbers can be continued by infinitely many rules, so a puzzle asking "what comes next?" is really asking for the simplest rule.
Famous failures
Pierre de Fermat guessed that 2^(2ⁿ) + 1 is always prime. It is for 3, 5, 17, 257 and 65,537. In 1732 Euler found the next one breaks.

items.w: It worked 5 times, so it's true
items.r: Only a proof covers every case

deep.x: No further prime of Fermat's form has ever been found, though they've been checked far beyond what Fermat could have imagined.
A pattern in examples is a hypothesis; only a proof makes it a fact.

cards.title: Olhe e diga
cards.text: 1, 11, 21, 1211, 111221… Cada termo descreve o anterior em voz alta: "um 1", "dois 1", "um 2, um 1". Um padrão baseado em palavras, não em aritmética.

deep.x: Each term describes the one before it, read aloud. The rule is about how numbers are written, not about their size.
Growing by a fixed rate

The terms get longer: 1, 2, 2, 4, 6, 6, 8, 10, 14, 20 digits for the first ten. In 1986 the mathematician John Conway proved that, in the long run, each term is about 30% longer than the last. The exact factor, **Conway's constant**, is about 1.3036.
Elements of the sequence
Conway showed that long terms split into 92 basic chunks that never interact again. He named them after the chemical elements, from hydrogen to uranium, and called the process "audioactive decay".

x: Starting from 1, only the digits 1, 2 and 3 ever appear
Start from 22 and you're stuck: "two 2s" is 22 again

deep.w: A real sequence needs a formula
deep.r: Some come from rules about writing and speaking numbers, and are still studied seriously

deep.x: Conway's constant is the root of a polynomial of degree 71, an unexpectedly deep answer to a word game.
A word game hides a precise growth rate of about 30% per step.

cards.title: Descubra a regra
cards.text: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26… As diferenças são 3, 5, 7, 9: números ímpares. A regra é n² + 1.

deep.x: When a sequence isn't obviously adding or multiplying, look at the **differences**: the gaps between neighbouring terms. If the gaps aren't constant, look at the gaps between the gaps.

steps: Gaps of gaps equal? n² rule
Fit the rule, then test it

x: constant second gaps → a rule with n²

deep.x: Fitting the formula
When the second gaps are constant, the number in front of n² is half that gap: here 2 ÷ 2 = 1. Compare n² with the sequence to find the rest.
Which kind of rule?
If the gaps look like the sequence itself (3, 6, 12, 24 has gaps 3, 6, 12), try dividing instead: it's geometric.
Charles Babbage's Difference Engine, designed in the 1820s, used exactly this method of differences to calculate tables of numbers using only addition, cranked by hand.
When you're stuck
The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences, started by Neil Sloane in 1964 and online since 1996, holds over 370,000 sequences. Type in a few terms and it suggests rules.
Look at the gaps, then the gaps of the gaps; whichever becomes constant tells you the type of rule.

quiz.q: O que vem depois: 2, 6, 18, 54, …?
Qual é o 4º número triangular?

lessons.title: Medidas e unidades
lessons.summary: Metros, quilos e por que eles importam.

cards.title: O sistema métrico
cards.text: Nascido na França revolucionária, na década de 1790, o sistema métrico usa potências de 10, então converter é só mover a vírgula decimal. Portugal o adotou em 1852.

deep.x: Before the metric system, units changed from town to town. In Portugal a *vara* was about 1.1 m, and an *alqueire* of grain differed between regions, which made trade and taxes a constant source of argument. Revolutionary France wanted units "for all people, for all time", based on nature rather than on a king's foot.
The original metre

In 1791 the metre was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured through Paris. Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, spent 1792–1798 surveying from Dunkirk to Barcelona to pin it down.
Powers of ten
Every unit grows or shrinks by the same prefixes, so converting means moving the decimal point.

Portugal's 1852 decree took decades to be fully obeyed, and old names linger: some rural markets still talk about alqueires. Portugal was also one of the 17 countries that signed the Metre Convention in 1875, which set up the international office that still looks after the units.
The 40,000 km circumference of the Earth isn't a coincidence: it follows directly from the original definition of the metre.
The metric system's power is that every conversion is just a shift of the decimal point.

cards.title: Sete unidades de base
cards.text: Todas as medidas são construídas a partir de sete unidades de base do SI. Desde 2019, todas são definidas por constantes fixas da natureza, e não por objetos físicos.

deep.x: Every quantity in science and engineering can be built from seven base units of the International System, the **SI**. Speed is metres per second; force, the newton, is kilograms × metres per second squared.
Defined by nature's constants
Since 20 May 2019, each base unit is fixed by giving an exact value to a constant of nature. Any well-equipped lab, anywhere, can reproduce them.

x: a caesium-133 atom's radiation oscillates 9,192,631,770 times
light travels exactly 299,792,458 m per second
1 metre = distance light covers in 1/299,792,458 s

deep.x: Derived units
The joule (energy), watt (power), volt and pascal are all combinations of base units. That's why a physics equation must balance in units as well as numbers: it is a free check on your working.
Portugal's national measurement laboratory, part of the Instituto Português da Qualidade in Caparica, keeps the reference standards that calibrate scales and fuel pumps across the country.
Seven units, each tied to a constant of nature, are enough to measure everything.

cards.title: Adeus, Le Grand K
cards.text: Durante 130 anos, o quilograma foi um cilindro de metal guardado num cofre perto de Paris. Em 2019, ele foi redefinido usando a constante de Planck.

deep.x: The International Prototype of the Kilogram was a cylinder of 90% platinum and 10% iridium, about 39 mm tall and 39 mm wide. Made in 1879 and officially adopted in 1889, it sat under three glass bell jars in a vault at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, just outside Paris.
The problem with a lump of metal

By definition, Le Grand K weighed exactly 1 kg forever. But when it was compared with its official copies over a century, they had drifted apart by about 50 micrograms: roughly the mass of a small grain of sand. Nobody could say which had changed, because the original couldn't be wrong by definition.
Weighing with electricity

A **Kibble balance** balances a mass against an electromagnetic force, which can be measured extremely precisely in terms of the Planck constant. Fix the constant's value exactly and you've defined the kilogram.

x: Planck constant h is fixed at exactly
the kilogram follows from h, the metre and the second

deep.x: Your kitchen scales didn't change on 20 May 2019. The new definition was chosen to match the old kilogram as closely as could be measured.

deep.w: The kilogram was redefined because Le Grand K got lighter
deep.r: Nobody knows whether it lost mass or its copies gained; the point was to stop relying on any object

deep.x: The last unit defined by a physical object was replaced by a constant of nature.

cards.title: Unidades de área e volume
cards.text: 1 m² são 10,000 cm², e não 100. 1 m³ são 1,000 litros. As unidades são elevadas ao quadrado e ao cubo junto com os comprimentos.

deep.x: Units of area are squares of length units, and volume units are cubes. A factor of 100 between metres and centimetres becomes 10,000 for area and a million for volume.
Handy links

x: Tiling a 4 m × 3 m floor with 30 cm tiles

deep.x: Scaling up

Double every length of a box and its surface area goes up 4 times, its volume 8 times. Galileo pointed out in 1638 that this is why a giant can't simply be a scaled-up human: weight grows with volume, but bone strength only with cross-sectional area.

deep.w: A metre is 100 cm, so a square metre is 100 square centimetres
deep.r: It's 100 × 100 = 10,000 cm²; the factor squares too

deep.x: Units square and cube along with the lengths, so conversion factors do too.

cards.title: Hectares
cards.text: Um hectare é 100 m × 100 m = 10,000 m², cerca de um campo de futebol e meio. Fazendas e florestas são medidas em hectares.

deep.x: The **are** is 10 m × 10 m = 100 m². A hectare is a hundred ares (*hecto* means 100), which works out to a square 100 m on each side. Ares are rare nowadays, but hectares are the standard unit for land across Europe.
Picturing a hectare
A professional football pitch is about 105 m × 68 m.
Portugal in hectares

Wildfire reports, farm subsidies and cork oak *montado* in Alentejo are all measured in hectares. In the terrible fire year of 2017, over half a million hectares burned in Portugal, roughly 5% of the country.
The old Portuguese *alqueire* was also used for land, meaning the area you could sow with an alqueire of seed, so its size varied by region and soil.
A hectare is a 100 m square, roughly one and a half football pitches.

cards.title: Unidades imperiais
cards.text: O Reino Unido e os EUA ainda usam milhas, libras e Fahrenheit. Conversões rápidas: 1 milha ≈ 1,6 km, 1 kg ≈ 2,2 lb, 1 polegada = 2,54 cm.

deep.x: Imperial units grew from body parts and everyday objects: the foot, the inch (a thumb's width), the mile from the Roman *mille passus*, a thousand double paces. Since 1959 they've been officially defined in terms of metric ones.

x: exact answer 68 °F: good enough for weather

deep.x: Who uses what
Same name, different size

A UK gallon is about 4.55 litres; a US gallon about 3.79 litres. A US "fuel economy" figure in miles per gallon can't be compared directly with a British one, and neither with European litres per 100 km.
The UK still weighs people in **stones**: 1 stone = 14 pounds ≈ 6.35 kg.

deep.w: The US doesn't use the metric system at all
deep.r: Its customary units are legally defined in metric, and science, medicine and the military use metric daily

deep.x: Learn three anchors, 2.54 cm, 1.6 km and 2.2 lb, and most conversions follow.

cards.title: A Mars Climate Orbiter
cards.text: Em 1999, uma sonda da NASA foi perdida em Marte porque uma equipe usou libras-força e outra, newtons. O erro de $125 milhões foi uma confusão de unidades.

deep.x: NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter launched in December 1998 to study the Martian atmosphere. On 23 September 1999, as it fired its engine to go into orbit, it passed behind Mars and was never heard from again.
What went wrong

Software from the spacecraft's builder, Lockheed Martin, reported small thruster firings in pound-force seconds. NASA's navigation team at JPL read the numbers as newton-seconds. Every correction was therefore underestimated by a factor of about 4.45.

x: each impulse was 4.45 × bigger than the navigators thought

deep.x: The errors added up over nine months. The orbiter arrived about 57 km above the surface, far lower than planned and below the roughly 80 km it could survive.
Not just NASA

In 1983 an Air Canada Boeing 767, later nicknamed the **Gimli Glider**, ran out of fuel mid-flight. The fuel had been worked out with a pounds conversion factor instead of kilograms, so it carried less than half what was needed. The crew glided to a disused airbase at Gimli, Manitoba; nobody died.

deep.w: The mistake was bad arithmetic
deep.r: The sums were fine; two teams silently assumed different units, and no check caught it

deep.x: A number without its unit is a disaster waiting for an interface.

cards.title: Algarismos significativos
cards.text: A precisão deve acompanhar a medição. Um cômodo medido como 4,2 m não tem uma área de exatamente 17,64 m²; diga cerca de 17,6 m².

deep.x: **Significant figures** are the digits that carry real information. "4.2 m" has two: it claims you measured to the nearest 10 cm, so the true length is somewhere between 4.15 m and 4.25 m.

x: but the true area could be anywhere from 17.2 to 18.1
so "about 17.6 m²" is the honest figure, and the last digit is shaky

deep.x: The rule of thumb
When multiplying or dividing, keep as many significant figures as the least precise number you started with. When adding, line up the decimal places with the least precise.
False precision
Extra digits look scientific but mislead. A forecast of "23.47% chance" or a population of "10,639,726" in a casual chat suggests certainty nobody has.
Normal body temperature was set at 37 °C in the 1800s, a rounded average. Converted to Fahrenheit it became 98.6 °F, which looks far more precise than the original measurement ever was.
A result can't be more precise than the measurements that went into it.

cards.title: Unidades de velocidade
cards.text: Divida km/h por 3,6 para obter metros por segundo. 120 km/h são cerca de 33 m/s: um carro percorre um campo de futebol a cada três segundos.

deep.x: There are 1,000 metres in a kilometre and 3,600 seconds in an hour, so 1 km/h = 1,000 ÷ 3,600 m/s. That's where the 3.6 comes from.

x: a 105 m football pitch in about 3.2 s

deep.x: Why m/s matters on the road
Before you even touch the brake, you travel at full speed for your reaction time.
Usain Bolt's 100 m world record of 9.58 s (2009) averages 10.4 m/s, about 37.6 km/h. Driving in town is faster than the fastest human ever ran.
Other speed units
A knot is one nautical mile per hour, and a nautical mile was originally one minute of arc of latitude: 1/60 of a degree along the Earth's surface.
Divide by 3.6 to go from km/h to m/s, and you can feel how far a car really travels each second.

cards.title: Unidades de energia
cards.text: Um quilowatt-hora mantém um aquecedor de 1,000 W ligado por uma hora. Uma Caloria dos alimentos são 1,000 calorias, cerca de 4,2 kJ. Um banho quente gasta cerca de 2–3 kWh.

deep.x: Energy is the capacity to do work; power is how fast you use it. A 1,000 W (1 kW) heater running for one hour uses one kilowatt-hour of energy, the unit on your electricity bill.
A shower and a day's food
Heating water takes about 4.2 kJ per litre per degree.

x: 10-minute shower at 8 L a minute = 80 L
≈ 2.3 kWh: about the same as one hot shower

deep.x: Calories and labels
Food labels in the EU must show energy in both kJ and kcal. The "Calorie" on a label is really a kilocalorie, 1,000 small calories, which is why packaging writes "kcal".

deep.w: kW and kWh are the same thing
deep.r: kW is a rate (power); kWh is an amount (energy), like km/h versus km

deep.x: Your body runs at roughly 100 W on average, about the same as an old incandescent light bulb: 2.3 kWh spread over 24 hours.
Power is the rate, energy is the amount: watts × hours gives the kilowatt-hours you pay for.

cards.title: A Torre de Hanói
cards.text: Mova uma pilha de discos para outro pino, um de cada vez, sem nunca colocar um disco maior sobre um menor. Com n discos, são necessários 2ⁿ − 1 movimentos.

deep.x: The French mathematician Édouard Lucas published the puzzle in 1883, with a legend about monks moving 64 golden discs. When they finish, the story goes, the world will end.
The recursive trick
To move n discs, you first have to move the n − 1 discs on top of the biggest one out of the way.

steps: Move top n − 1 to spare peg

deep.x: Each step of moving n − 1 discs is itself the same puzzle, one size smaller. So the number of moves more than doubles with each extra disc.
moves(n) = 2 × moves(n − 1) + 1, which gives 2ⁿ − 1
The monks' timetable

x: at one move per second ≈ 585 billion years

deep.x: That is over 40 times the age of the universe (about 13.8 billion years). The world is safe.
Computer backup software has used a "Tower of Hanoi" rotation to decide which backup tape to overwrite each day, keeping copies at doubling ages.
Solve a big problem by assuming you can solve a slightly smaller one: that's recursion.

cards.title: O quadrado que falta

items.r: As bordas são levemente tortas: as figuras não são iguais

cards.text: Rearrumar quatro peças de um triângulo parece criar um buraco. O truque: as "hipotenusas" não são retas, então as figuras são ligeiramente diferentes.

deep.x: The best-known version, often called Curry's paradox after the magician Paul Curry, uses a "triangle" 13 squares wide and 5 high, cut into two small triangles and two L-shapes. Rearranged, the same pieces leave a one-square hole.
Check the slopes

The two small triangles have different slopes, so when placed end to end their long sides don't form one straight line. In one arrangement the edge bends slightly inwards; in the other, slightly outwards.
Count the areas
The extra half-square on each side is spread along a very thin sliver, too thin for the eye to notice.
Fibonacci again
The side lengths 2, 3, 5, 8 and 13 are Fibonacci numbers. Their ratios are all close to the golden ratio, which is why the bend is so slight.
When a picture seems to break the rules, check whether the lines are really straight.

cards.title: O problema dos apertos de mão
cards.text: Se 10 pessoas se cumprimentam uma vez cada, quantos apertos de mão acontecem? Cada uma aperta 9 mãos, mas cada aperto envolve duas pessoas: 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45.

deep.x: There are two ways to count, and both give the same answer. Count each person's handshakes and divide by two, or count the pairs of people directly.
handshakes among n people = n × (n − 1) ÷ 2
The answers 3, 6, 10, 15… are the triangular numbers: the 10th person shakes 9 new hands, the 9th shakes 8 new ones, and so on, so the total is 9 + 8 + … + 1.
The same sum everywhere

x: 18 × 17 ÷ 2 = 153 pairings, each played home and away

deep.x: Why it matters

The number of pairs grows roughly with the square of the group size. That's why the birthday problem surprises people: 23 people sounds few, but 253 pairs gives about a 50.7% chance that two share a birthday. It's also why telephone networks use exchanges and hubs instead of wiring every phone to every other.
In a team of 5, there are 10 pairs of people who need to communicate; in a team of 50, there are 1,225. Coordination costs grow much faster than headcount.
Count from each person, then divide by two, because every handshake has two ends.

cards.title: O princípio da casa dos pombos

steps: Pelo menos uma caixa tem dois

cards.text: Se você colocar 13 meias em 12 gavetas, pelo menos uma gaveta fica com duas. Simples, mas poderoso: em Lisboa, pelo menos duas pessoas têm exatamente o mesmo número de fios de cabelo na cabeça.

deep.x: If there are more items than boxes, some box must hold at least two. It sounds too obvious to be useful, yet it proves things you could never check directly. The German mathematician Dirichlet used it in 1834; in Portuguese it is often called the *princípio das gavetas*, the drawer principle.
n items in k boxes → some box holds at least n ÷ k, rounded up
The hair proof
Nobody has more than a couple of hundred thousand hairs on their head; a typical count is around 100,000–150,000.

x: Allow 0 to 200,000 hairs: 200,001 possible counts (the boxes)
545,000 ÷ 200,001 ≈ 2.7, so at least 3 people share the exact same count

deep.x: You can't name them, but they must exist.
More examples

The last one matters in computing. There are more files of 1,000 bits than files of all shorter lengths put together, so no compressor can make every file smaller: some must stay the same size or grow.

deep.w: You need to find the pair to prove it exists
deep.r: Pigeonhole proves existence without pointing at any example

deep.x: More items than boxes guarantees a shared box, even when you can't say which.

cards.title: O enigma do 0,999…
cards.text: 0,999…, com o 9 se repetindo para sempre, é exatamente igual a 1. Uma prova: 1/3 = 0,333…, então 3 × 1/3 = 0,999… = 1.

deep.x: The dots mean the 9s never stop. It isn't a number creeping towards 1; it is a fixed number, and that number is exactly 1. Three different arguments agree.
Nothing in between

Two different numbers always have another number between them, such as their average. Try to find one between 0.999… and 1: any decimal smaller than 1 differs from 1 at some digit, so it's smaller than 0.999… too. No gap means they are the same number.
Two ways to write one number
Every decimal that stops has a twin that ends in endless 9s: 2.5 = 2.4999…, and 0.37 = 0.36999…. Different symbols, one value, like ½ and 2/4.
Surveys of students regularly find many reject 0.999… = 1 at first. The discomfort comes from treating "infinitely many 9s" as a process rather than a finished number.
0.999… and 1 are two names for the same number.

cards.title: O hotel de Hilbert
cards.text: Um hotel com infinitos quartos está lotado. Chega um novo hóspede: passe todo mundo do quarto n para o quarto n + 1, e o quarto 1 fica livre. O infinito se comporta de um jeito estranho.

deep.x: The German mathematician David Hilbert described the hotel in a 1924 lecture; the physicist George Gamow made it famous in his 1947 book *One Two Three… Infinity*. It shows that infinite sets break rules that are obvious for finite ones.
One new guest
Everyone moves from room n to room n + 1. Nobody is left without a room, because there is no last room to fall off the end. Room 1 is now free.
An infinite coach
An endless coach of new guests arrives. Move everyone from room n to room 2n.
Even infinitely many coaches can be housed, with a cleverer numbering scheme.
Some infinities are bigger

In the 1870s and 1890s Georg Cantor proved that the real numbers, all the decimals, can't be listed one by one at all. A hotel with rooms numbered 1, 2, 3… could never fit a guest for every decimal between 0 and 1. That infinity is strictly bigger.

deep.w: Infinity plus one is bigger than infinity
deep.r: For the counting infinity, adding one, or even doubling, gives the same size

deep.x: With infinitely many rooms, "full" doesn't mean "no space".

cards.title: Os que dizem a verdade e os mentirosos
cards.text: Numa ilha, os cavaleiros sempre dizem a verdade e os patifes sempre mentem. Pergunte a qualquer um "o que o outro diria?" e você pode inverter a resposta para descobrir a verdade.

deep.x: These puzzles were made famous by the American logician Raymond Smullyan, especially in his 1978 book *What Is the Name of This Book?*. They train the same reasoning computers use: follow each possibility and throw out the ones that contradict themselves.
Two doors, two guards
One door leads out, one doesn't. One guard always tells the truth, the other always lies, and you don't know which is which. Ask either guard: "Which door would the other guard say is the way out?"
Both routes pass through exactly one lie, so the answer is always wrong, and reliably so.
Solving by cases
On the island, A says: "We are both knaves."

x: then the sentence is true, so A is a knave
contradiction, so A is a knave
A is a knave, so the sentence is false
"both knaves" is false, but A is one
so B must be a knight

deep.x: A version of the two-door puzzle appears in Jim Henson's 1986 film *Labyrinth*. In 1996 the philosopher George Boolos published "the hardest logic puzzle ever", with three gods: one truthful, one lying and one answering at random.
A question routed through a liar flips the answer predictably, and a predictable lie is as useful as the truth.

cards.title: Sudoku é lógica
cards.text: O sudoku não exige aritmética, só lógica: cada linha, coluna e quadrado tem os números de 1 a 9 uma única vez. Um bom sudoku tem exatamente uma solução.

deep.x: The digits 1 to 9 are just nine different symbols. Sudoku could use letters, colours or animals and nothing would change: no adding, only deduction about where each symbol can go.
Two basic moves

items.b: a cell with only one option
a digit with only one home

deep.x: Harder puzzles need longer chains: "if this cell were 4, that row would have no 7, so it isn't 4."
Numbers about Sudoku

In 2005 Bertram Felgenhauer and Frazer Jarvis counted the possible completed grids: about 6.67 × 10²¹. In 2012 an exhaustive computer search by Gary McGuire's team showed no proper Sudoku can have fewer than 17 clues.

x: 64 cells to deduce, with exactly one solution

deep.x: A short history

The modern puzzle was designed by Howard Garns in the USA; the Japanese publisher Nikoli gave it its name. A Sudoku solution is a special **Latin square**, a grid where each symbol appears once per row and column, studied by Euler in the 1780s.

deep.w: You need to be good at maths to do Sudoku
deep.r: It uses no arithmetic at all, only careful logical elimination

deep.x: Sudoku is pure deduction: the digits are just labels.

cards.title: As Sete Pontes hoje
cards.text: A ideia de Euler é usada na coleta de lixo e nas rotas dos carteiros: planejar trajetos que passem por todas as ruas uma vez, voltando pelo mesmo caminho o mínimo possível.

deep.x: In 1736 Leonhard Euler showed you couldn't walk around Königsberg crossing each of its seven bridges exactly once. His trick was to ignore everything except what connects to what: land became dots (nodes), bridges became lines (edges). That founded **graph theory**.
Euler's rule
Every time you pass through a place you use two bridges, one in and one out. So only the start and end can have an odd number of bridges.
A route using every edge once exists only if 0 or 2 nodes have an odd number of edges

x: Königsberg's four land masses had 5, 3, 3 and 3 bridges
more than 2, so no such walk

deep.x: Streets as a graph

A bin lorry, a snow plough or a street sweeper must cover every street, not just visit every junction. Real street maps usually have many odd junctions, so some streets must be driven twice. The trick is to choose the shortest set of repeats.
This is the **Chinese postman problem**, posed by the mathematician Meigu Guan in 1962 while thinking about postal routes.
Königsberg is now Kaliningrad, in Russia. Wartime bombing and rebuilding changed the bridges; with today's layout, a walk crossing each once is possible, though you can't finish where you started.
Turn the map into dots and lines, count the odd junctions, and you know how much doubling back is unavoidable.

cards.title: O lobo, a cabra e o repolho: solução
cards.text: O pulo do gato foi levar algo de volta. Muitos enigmas exigem um passo que parece um retrocesso, uma lição que vale também para resolver problemas reais.

deep.x: The puzzle appears in a collection attributed to Alcuin of York, around 800 AD, called *Problems to Sharpen the Young*. A farmer's boat carries him and one item. Left alone, the wolf eats the goat and the goat eats the cabbage.
The solution: seven crossings
The surprising move is bringing the goat back. It seems to undo progress, but it's the only way to avoid leaving a dangerous pair together.

x: goat over, return empty, wolf over, goat back
cabbage over, return empty, goat over: 7

deep.x: Swapping the roles of wolf and cabbage gives the only other seven-crossing solution.
Thinking in states

Each situation is a state: which bank the farmer, wolf, goat and cabbage are on. There are 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 states, of which 10 are safe. Solving the puzzle means finding a path through the safe states, exactly how computers solve route and planning problems.
Going backwards to go forwards
Many problems punish always moving towards the goal. A Rubik's cube solver breaks finished layers to place pieces; a chess player sacrifices a piece; a detour round traffic arrives sooner.

deep.w: Every good step should get you closer to the goal
deep.r: Sometimes the only path goes through a step that looks backwards

deep.x: Being willing to undo progress is often what finally unlocks a problem.
